lessons.title: Containerize the complete application
lessons.content:
# Containerize the complete application ## Learning progression and project preparation ## Before this session Bring your notes and observed output from **Observability, cost, and latency budgets**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary. ### Specific preparation - Observability, cost, and latency budgets (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:18`) If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required. ## Readiness check from the previous session Explain **Run trace** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: Structured observations such as stage duration, source revision, tool outcome and retry count. Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract. ## Carry work forward Build toward **a container, recovery transcript and orchestration decision**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees. ## Next checkpoint Next: **Failure recovery and release checklists**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline. ## Understand the decision: Containerize the complete application ## Before you begin Complete sessions 1–18 in this bootcamp. Keep your policy fixtures and evaluation labels in your own workspace. The example below runs independently so a prior missing file cannot block understanding. ## Why this decision matters A working local Python process is only one part of the release. A complete deployment needs a frontend, API, database, configuration, networking, static assets, startup ordering, and health checks. Container images package code and dependencies; named volumes preserve database data beyond a container’s lifetime. Keep credentials in runtime configuration. A database port does not need to be public when only the API uses it. Understand the difference between container-local hostnames and browser-visible URLs: the browser cannot resolve a Compose service name. Use a frontend proxy so requests remain on the same origin. Test the built frontend rather than only a development server. ## Vocabulary used in this session ### Container network A private network where service names resolve for containers, not necessarily for a browser. ### Persistent volume Storage that survives removal or replacement of a container. ### Readiness probe A check of the dependency needed for the service to fulfill its readiness claim. ## Learn each concept step by step Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions. ## Step 1 · Container network A container network provides service names to containers, not to the browser. The page requests relative /api URLs; Nginx resolves backend internally, and the backend resolves db. Publishing PostgreSQL is unnecessary for this path. Trace browser → proxy → API → database before debugging individual endpoints so localhost is not mistaken for the same host everywhere. ## Step 2 · Persistent volume A persistent volume stores database files outside a replaceable container. Recreating the backend should preserve the saved draft because its data lives in PostgreSQL. A named volume is not a tested backup; deleting it removes the synthetic records. The supplied lab binds only loopback and uses synthetic runtime configuration; it is not an authenticated production deployment. ## Step 3 · Readiness probe A readiness probe checks a required dependency through an actual query. A running process can still return 503 when PostgreSQL is stopped. Wait for readiness before writing, record the returned draft ID and read it after replacement. Building an image or creating source files alone does not demonstrate end-to-end persistence. ## Worked implementation: Containerize the complete application ## Walk through the data and decision 1. The supplied seven files place browser traffic through Nginx and keep the database internal. 2. The backend reads runtime configuration and PostgreSQL stores rows in its named volume. 3. The procedure saves a draft, replaces backend, then checks readback and database-outage readiness. ## Follow the network and storage boundaries This file creates every source file for a small DRF/PostgreSQL/Nginx experiment. Inspect the generated files before building. The deliberately plain browser page isolates network and persistence concepts; it is not a replacement for your capstone React interface. The database port stays private, the browser uses relative /api URLs, and Nginx resolves backend on the container network. A PostgreSQL SELECT backs readiness. Named volume lab-data preserves records. Credentials enter at runtime. This unauthenticated, loopback-only synthetic lab uses table creation in the handler solely to remain self-contained; your capstone must use authenticated owner scopes and Django migrations. ### backend/requirements.txt ```text Django==5.2.7 djangorestframework==3.16.1 psycopg[binary]==3.2.10 gunicorn==23.0.0 ``` ### backend/Dockerfile ```text FROM python:3.12-slim WORKDIR /app COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt && useradd --create-home learner COPY app.py . USER learner EXPOSE 8000 CMD ["gunicorn", "app:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "1"] ``` ### backend/app.py ```python import os from django.conf import settings settings.configure( SECRET_KEY=os.environ["DJANGO_SECRET_KEY"], DEBUG=False, ALLOWED_HOSTS=["localhost","127.0.0.1","backend"], ROOT_URLCONF=__name__, DATABASES={"default":{"ENGINE":"django.db.backends.postgresql", "NAME":os.environ["POSTGRES_DB"], "USER":os.environ["POSTGRES_USER"], "PASSWORD":os.environ["POSTGRES_PASSWORD"], "HOST":"db", "PORT":"5432"}}, INSTALLED_APPS=["rest_framework"], REST_FRAMEWORK={"UNAUTHENTICATED_USER":None}, ) import django django.setup() from django.db import connection from django.urls import path from django.core.wsgi import get_wsgi_application from rest_framework.decorators import api_view from rest_framework.response import Response @api_view(["GET"]) def health(request): try: with connection.cursor() as cursor: cursor.execute("SELECT 1") cursor.fetchone() return Response({"database":"postgresql","ready":True}) except Exception: return Response({"ready":False,"error":"database_unavailable"},status=503) @api_view(["GET","POST"]) def drafts(request): # Dedicated synthetic local lab only; no authentication or production migration system. with connection.cursor() as cursor: cursor.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS lab_drafts(id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT NOT NULL)") if request.method=="POST": body=request.data.get("body") if type(body) is not str or not body.strip() or len(body)>500: return Response({"error":"body_required_max_500"},status=400) cursor.execute("INSERT INTO lab_drafts(body) VALUES(%s) RETURNING id",[body.strip()]) return Response({"id":cursor.fetchone()[0],"body":body.strip()},status=201) cursor.execute("SELECT id,body FROM lab_drafts ORDER BY id") return Response([{"id":row[0],"body":row[1]} for row in cursor.fetchall()]) urlpatterns=[path("api/health/",health),path("api/drafts/",drafts)] application=get_wsgi_application() ``` ### frontend/Dockerfile ```text FROM nginx:1.28-alpine COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html ``` ### frontend/nginx.conf ```text server { listen 80; server_name localhost; root /usr/share/nginx/html; location /api/ { proxy_pass http://backend:8000; proxy_set_header Host $host; } location / { try_files $uri /index.html; } } ``` ### frontend/index.html ```html Persistence boundary lab

Synthetic draft store

Local unauthenticated lab. Use synthetic text only.



```

### compose.yaml

```yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: lab
      POSTGRES_USER: lab
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${LAB_DB_PASSWORD:?Set LAB_DB_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - lab-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U lab -d lab"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 30
  backend:
    build: ./backend
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: lab
      POSTGRES_USER: lab
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${LAB_DB_PASSWORD:?Set LAB_DB_PASSWORD}
      DJANGO_SECRET_KEY: ${LAB_DJANGO_SECRET:?Set LAB_DJANGO_SECRET}
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  frontend:
    build: ./frontend
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${LAB_PORT:-8091}:80"
    depends_on:
      - backend
volumes:
  lab-data:
```

### Run the isolated container experiment

Prerequisite: Docker Engine with Compose available. This is an optional local build; it uses no model key. Save the seven files above under a new `container-lab` folder with exactly the shown paths. Never run this unauthenticated experiment on a public interface or put real content in it. Its static page isolates networking and persistence; keep React for your own capstone.

```sh
cd container-lab
export LAB_DB_PASSWORD=synthetic-local-lab-password
export LAB_DJANGO_SECRET=synthetic-local-lab-secret-for-testing-only
export LAB_PORT=8091
docker compose -p academy-student-lab up -d --build
curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8091/api/health/
curl --fail -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"body":"restart-proof-draft"}' http://127.0.0.1:8091/api/drafts/
docker compose -p academy-student-lab up -d --force-recreate backend
curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8091/api/drafts/
```

Wait for the health request to succeed before the POST; startup ordering alone does not establish HTTP readiness. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8091/` and use the form, then reload. The same saved record must return from the API. Stop only the lab database with `docker compose -p academy-student-lab stop db`; a health request must return HTTP 503. Restart it with `docker compose -p academy-student-lab start db` and repeat readiness/readback. A process can be running while its dependency is unavailable.

Clean up using `docker compose -p academy-student-lab down`. This preserves the named volume. Add `--volumes` only when you deliberately want to delete this lab's synthetic records. Do not substitute your capstone or academy Compose project name.


## Extend the example

Run the Docker procedure below, save a unique synthetic draft, replace the backend container and read it again. Then stop the database and check that /api/health/ returns 503. Record HTTP status and actual record ID; creating files or building an image alone does not pass the exercise.

The assertions demonstrate only the named local behavior. They do not execute your capstone, grade factual judgments, or prove that a real provider or external integration works.

## Connect the taught pieces before the capstone

# ai-agent-bootcamp: complete independent student capstone

## Product and prerequisite contract

Ask a supported refund question; an unsupported topic must abstain and a requested write must be denied. The bounded loop permits search and draft only, enforces evidence-before-draft and stops at its step budget. Confirm a stored draft with a reviewer and prove replay creates the same local receipt.

Sessions 4–6 define the model contract and budget; 7–9 teach source identity and grounding; 10–12 teach bounded actions and approval; 13–14 teach HTTP/data ownership; 16–20 teach tests, traces, containers and recovery.

The assembly mechanics below repair the previously missing connection between separate lesson examples. Read them before attempting the final project. Every file follows inline in the course; the optional program download contains the identical capstone/ directory. Python 3.12 and Docker Compose are required. There is no import from another academy program, Workshop checkout or private app database.

## Connect the pieces before changing them

1. Read core.py first. Its process(input, mode, documents) function returns a status, text and evidence IDs. It must never receive the expected test answer. The provider is a named scripted fixture, so a passing run proves control flow, not model quality.
2. Read app.py's exact and identity functions. Reject extra fields and blank input before retrieval. Demo bearer strings resolve to a trusted owner/role at the server; a JSON owner field is rejected. These published fixture tokens are local teaching identities, not production authentication.
3. Trace ask: validate → owner-filter persisted sources → core workflow → save result → return ID. A timeout is a stored failed result, not an empty successful answer. Health runs a real query against the required table.
4. initialize is a one-shot schema release job. It creates the records and quota tables before Gunicorn starts. PostgreSQL bucket is a fixed-minute quota window: avoid the reserved SQL word window. Parameterized values stay outside SQL syntax. The ON CONFLICT increment is atomic across both HTTP workers; a Python dictionary counter would not be shared.
5. PostgreSQL JSONB stores an object, but Django raw cursors may return its JSON text. Decode a string at the storage boundary before accessing fields. Do not serialize an already serialized value twice. All reads include owner before payload leaves the database.
6. Approval digests bind text, source version and citations using one canonical server serialization. The UI uses the server's digest rather than trying to recreate Python JSON spacing in JavaScript. The submitted version and digest must match the row locked by SELECT FOR UPDATE. Only reviewer-one can approve owner one's draft. The effect is a local outbox row, never an external message, refund or calendar event.
7. The same transaction writes the local effect and approval status. A stable effect key plus the row lock makes simultaneous duplicate confirmation return the same receipt. A timed-out external write would need reconciliation; this local transaction does not claim distributed exactly-once delivery.
8. Browser code displays response text with textContent and retains the input on errors. It shows the stored result before review. An HTTP 201 says a result was saved; inspect status to distinguish needs_review, failed, abstain, denied or needs_correction.
9. Compose starts an isolated PostgreSQL volume, runs the schema job once, and publishes only the API on loopback. Recreating an API container must retain records because the database volume is separate. Dependency outage yields 503; health is not a substitute for the full check script.
10. check.py sends real HTTP requests and reads back their actual IDs. It tests changed approvals, wrong owners, malformed input, failures and concurrent duplicate review. Latency is measured around actual requests. Unknown token usage and spend remain null, not fabricated zero. This sequential local sample is not a cloud concurrency benchmark.

## Make the three pillars observable

Compare two core candidates on the same unchanged cases; retain failed and rejected work in the report. Measure HTTP latency separately from any future provider latency and report accepted-output quality. Preserve exact deterministic invariants while recording factual review separately. Context budgets here are explicitly characters; token accounting belongs in an actual model adapter. Scope and source revisions belong in any future cache key; no cache-hit or savings claim is made by these local projects.

## Diagnose a failed build or check

If schema exits nonzero, inspect that service's log before testing the API. If HTTP succeeds but the saved result differs, inspect core.process and the stored JSON separately. If a restart loses data, inspect the named volume and compose project name. If a duplicate approval changes receipts, inspect the row-lock/transaction boundary, not the prompt. Preserve the failed output with its repaired rerun.


## Student build walkthrough — trace one draft all the way to its receipt

This project has two layers. `core.py` is the scripted, bounded read-only agent. `app.py` is the HTTP, identity, quota and PostgreSQL adapter. Keep those responsibilities separate: a proposal function never receives a database connection or reviewer authority. Sessions 5 and 14 now contain runtime studios for actual asynchronous deadlines and transaction rollback; complete those before this integration.

### Step 1 — prove the pure control flow before starting containers

From your fresh capstone directory, run:

```sh
python3.12 -m unittest -v test_core
```

Read each assertion in `test_core.py`. A one-step allowance permits a search but cannot also finish. A proposal to draft before searching raises an evidence error. A proposal with an extra owner field fails its exact shape check; an unknown operation is denied. The policy contains both the refund rule and the opened-item exclusion. A known negative policy answer must preserve that exclusion, while an unrelated wallpaper question abstains. These are actual control-flow assertions over a scripted fixture, not tests of a model’s understanding.

Prediction checkpoint: `run('refund','fixture',max_steps=1)` must return failed/step_budget, not needs_review. If it succeeds, inspect where the step counter is decremented. Do not increase the expected budget just to hide a missing transition.

### Step 2 — trace request validation and persisted failure

Start Compose and run the complete HTTP check from the earlier section. Follow one request through these statements in `app.py`:

1. `identity` maps the demo bearer token to a trusted owner and role. `exact` rejects a client-provided owner. Admission uses the shared PostgreSQL quota rather than a process-local dictionary.
2. `ask` validates input and fixture mode, then calls `process`. The policy corpus in this Bootcamp build is the explicit constant in `core.py`; `documents` is an intentionally unused common adapter parameter. There is no hidden upload or vector-search feature.
3. `TimeoutError` becomes a failed result with provider_timeout, null text and no citations. The route then saves that result. Inspect the returned status as well as HTTP 201: 201 means this result record was created, not that generation succeeded.
4. `record` binds JSON as a parameter and stores it in JSONB. `get_record` includes owner in the SQL query and decodes raw JSON text if required by the driver. Use the returned ID to read the same stored input/result.

This failure mode is injection at the workflow boundary. It does not enforce a real provider network deadline; the earlier asynchronous studio teaches that adapter responsibility.

### Step 3 — bind review to exactly what was displayed

The server computes approval_digest over text, citation IDs and source version with one canonical serialization. Copy that returned digest and version when approving. Never reconstruct the hash from JavaScript object formatting. Inside `transaction.atomic`, `get_record(..., lock=True)` locks the owner-scoped row. Only after role, version, digest and state checks succeed can it insert the deterministic `effect:` local receipt and update the draft.

Predict the two concurrent callers: the first holds the lock and commits one receipt; the second then reads approved and returns that receipt. The HTTP check exercises four replays. This proves a local database boundary. It does not mean a remote refund or message can be retried safely after a lost response.

### Step 4 — break, diagnose and repair the integrated path

| Observed result | First boundary to inspect | Required evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unsupported question gets a policy answer | `process` topic gate and unchanged unknown-topic case | Actual request, status, text and citations |
| Wrong owner reads the draft | Owner predicate in `get_record`, before JSON leaves SQL | Same stored ID, two identities, 200 versus 404 |
| Stale approval succeeds | Version/digest comparison inside the lock | Changed digest gets 409 and no receipt |
| Timeout returns plausible text | Exception classification before saving | Failed record read back under the original ID |
| Recreated API loses the result | Compose database volume and project name | Same ID and payload before/after replacement |

Student variation: add one explicit forbidden operation and its case to `test_core.py` before changing the gate. Preserve the unsupported-topic and opened-item exclusion cases. Run the pure tests, actual HTTP checks, restart readback and fresh restore comparison. Your release evidence must include the failed case and corrected rerun; a successful browser button alone is insufficient.

### Read a failed acceptance report

The HTTP check starts a fresh report before its first request and updates it as checks run. A failed assertion or dependency exception leaves completed=false, the checks observed so far and error_type; it still exits nonzero. A completed=true report means the whole procedure finished. Latency p95 uses nearest rank, ceil(.95*n)-1, over its labeled sample. Do not reuse an older successful report after a new failed run, and do not mistake twelve sequential observations for a capacity benchmark.




The final project chapter in this program provides every file, exact commands and the failure checks. Explain the storage, ownership and observed-result boundaries above before proceeding. No code from another program is required.

## Bounded first practice

## Practice acceptance

## Integrate after practice

## Worked example

A Compose network contains `frontend`, `backend`, and `db`. Django connects to `db:5432`; the browser connects to `localhost:8080/api/` through Nginx. A health probe should prove the dependency your readiness claim relies on, not just return a hard-coded string.

## Build it yourself

1. Write Dockerfiles and a Compose file for your capstone.
2. Add database readiness, migrations, a non-root application user, and an HTTP health endpoint.
3. Bring up the stack and verify the actual database vendor from the running API container.
4. Restart services and confirm saved synthetic records remain.

## Break it deliberately

Point the API at an unavailable database. The service should fail readiness and expose a useful operational failure rather than advertise healthy persisted behavior.

## Acceptance checks

- The production frontend can call the containerized API.
- A database record survives a service restart.
- No database credential is baked into the image.

## Deliverable

Save **`compose.yaml`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

## Full project sequence

1. Write Dockerfiles and a Compose file for your capstone.
2. Add database readiness, migrations, a non-root application user, and an HTTP health endpoint.
3. Bring up the stack and verify the actual database vendor from the running API container.
4. Restart services and confirm saved synthetic records remain.

## Integration acceptance

- The production frontend can call the containerized API.
- A database record survives a service restart.
- No database credential is baked into the image.

## Apply the three engineering pillars

## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to A multi-user AI service deployed from containers

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Load-test offered vs. completed work, p95 and cost per accepted result at stated concurrency. Autoscaling settings are hypotheses until observed against downstream/GPU limits.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Test readiness against the actual database, restart/readback, isolated restore, denied owner access, overload rejection and a dependency outage on the deployed revision.

### Context Management

Budget resident model memory/KV cache and per-request context separately. Keep tenant/revision-aware application caches; never assume a process-local cache is shared across replicas.

## Failure and deployment work

Separate request concurrency, worker capacity and model/GPU capacity. Add admission control, shared quotas, bounded queues, maximum instances and a documented fallback/stop budget.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

chapters.body:
## Before you begin

Complete sessions 1–18 in this bootcamp. Keep your policy fixtures and evaluation labels in your own workspace. The example below runs independently so a prior missing file cannot block understanding.

## Why this decision matters

A working local Python process is only one part of the release. A complete deployment needs a frontend, API, database, configuration, networking, static assets, startup ordering, and health checks. Container images package code and dependencies; named volumes preserve database data beyond a container’s lifetime.

Keep credentials in runtime configuration. A database port does not need to be public when only the API uses it. Understand the difference between container-local hostnames and browser-visible URLs: the browser cannot resolve a Compose service name. Use a frontend proxy so requests remain on the same origin. Test the built frontend rather than only a development server.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Container network

A private network where service names resolve for containers, not necessarily for a browser.

### Persistent volume

Storage that survives removal or replacement of a container.

### Readiness probe

A check of the dependency needed for the service to fulfill its readiness claim.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Container network

A container network provides service names to containers, not to the browser. The page requests relative /api URLs; Nginx resolves backend internally, and the backend resolves db. Publishing PostgreSQL is unnecessary for this path. Trace browser → proxy → API → database before debugging individual endpoints so localhost is not mistaken for the same host everywhere.

## Step 2 · Persistent volume

A persistent volume stores database files outside a replaceable container. Recreating the backend should preserve the saved draft because its data lives in PostgreSQL. A named volume is not a tested backup; deleting it removes the synthetic records. The supplied lab binds only loopback and uses synthetic runtime configuration; it is not an authenticated production deployment.

## Step 3 · Readiness probe

A readiness probe checks a required dependency through an actual query. A running process can still return 503 when PostgreSQL is stopped. Wait for readiness before writing, record the returned draft ID and read it after replacement. Building an image or creating source files alone does not demonstrate end-to-end persistence.

chapters.title: Worked implementation: Containerize the complete application
chapters.body:
## Walk through the data and decision 1. The supplied seven files place browser traffic through Nginx and keep the database internal. 2. The backend reads runtime configuration and PostgreSQL stores rows in its named volume. 3. The procedure saves a draft, replaces backend, then checks readback and database-outage readiness. ## Follow the network and storage boundaries This file creates every source file for a small DRF/PostgreSQL/Nginx experiment. Inspect the generated files before building. The deliberately plain browser page isolates network and persistence concepts; it is not a replacement for your capstone React interface. The database port stays private, the browser uses relative /api URLs, and Nginx resolves backend on the container network. A PostgreSQL SELECT backs readiness. Named volume lab-data preserves records. Credentials enter at runtime. This unauthenticated, loopback-only synthetic lab uses table creation in the handler solely to remain self-contained; your capstone must use authenticated owner scopes and Django migrations. ### backend/requirements.txt ```text Django==5.2.7 djangorestframework==3.16.1 psycopg[binary]==3.2.10 gunicorn==23.0.0 ``` ### backend/Dockerfile ```text FROM python:3.12-slim WORKDIR /app COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt && useradd --create-home learner COPY app.py . USER learner EXPOSE 8000 CMD ["gunicorn", "app:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "1"] ``` ### backend/app.py ```python import os from django.conf import settings settings.configure( SECRET_KEY=os.environ["DJANGO_SECRET_KEY"], DEBUG=False, ALLOWED_HOSTS=["localhost","127.0.0.1","backend"], ROOT_URLCONF=__name__, DATABASES={"default":{"ENGINE":"django.db.backends.postgresql", "NAME":os.environ["POSTGRES_DB"], "USER":os.environ["POSTGRES_USER"], "PASSWORD":os.environ["POSTGRES_PASSWORD"], "HOST":"db", "PORT":"5432"}}, INSTALLED_APPS=["rest_framework"], REST_FRAMEWORK={"UNAUTHENTICATED_USER":None}, ) import django django.setup() from django.db import connection from django.urls import path from django.core.wsgi import get_wsgi_application from rest_framework.decorators import api_view from rest_framework.response import Response @api_view(["GET"]) def health(request): try: with connection.cursor() as cursor: cursor.execute("SELECT 1") cursor.fetchone() return Response({"database":"postgresql","ready":True}) except Exception: return Response({"ready":False,"error":"database_unavailable"},status=503) @api_view(["GET","POST"]) def drafts(request): # Dedicated synthetic local lab only; no authentication or production migration system. with connection.cursor() as cursor: cursor.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS lab_drafts(id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT NOT NULL)") if request.method=="POST": body=request.data.get("body") if type(body) is not str or not body.strip() or len(body)>500: return Response({"error":"body_required_max_500"},status=400) cursor.execute("INSERT INTO lab_drafts(body) VALUES(%s) RETURNING id",[body.strip()]) return Response({"id":cursor.fetchone()[0],"body":body.strip()},status=201) cursor.execute("SELECT id,body FROM lab_drafts ORDER BY id") return Response([{"id":row[0],"body":row[1]} for row in cursor.fetchall()]) urlpatterns=[path("api/health/",health),path("api/drafts/",drafts)] application=get_wsgi_application() ``` ### frontend/Dockerfile ```text FROM nginx:1.28-alpine COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html ``` ### frontend/nginx.conf ```text server { listen 80; server_name localhost; root /usr/share/nginx/html; location /api/ { proxy_pass http://backend:8000; proxy_set_header Host $host; } location / { try_files $uri /index.html; } } ``` ### frontend/index.html ```html Persistence boundary lab

Synthetic draft store

Local unauthenticated lab. Use synthetic text only.



```

### compose.yaml

```yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: lab
      POSTGRES_USER: lab
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${LAB_DB_PASSWORD:?Set LAB_DB_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - lab-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U lab -d lab"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 30
  backend:
    build: ./backend
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: lab
      POSTGRES_USER: lab
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${LAB_DB_PASSWORD:?Set LAB_DB_PASSWORD}
      DJANGO_SECRET_KEY: ${LAB_DJANGO_SECRET:?Set LAB_DJANGO_SECRET}
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  frontend:
    build: ./frontend
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${LAB_PORT:-8091}:80"
    depends_on:
      - backend
volumes:
  lab-data:
```

### Run the isolated container experiment

Prerequisite: Docker Engine with Compose available. This is an optional local build; it uses no model key. Save the seven files above under a new `container-lab` folder with exactly the shown paths. Never run this unauthenticated experiment on a public interface or put real content in it. Its static page isolates networking and persistence; keep React for your own capstone.

```sh
cd container-lab
export LAB_DB_PASSWORD=synthetic-local-lab-password
export LAB_DJANGO_SECRET=synthetic-local-lab-secret-for-testing-only
export LAB_PORT=8091
docker compose -p academy-student-lab up -d --build
curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8091/api/health/
curl --fail -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"body":"restart-proof-draft"}' http://127.0.0.1:8091/api/drafts/
docker compose -p academy-student-lab up -d --force-recreate backend
curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8091/api/drafts/
```

Wait for the health request to succeed before the POST; startup ordering alone does not establish HTTP readiness. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8091/` and use the form, then reload. The same saved record must return from the API. Stop only the lab database with `docker compose -p academy-student-lab stop db`; a health request must return HTTP 503. Restart it with `docker compose -p academy-student-lab start db` and repeat readiness/readback. A process can be running while its dependency is unavailable.

Clean up using `docker compose -p academy-student-lab down`. This preserves the named volume. Add `--volumes` only when you deliberately want to delete this lab's synthetic records. Do not substitute your capstone or academy Compose project name.


## Extend the example

Run the Docker procedure below, save a unique synthetic draft, replace the backend container and read it again. Then stop the database and check that /api/health/ returns 503. Record HTTP status and actual record ID; creating files or building an image alone does not pass the exercise.

The assertions demonstrate only the named local behavior. They do not execute your capstone, grade factual judgments, or prove that a real provider or external integration works.

chapters.title: Connect the taught pieces before the capstone
chapters.body:
# ai-agent-bootcamp: complete independent student capstone

## Product and prerequisite contract

Ask a supported refund question; an unsupported topic must abstain and a requested write must be denied. The bounded loop permits search and draft only, enforces evidence-before-draft and stops at its step budget. Confirm a stored draft with a reviewer and prove replay creates the same local receipt.

Sessions 4–6 define the model contract and budget; 7–9 teach source identity and grounding; 10–12 teach bounded actions and approval; 13–14 teach HTTP/data ownership; 16–20 teach tests, traces, containers and recovery.

The assembly mechanics below repair the previously missing connection between separate lesson examples. Read them before attempting the final project. Every file follows inline in the course; the optional program download contains the identical capstone/ directory. Python 3.12 and Docker Compose are required. There is no import from another academy program, Workshop checkout or private app database.

## Connect the pieces before changing them

1. Read core.py first. Its process(input, mode, documents) function returns a status, text and evidence IDs. It must never receive the expected test answer. The provider is a named scripted fixture, so a passing run proves control flow, not model quality.
2. Read app.py's exact and identity functions. Reject extra fields and blank input before retrieval. Demo bearer strings resolve to a trusted owner/role at the server; a JSON owner field is rejected. These published fixture tokens are local teaching identities, not production authentication.
3. Trace ask: validate → owner-filter persisted sources → core workflow → save result → return ID. A timeout is a stored failed result, not an empty successful answer. Health runs a real query against the required table.
4. initialize is a one-shot schema release job. It creates the records and quota tables before Gunicorn starts. PostgreSQL bucket is a fixed-minute quota window: avoid the reserved SQL word window. Parameterized values stay outside SQL syntax. The ON CONFLICT increment is atomic across both HTTP workers; a Python dictionary counter would not be shared.
5. PostgreSQL JSONB stores an object, but Django raw cursors may return its JSON text. Decode a string at the storage boundary before accessing fields. Do not serialize an already serialized value twice. All reads include owner before payload leaves the database.
6. Approval digests bind text, source version and citations using one canonical server serialization. The UI uses the server's digest rather than trying to recreate Python JSON spacing in JavaScript. The submitted version and digest must match the row locked by SELECT FOR UPDATE. Only reviewer-one can approve owner one's draft. The effect is a local outbox row, never an external message, refund or calendar event.
7. The same transaction writes the local effect and approval status. A stable effect key plus the row lock makes simultaneous duplicate confirmation return the same receipt. A timed-out external write would need reconciliation; this local transaction does not claim distributed exactly-once delivery.
8. Browser code displays response text with textContent and retains the input on errors. It shows the stored result before review. An HTTP 201 says a result was saved; inspect status to distinguish needs_review, failed, abstain, denied or needs_correction.
9. Compose starts an isolated PostgreSQL volume, runs the schema job once, and publishes only the API on loopback. Recreating an API container must retain records because the database volume is separate. Dependency outage yields 503; health is not a substitute for the full check script.
10. check.py sends real HTTP requests and reads back their actual IDs. It tests changed approvals, wrong owners, malformed input, failures and concurrent duplicate review. Latency is measured around actual requests. Unknown token usage and spend remain null, not fabricated zero. This sequential local sample is not a cloud concurrency benchmark.

## Make the three pillars observable

Compare two core candidates on the same unchanged cases; retain failed and rejected work in the report. Measure HTTP latency separately from any future provider latency and report accepted-output quality. Preserve exact deterministic invariants while recording factual review separately. Context budgets here are explicitly characters; token accounting belongs in an actual model adapter. Scope and source revisions belong in any future cache key; no cache-hit or savings claim is made by these local projects.

## Diagnose a failed build or check

If schema exits nonzero, inspect that service's log before testing the API. If HTTP succeeds but the saved result differs, inspect core.process and the stored JSON separately. If a restart loses data, inspect the named volume and compose project name. If a duplicate approval changes receipts, inspect the row-lock/transaction boundary, not the prompt. Preserve the failed output with its repaired rerun.

<!-- student-depth:start -->
## Student build walkthrough — trace one draft all the way to its receipt

This project has two layers. `core.py` is the scripted, bounded read-only agent. `app.py` is the HTTP, identity, quota and PostgreSQL adapter. Keep those responsibilities separate: a proposal function never receives a database connection or reviewer authority. Sessions 5 and 14 now contain runtime studios for actual asynchronous deadlines and transaction rollback; complete those before this integration.

### Step 1 — prove the pure control flow before starting containers

From your fresh capstone directory, run:

```sh
python3.12 -m unittest -v test_core
```

Read each assertion in `test_core.py`. A one-step allowance permits a search but cannot also finish. A proposal to draft before searching raises an evidence error. A proposal with an extra owner field fails its exact shape check; an unknown operation is denied. The policy contains both the refund rule and the opened-item exclusion. A known negative policy answer must preserve that exclusion, while an unrelated wallpaper question abstains. These are actual control-flow assertions over a scripted fixture, not tests of a model’s understanding.

Prediction checkpoint: `run('refund','fixture',max_steps=1)` must return failed/step_budget, not needs_review. If it succeeds, inspect where the step counter is decremented. Do not increase the expected budget just to hide a missing transition.

### Step 2 — trace request validation and persisted failure

Start Compose and run the complete HTTP check from the earlier section. Follow one request through these statements in `app.py`:

1. `identity` maps the demo bearer token to a trusted owner and role. `exact` rejects a client-provided owner. Admission uses the shared PostgreSQL quota rather than a process-local dictionary.
2. `ask` validates input and fixture mode, then calls `process`. The policy corpus in this Bootcamp build is the explicit constant in `core.py`; `documents` is an intentionally unused common adapter parameter. There is no hidden upload or vector-search feature.
3. `TimeoutError` becomes a failed result with provider_timeout, null text and no citations. The route then saves that result. Inspect the returned status as well as HTTP 201: 201 means this result record was created, not that generation succeeded.
4. `record` binds JSON as a parameter and stores it in JSONB. `get_record` includes owner in the SQL query and decodes raw JSON text if required by the driver. Use the returned ID to read the same stored input/result.

This failure mode is injection at the workflow boundary. It does not enforce a real provider network deadline; the earlier asynchronous studio teaches that adapter responsibility.

### Step 3 — bind review to exactly what was displayed

The server computes approval_digest over text, citation IDs and source version with one canonical serialization. Copy that returned digest and version when approving. Never reconstruct the hash from JavaScript object formatting. Inside `transaction.atomic`, `get_record(..., lock=True)` locks the owner-scoped row. Only after role, version, digest and state checks succeed can it insert the deterministic `effect:<draft_id>` local receipt and update the draft.

Predict the two concurrent callers: the first holds the lock and commits one receipt; the second then reads approved and returns that receipt. The HTTP check exercises four replays. This proves a local database boundary. It does not mean a remote refund or message can be retried safely after a lost response.

### Step 4 — break, diagnose and repair the integrated path

| Observed result | First boundary to inspect | Required evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unsupported question gets a policy answer | `process` topic gate and unchanged unknown-topic case | Actual request, status, text and citations |
| Wrong owner reads the draft | Owner predicate in `get_record`, before JSON leaves SQL | Same stored ID, two identities, 200 versus 404 |
| Stale approval succeeds | Version/digest comparison inside the lock | Changed digest gets 409 and no receipt |
| Timeout returns plausible text | Exception classification before saving | Failed record read back under the original ID |
| Recreated API loses the result | Compose database volume and project name | Same ID and payload before/after replacement |

Student variation: add one explicit forbidden operation and its case to `test_core.py` before changing the gate. Preserve the unsupported-topic and opened-item exclusion cases. Run the pure tests, actual HTTP checks, restart readback and fresh restore comparison. Your release evidence must include the failed case and corrected rerun; a successful browser button alone is insufficient.

### Read a failed acceptance report

The HTTP check starts a fresh report before its first request and updates it as checks run. A failed assertion or dependency exception leaves completed=false, the checks observed so far and error_type; it still exits nonzero. A completed=true report means the whole procedure finished. Latency p95 uses nearest rank, ceil(.95*n)-1, over its labeled sample. Do not reuse an older successful report after a new failed run, and do not mistake twelve sequential observations for a capacity benchmark.
<!-- student-depth:end -->



The final project chapter in this program provides every file, exact commands and the failure checks. Explain the storage, ownership and observed-result boundaries above before proceeding. No code from another program is required.

chapters.title: Practice first, then integrate
chapters.body:
## Bounded first practice

Create the supplied lab, run its Docker procedure and record one saved ID/body after backend replacement plus a 503 when only the lab database is stopped.

## Practice acceptance

- The completed baseline/specimen is explained using the lesson walkthrough, with fixture assumptions distinguished from observations.
- Create the supplied lab, run its Docker procedure and record one saved ID/body after backend replacement plus a 503 when only the lab database is stopped.
- The implementation includes positive and negative checks, actual output and explicit limits on what those checks establish.

## Integrate after practice

## Worked example

A Compose network contains `frontend`, `backend`, and `db`. Django connects to `db:5432`; the browser connects to `localhost:8080/api/` through Nginx. A health probe should prove the dependency your readiness claim relies on, not just return a hard-coded string.

## Build it yourself

1. Write Dockerfiles and a Compose file for your capstone.
2. Add database readiness, migrations, a non-root application user, and an HTTP health endpoint.
3. Bring up the stack and verify the actual database vendor from the running API container.
4. Restart services and confirm saved synthetic records remain.

## Break it deliberately

Point the API at an unavailable database. The service should fail readiness and expose a useful operational failure rather than advertise healthy persisted behavior.

## Acceptance checks

- The production frontend can call the containerized API.
- A database record survives a service restart.
- No database credential is baked into the image.

## Deliverable

Save **`compose.yaml`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

## Full project sequence

1. Write Dockerfiles and a Compose file for your capstone.
2. Add database readiness, migrations, a non-root application user, and an HTTP health endpoint.
3. Bring up the stack and verify the actual database vendor from the running API container.
4. Restart services and confirm saved synthetic records remain.

## Integration acceptance

- The production frontend can call the containerized API.
- A database record survives a service restart.
- No database credential is baked into the image.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to A multi-user AI service deployed from containers

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Load-test offered vs. completed work, p95 and cost per accepted result at stated concurrency. Autoscaling settings are hypotheses until observed against downstream/GPU limits.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Test readiness against the actual database, restart/readback, isolated restore, denied owner access, overload rejection and a dependency outage on the deployed revision.

### Context Management

Budget resident model memory/KV cache and per-request context separately. Keep tenant/revision-aware application caches; never assume a process-local cache is shared across replicas.

## Failure and deployment work

Separate request concurrency, worker capacity and model/GPU capacity. Add admission control, shared quotas, bounded queues, maximum instances and a documented fallback/stop budget.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

lessons.title: Failure recovery and release checklists
lessons.content:
# Failure recovery and release checklists

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Containerize the complete application**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Containerize the complete application (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:19`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Container network** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: A private network where service names resolve for containers, not necessarily for a browser.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **a container, recovery transcript and orchestration decision**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Choose orchestration complexity deliberately**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Failure recovery and release checklists

## Before you begin

Complete sessions 1–19 in this bootcamp. Keep your policy fixtures and evaluation labels in your own workspace. The example below runs independently so a prior missing file cannot block understanding.

## Why this decision matters

A release plan specifies what you will check, what failure means, and how you will recover. Back up data before applying schema changes. Test a restore into an isolated target rather than assuming a generated backup file is sufficient. A rollback of code does not automatically undo a destructive database migration.

Exercise failure modes deliberately in a local environment: provider unavailable, database restarting, missing static assets, wrong configuration, and oversized requests. Record which data is preserved and which requests must be retried. An operational runbook should let another person diagnose these failures without needing your memory.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Restore verification

Recovering a backup into an isolated target and checking its actual contents.

### Rollback boundary

Code rollback and data-schema recovery are distinct operations.

### Runbook

Concrete diagnosis and recovery steps that another operator can follow.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Restore verification

Restore verification checks a backup by restoring into an isolated target and comparing meaningful records. A backup file’s existence or size does not show it can be recovered. In the baseline two SQLite backup operations construct a separate restore database, and the assertion checks both ID and body without altering the source.

## Step 2 · Rollback boundary

A rollback boundary separates code, schema, data and external effects. Returning to an earlier image may not reverse a migrated schema or a message already delivered. State which revisions remain compatible and when operator review is needed. Never rehearse destructive steps against the academy or a real client database.

## Step 3 · Runbook

A runbook gives a fresh operator prerequisites, exact commands, decision points and expected observations. Record snapshot time, source revision and measured restore duration; these determine what recovery claims are defensible. The inline PostgreSQL drill extends the small SQLite mechanism into a real isolated container experiment without pretending it is a disaster-recovery certification.

## Worked implementation: Failure recovery and release checklists

## Walk through the data and decision

1. source.backup writes a consistent source snapshot to the backup database.

2. Restoring to a separate target preserves the live source row.

3. Representative ID/body equality, not filename existence, establishes the shown recovery observation.

## Predict before running

Read the assertions and predict the output and rejected cases. Save the **entire** following block as `example.py` in a new scratch folder. Use Python 3.12; every import and synthetic fixture required for this example is included. Run `python3 -I example.py`. Assertions must be enabled; do not use `-O`. No model, network, database service or third-party package is required. SQLite examples create a temporary database and clean it up.

```python
import sqlite3
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
from pathlib import Path
with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    root = Path(folder)
    source = sqlite3.connect(root/'source.sqlite')
    source.execute('CREATE TABLE drafts(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT)')
    source.execute('INSERT INTO drafts VALUES(?,?)',('d7','reviewed policy draft'))
    source.commit()
    backup = sqlite3.connect(root/'backup.sqlite')
    source.backup(backup)
    backup.close()
    restore = sqlite3.connect(root/'restore.sqlite')
    backup = sqlite3.connect(root/'backup.sqlite')
    backup.backup(restore)
    assert restore.execute('SELECT id,body FROM drafts').fetchall() == [('d7','reviewed policy draft')]
    assert source.execute('SELECT count(*) FROM drafts').fetchone()[0] == 1
    for connection in (source,backup,restore): connection.close()
print('isolated restore verified by representative content; live source unchanged')
```

## Expected observation

```text
isolated restore verified by representative content; live source unchanged
```

## Walk through the mechanism and its limits

SQLite’s backup API copies a consistent database into another file. A second copy restores it into an isolated target; comparing a representative body checks more than row counts. The original remains unchanged. This is a local recovery mechanism, not a PostgreSQL backup recipe. A production runbook also needs backup age, access, retention, restoration time and acceptable data loss.

## Rehearse the PostgreSQL restore in your previous lab

exercise.solution:
## Complete guided-practice reference

Save the entire block as solution.py in a new scratch directory. Use Python 3.12 and run `python3 -I solution.py` with assertions enabled. All imports and synthetic data are included. The Python checks use the standard library and no provider account. This reference covers the bounded practice, not the completed integration project.



```python
import sqlite3
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
from pathlib import Path
with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    root = Path(folder)
    source = sqlite3.connect(root/'source.sqlite')
    source.execute('CREATE TABLE drafts(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT)')
    source.execute('INSERT INTO drafts VALUES(?,?)',('d7','reviewed policy draft'))
    source.commit()
    backup = sqlite3.connect(root/'backup.sqlite')
    source.backup(backup)
    backup.close()
    restore = sqlite3.connect(root/'restore.sqlite')
    backup = sqlite3.connect(root/'backup.sqlite')
    backup.backup(restore)
    assert restore.execute('SELECT id,body FROM drafts').fetchall() == [('d7','reviewed policy draft')]
    assert source.execute('SELECT count(*) FROM drafts').fetchone()[0] == 1
    for connection in (source,backup,restore): connection.close()
print('isolated restore verified by representative content; live source unchanged')

# Complete guided-practice reference change
with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    root=Path(folder);live=sqlite3.connect(root/'live.sqlite');snap=sqlite3.connect(root/'snap.sqlite')
    live.execute('CREATE TABLE drafts(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,body TEXT)')
    with live:live.execute('INSERT INTO drafts VALUES(?,?)',('r1','before'))
    live.backup(snap)
    with live:live.execute('UPDATE drafts SET body=? WHERE id=?',('after','r1'))
    restored=sqlite3.connect(root/'restored.sqlite');snap.backup(restored)
    assert restored.execute('SELECT body FROM drafts').fetchone()==('before',)
    assert live.execute('SELECT body FROM drafts').fetchone()==('after',)
    for connection in (live,snap,restored):connection.close()
print('practice: isolated restore contains snapshot before; live after preserved; recovery point made visible')
```

## Expected reference observation

```text
isolated restore verified by representative content; live source unchanged
practice: isolated restore contains snapshot before; live after preserved; recovery point made visible
```

## If your result differs

If restored contains after, you may have restored from the wrong source or captured the backup too late. A legitimate earlier snapshot has a recovery-point gap that the runbook must disclose.

Name the decision or invariant your change protects. Compare the baseline with your result, retain the failed case, and state what remains untested in the larger project.

# Choose orchestration complexity deliberately

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Failure recovery and release checklists**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Failure recovery and release checklists (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:20`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Restore verification** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: Recovering a backup into an isolated target and checking its actual contents.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **a container, recovery transcript and orchestration decision**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

## Understand the decision: Choose orchestration complexity deliberately

## Before you begin

Complete sessions 1–20 in this bootcamp. Keep your policy fixtures and evaluation labels in your own workspace. The example below runs independently so a prior missing file cannot block understanding.

## Why this decision matters

Graphs, durable workflows, and multi-agent systems solve different coordination problems. A graph makes state transitions explicit. Durability preserves progress across interruption. Multiple agents introduce communication and responsibility boundaries. None automatically improves answer quality or removes the need for authorization.

Use your observed capstone failures to choose an extension. A fixed pipeline may already be sufficient. If a job must pause for human review and resume after restart, durable state matters more than adding a second model persona. Write the decision in terms of correctness, recovery, latency, and maintenance rather than fashionable tool names.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Explicit graph

A representation of permitted workflow states and transitions.

### Durability

Progress survives interruption because required state is persisted outside the process.

### Architecture baseline

The simpler design against which added complexity is evaluated.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Explicit graph

An explicit graph names states and permitted edges such as draft → waiting_review → ready. It helps when the workflow has branches, pauses or retries that need inspection. A graph framework does not remove the need for owner checks, versioning and stop conditions. Compare its operational cost with a fixed function chain before adopting it.

## Step 2 · Durability

Durability means state survives the relevant process boundary. An in-memory variable cannot resume after a restart. Persist state and version, reopen storage and apply a conditional transition so an old review does not replay work. The SQLite fixture demonstrates a single-record transition, not durable remote effects or multi-region coordination.

## Step 3 · Architecture baseline

An architecture baseline keeps the task and dataset fixed while comparing implementations. Count added coordination calls, latency, failure modes and review quality. Choose a framework because it resolves an observed requirement such as a durable pause, not because a multi-agent diagram looks sophisticated. Keep one simpler implementation to reveal whether complexity adds value.

## Worked implementation: Choose orchestration complexity deliberately

## Walk through the data and decision

1. The job is committed as waiting_review version 2 before closing the connection.

2. resume changes only the matching waiting version to ready version 3.

3. A duplicate version-2 resume updates zero rows.

## Predict before running

Read the assertions and predict the output and rejected cases. Save the **entire** following block as `example.py` in a new scratch folder. Use Python 3.12; every import and synthetic fixture required for this example is included. Run `python3 -I example.py`. Assertions must be enabled; do not use `-O`. No model, network, database service or third-party package is required. SQLite examples create a temporary database and clean it up.

```python
import sqlite3
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
from pathlib import Path
with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path = Path(folder)/'jobs.sqlite'
    db = sqlite3.connect(path)
    db.execute('CREATE TABLE jobs(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,state TEXT,version INT)')
    db.execute('INSERT INTO jobs VALUES(?,?,?)',('j1','waiting_review',2))
    db.commit(); db.close()
    db = sqlite3.connect(path)
    def resume(expected):
        with db:
            return db.execute("UPDATE jobs SET state='ready',version=version+1 WHERE id='j1' AND state='waiting_review' AND version=?",(expected,)).rowcount
    assert resume(2)==1 and resume(2)==0
    assert db.execute('SELECT state,version FROM jobs').fetchone()==('ready',3)
    db.close()
print('resume survives reopen; duplicate version-2 transition has zero effect')
```

## Expected observation

```text
resume survives reopen; duplicate version-2 transition has zero effect
```

## Walk through the mechanism and its limits

The persisted waiting state survives closing the connection. A conditional transition consumes a particular version once, so replaying the same review cannot advance it twice. This solves one requirement—durable review resumption—without introducing multiple agents. It does not make a subsequent external send atomic; that still requires the effect ledger from the approval lesson.

## Extend the example

Compare this state machine with the earlier bounded loop. Interrupt before and after the conditional update and explain which work may be repeated. Add two independent connections to verify your actual database’s contention behavior.

The assertions demonstrate only the named local behavior. They do not execute your capstone, grade factual judgments, or prove that a real provider or external integration works.

The SQLite fixture demonstrates a single-record transition, not durable remote effects or multi-region coordination.

## Step 3 · Architecture baseline

An architecture baseline keeps the task and dataset fixed while comparing implementations. Count added coordination calls, latency, failure modes and review quality. Choose a framework because it resolves an observed requirement such as a durable pause, not because a multi-agent diagram looks sophisticated. Keep one simpler implementation to reveal whether complexity adds value.

chapters.title: Worked implementation: Choose orchestration complexity deliberately
chapters.body:
## Walk through the data and decision

1. The job is committed as waiting_review version 2 before closing the connection.

2. resume changes only the matching waiting version to ready version 3.

3. A duplicate version-2 resume updates zero rows.

## Predict before running

Read the assertions and predict the output and rejected cases. Save the **entire** following block as `example.py` in a new scratch folder. Use Python 3.12; every import and synthetic fixture required for this example is included. Run `python3 -I example.py`. Assertions must be enabled; do not use `-O`. No model, network, database service or third-party package is required. SQLite examples create a temporary database and clean it up.

```python
import sqlite3
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
from pathlib import Path
with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path = Path(folder)/'jobs.sqlite'
    db = sqlite3.connect(path)
    db.execute('CREATE TABLE jobs(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,state TEXT,version INT)')
    db.execute('INSERT INTO jobs VALUES(?,?,?)',('j1','waiting_review',2))
    db.commit(); db.close()
    db = sqlite3.connect(path)
    def resume(expected):
        with db:
            return db.execute("UPDATE jobs SET state='ready',version=version+1 WHERE id='j1' AND state='waiting_review' AND version=?",(expected,)).rowcount
    assert resume(2)==1 and resume(2)==0
    assert db.execute('SELECT state,version FROM jobs').fetchone()==('ready',3)
    db.close()
print('resume survives reopen; duplicate version-2 transition has zero effect')
```

## Expected observation

```text
resume survives reopen; duplicate version-2 transition has zero effect
```

## Walk through the mechanism and its limits

The persisted waiting state survives closing the connection. A conditional transition consumes a particular version once, so replaying the same review cannot advance it twice. This solves one requirement—durable review resumption—without introducing multiple agents. It does not make a subsequent external send atomic; that still requires the effect ledger from the approval lesson.

## Extend the example

Compare this state machine with the earlier bounded loop. Interrupt before and after the conditional update and explain which work may be repeated. Add two independent connections to verify your actual database’s contention behavior.

The assertions demonstrate only the named local behavior. They do not execute your capstone, grade factual judgments, or prove that a real provider or external integration works.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to A multi-user AI service deployed from containers

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Load-test offered vs. completed work, p95 and cost per accepted result at stated concurrency. Autoscaling settings are hypotheses until observed against downstream/GPU limits.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Test readiness against the actual database, restart/readback, isolated restore, denied owner access, overload rejection and a dependency outage on the deployed revision.

### Context Management

Budget resident model memory/KV cache and per-request context separately. Keep tenant/revision-aware application caches; never assume a process-local cache is shared across replicas.

## Failure and deployment work

Separate request concurrency, worker capacity and model/GPU capacity. Add admission control, shared quotas, bounded queues, maximum instances and a documented fallback/stop budget.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.
