# Capstone build: support-agent vertical slice

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Choose orchestration complexity deliberately**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- From prompts to useful systems (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:01`)
- Build a small evaluation dataset first (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:03`)
- Prompt contracts and structured outputs (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:04`)
- Provider adapters, timeouts, and failures (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:05`)
- Context budgets and source selection (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:06`)
- Ingestion, normalization, and versioning (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:07`)
- Chunking and a lexical retrieval baseline (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:08`)
- Grounding, citations, and abstention (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:09`)
- Tools as typed, permissioned interfaces (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:10`)
- State machines and bounded agent loops (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:11`)
- Human approval and idempotent actions (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:12`)
- HTTP contracts and a usable API (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:13`)
- Persistence, transactions, and data ownership (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:14`)
- Build a regression harness (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:16`)
- Prompt injection and untrusted documents (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:17`)
- Observability, cost, and latency budgets (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:18`)
- Containerize the complete application (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:19`)
- Failure recovery and release checklists (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:20`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Explicit graph** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: A representation of permitted workflow states and transitions.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **the support-agent release packet**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Taught-to-project evidence map

- **scope and labeled cases** — taught in From prompts to useful systems, Build a small evaluation dataset first. Evidence: retain those lessons’ successful case and negative check in the project report.
- **contract, timeout and bounded evidence** — taught in Prompt contracts and structured outputs, Provider adapters, timeouts, and failures, Context budgets and source selection. Evidence: retain those lessons’ successful case and negative check in the project report.
- **authorized retrieval and grounded abstention** — taught in Ingestion, normalization, and versioning, Chunking and a lexical retrieval baseline, Grounding, citations, and abstention. Evidence: retain those lessons’ successful case and negative check in the project report.
- **allowlisted loop, approval and replay protection** — taught in Tools as typed, permissioned interfaces, State machines and bounded agent loops, Human approval and idempotent actions. Evidence: retain those lessons’ successful case and negative check in the project report.
- **HTTP and persistent ownership boundary** — taught in HTTP contracts and a usable API, Persistence, transactions, and data ownership. Evidence: retain those lessons’ successful case and negative check in the project report.
- **regression, injection and measured trace** — taught in Build a regression harness, Prompt injection and untrusted documents, Observability, cost, and latency budgets. Evidence: retain those lessons’ successful case and negative check in the project report.
- **container and recovery evidence** — taught in Containerize the complete application, Failure recovery and release checklists. Evidence: retain those lessons’ successful case and negative check in the project report.

## Assemble, then test

Choose the support workflow from session 1. Reuse the case labels from 3 without changing expected answers to fit the candidate. Wire the adapter, retrieval and dispatcher through the API boundary. Record one supported question, one unsupported question, one denied action and one timeout as full request/result traces. Carry unresolved defects into sessions 23–24; a fixture-only run stays labeled local.

## Feedback when integration fails

Find the first boundary whose actual output differs from its contract. Rerun that lesson’s isolated positive and negative checks. If they pass, inspect the connecting field names, owner/source IDs, units and state transitions; do not weaken the gold labels or bypass a denied path. Record the failing input and unresolved result. Passing a single variation does not establish the whole project.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Capstone evaluation and peer critique**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Capstone build: support-agent vertical slice

## Before you begin

Complete sessions 1–21 in this bootcamp. Keep your policy fixtures and evaluation labels in your own workspace. The example below runs independently so a prior missing file cannot block understanding.

## Why this decision matters

A vertical slice connects a real user action through UI, API, retrieval, draft generation, persistence, and visible result. It is more valuable than six disconnected components that each work alone. Freeze your release scope to the read-only policy assistant and optional fake approval action. Use synthetic data, a fake provider, and your existing evaluation dataset before a live integration.

Keep an evidence bundle as you build. Include the exact setup, observed outputs, tests, source revisions, and failure investigations. A screenshot of a plausible answer cannot prove retrieval correctness or data isolation. Demonstrate those claims through targeted checks and traceable artifacts.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Vertical slice

One complete user path through interface, API, application logic, storage and visible result.

### Evidence bundle

Inputs, observed outputs, versions, tests and limitations supporting a project claim.

### Offline baseline

A runnable deterministic path requiring no model credentials or network call.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Vertical slice

A vertical slice connects one real user-visible path from input through result and saved readback. It is narrower than many disconnected features. Build normal, clarify, abstain and failure states around the same policy fixtures. The supplied application-layer slice saves a scoped source reference; your final API needs original question and full result as well.

## Step 2 · Evidence bundle

An evidence bundle links each claim to a fixture revision, candidate, actual observation and limitation. A console assertion is evidence for that function call; it does not prove the browser showed a failure correctly. Collect the UI, HTTP and datastore observations needed for each acceptance scenario rather than presenting screenshots as interchangeable proof.

## Step 3 · Offline baseline

An offline baseline uses a fake adapter deliberately to isolate orchestration. It allows repeatable failures and no paid account requirement. Its perfect text echo is not model quality, and a citation ID is not semantic support. Add real-provider comparisons only after the mechanical slice works, retaining the same workload and reviewed acceptance bar.

## Worked implementation: Capstone build: support-agent vertical slice

## Walk through the data and decision

1. The fake provider echoes the approved policy into a needs_review result.

2. SQLite reopen retrieves the source for acme and not another owner.

3. Missing condition, unsupported condition and timeout produce distinct outcomes.

## Predict before running

Read the assertions and predict the output and rejected cases. Save the **entire** following block as `example.py` in a new scratch folder. Use Python 3.12; every import and synthetic fixture required for this example is included. Run `python3 -I example.py`. Assertions must be enabled; do not use `-O`. No model, network, database service or third-party package is required. SQLite examples create a temporary database and clean it up.

```python
import sqlite3
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
from pathlib import Path
POLICY = {'id':'returns-v1','text':'Only unopened items within 14 days; opened items excluded.'}
def draft(condition, provider):
    if condition is None: return {'status':'clarify','citations':[]}
    if condition not in {'unopened','opened'}: return {'status':'abstain','citations':[]}
    try: answer = provider(POLICY['text'])
    except TimeoutError: return {'status':'generation_failed','citations':[]}
    return {'status':'needs_review','answer':answer,'citations':[POLICY['id']]}
def offline(text): return text  # Deterministic fake provider, not a trained model.
with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path=Path(folder)/'runs.sqlite'
    db=sqlite3.connect(path)
    db.execute('CREATE TABLE runs(id TEXT,owner TEXT,status TEXT,source TEXT)')
    result=draft('unopened',offline)
    with db: db.execute('INSERT INTO runs VALUES(?,?,?,?)',('r1','acme',result['status'],result['citations'][0]))
    db.close(); db=sqlite3.connect(path)
    assert db.execute('SELECT source FROM runs WHERE id=? AND owner=?',('r1','acme')).fetchone()==('returns-v1',)
    assert db.execute('SELECT source FROM runs WHERE id=? AND owner=?',('r1','other')).fetchone() is None
    assert draft(None,offline)['status']=='clarify'
    assert draft('commercial-contract',offline)['status']=='abstain'
    assert draft('opened',offline)['status']=='needs_review'
    def unavailable(text): raise TimeoutError()
    assert draft('unopened',unavailable)['status']=='generation_failed'
    db.close()
print('offline application slice: draft, clarify, abstain, failure, durable scoped readback')
```

## Expected observation

```text
offline application slice: draft, clarify, abstain, failure, durable scoped readback
```

## Walk through the mechanism and its limits

This deliberately small application-layer slice connects policy selection, fake drafting, an explicit status, a source revision and durable owner-scoped readback. It is not a UI/API capstone by itself. The hard-coded condition supports only this synthetic policy, not free-text eligibility reasoning. It gives you a known baseline to connect to your own actual browser and DRF endpoint.

## Extend the example

Connect this behavior to your own UI and API, then replay all five paths through HTTP. Store the original question and full result in your actual schema. Distinguish observed browser behavior from this application-layer test.

The assertions demonstrate only the named local behavior. They do not execute your capstone, grade factual judgments, or prove that a real provider or external integration works.

## Build the complete final project from these files

# ai-agent-bootcamp: complete independent student capstone

## Product and prerequisite contract

Ask a supported refund question; an unsupported topic must abstain and a requested write must be denied. The bounded loop permits search and draft only, enforces evidence-before-draft and stops at its step budget. Confirm a stored draft with a reviewer and prove replay creates the same local receipt.

Sessions 4–6 define the model contract and budget; 7–9 teach source identity and grounding; 10–12 teach bounded actions and approval; 13–14 teach HTTP/data ownership; 16–20 teach tests, traces, containers and recovery.

The assembly mechanics below repair the previously missing connection between separate lesson examples. Read them before attempting the final project. Every file follows inline in the course; the optional program download contains the identical capstone/ directory. Python 3.12 and Docker Compose are required. There is no import from another academy program, Workshop checkout or private app database.

## Connect the pieces before changing them

1. Read core.py first. Its process(input, mode, documents) function returns a status, text and evidence IDs. It must never receive the expected test answer. The provider is a named scripted fixture, so a passing run proves control flow, not model quality.
2. Read app.py's exact and identity functions. Reject extra fields and blank input before retrieval. Demo bearer strings resolve to a trusted owner/role at the server; a JSON owner field is rejected. These published fixture tokens are local teaching identities, not production authentication.
3. Trace ask: validate → owner-filter persisted sources → core workflow → save result → return ID. A timeout is a stored failed result, not an empty successful answer. Health runs a real query against the required table.
4. initialize is a one-shot schema release job. It creates the records and quota tables before Gunicorn starts. PostgreSQL bucket is a fixed-minute quota window: avoid the reserved SQL word window. Parameterized values stay outside SQL syntax. The ON CONFLICT increment is atomic across both HTTP workers; a Python dictionary counter would not be shared.
5. PostgreSQL JSONB stores an object, but Django raw cursors may return its JSON text. Decode a string at the storage boundary before accessing fields. Do not serialize an already serialized value twice. All reads include owner before payload leaves the database.
6. Approval digests bind text, source version and citations using one canonical server serialization. The UI uses the server's digest rather than trying to recreate Python JSON spacing in JavaScript. The submitted version and digest must match the row locked by SELECT FOR UPDATE. Only reviewer-one can approve owner one's draft. The effect is a local outbox row, never an external message, refund or calendar event.
7. The same transaction writes the local effect and approval status. A stable effect key plus the row lock makes simultaneous duplicate confirmation return the same receipt. A timed-out external write would need reconciliation; this local transaction does not claim distributed exactly-once delivery.
8. Browser code displays response text with textContent and retains the input on errors. It shows the stored result before review. An HTTP 201 says a result was saved; inspect status to distinguish needs_review, failed, abstain, denied or needs_correction.
9. Compose starts an isolated PostgreSQL volume, runs the schema job once, and publishes only the API on loopback. Recreating an API container must retain records because the database volume is separate. Dependency outage yields 503; health is not a substitute for the full check script.
10. check.py sends real HTTP requests and reads back their actual IDs. It tests changed approvals, wrong owners, malformed input, failures and concurrent duplicate review. Latency is measured around actual requests. Unknown token usage and spend remain null, not fabricated zero. This sequential local sample is not a cloud concurrency benchmark.

## Make the three pillars observable

Compare two core candidates on the same unchanged cases; retain failed and rejected work in the report. Measure HTTP latency separately from any future provider latency and report accepted-output quality. Preserve exact deterministic invariants while recording factual review separately. Context budgets here are explicitly characters; token accounting belongs in an actual model adapter. Scope and source revisions belong in any future cache key; no cache-hit or savings claim is made by these local projects.

## Diagnose a failed build or check

If schema exits nonzero, inspect that service's log before testing the API. If HTTP succeeds but the saved result differs, inspect core.process and the stored JSON separately. If a restart loses data, inspect the named volume and compose project name. If a duplicate approval changes receipts, inspect the row-lock/transaction boundary, not the prompt. Preserve the failed output with its repaired rerun.

<!-- student-depth:start -->
## Student build walkthrough — trace one draft all the way to its receipt

This project has two layers. `core.py` is the scripted, bounded read-only agent. `app.py` is the HTTP, identity, quota and PostgreSQL adapter. Keep those responsibilities separate: a proposal function never receives a database connection or reviewer authority. Sessions 5 and 14 now contain runtime studios for actual asynchronous deadlines and transaction rollback; complete those before this integration.

### Step 1 — prove the pure control flow before starting containers

From your fresh capstone directory, run:

```sh
python3.12 -m unittest -v test_core
```

Read each assertion in `test_core.py`. A one-step allowance permits a search but cannot also finish. A proposal to draft before searching raises an evidence error. A proposal with an extra owner field fails its exact shape check; an unknown operation is denied. The policy contains both the refund rule and the opened-item exclusion. A known negative policy answer must preserve that exclusion, while an unrelated wallpaper question abstains. These are actual control-flow assertions over a scripted fixture, not tests of a model’s understanding.

Prediction checkpoint: `run('refund','fixture',max_steps=1)` must return failed/step_budget, not needs_review. If it succeeds, inspect where the step counter is decremented. Do not increase the expected budget just to hide a missing transition.

### Step 2 — trace request validation and persisted failure

Start Compose and run the complete HTTP check from the earlier section. Follow one request through these statements in `app.py`:

1. `identity` maps the demo bearer token to a trusted owner and role. `exact` rejects a client-provided owner. Admission uses the shared PostgreSQL quota rather than a process-local dictionary.
2. `ask` validates input and fixture mode, then calls `process`. The policy corpus in this Bootcamp build is the explicit constant in `core.py`; `documents` is an intentionally unused common adapter parameter. There is no hidden upload or vector-search feature.
3. `TimeoutError` becomes a failed result with provider_timeout, null text and no citations. The route then saves that result. Inspect the returned status as well as HTTP 201: 201 means this result record was created, not that generation succeeded.
4. `record` binds JSON as a parameter and stores it in JSONB. `get_record` includes owner in the SQL query and decodes raw JSON text if required by the driver. Use the returned ID to read the same stored input/result.

This failure mode is injection at the workflow boundary. It does not enforce a real provider network deadline; the earlier asynchronous studio teaches that adapter responsibility.

### Step 3 — bind review to exactly what was displayed

The server computes approval_digest over text, citation IDs and source version with one canonical serialization. Copy that returned digest and version when approving. Never reconstruct the hash from JavaScript object formatting. Inside `transaction.atomic`, `get_record(..., lock=True)` locks the owner-scoped row. Only after role, version, digest and state checks succeed can it insert the deterministic `effect:<draft_id>` local receipt and update the draft.

Predict the two concurrent callers: the first holds the lock and commits one receipt; the second then reads approved and returns that receipt. The HTTP check exercises four replays. This proves a local database boundary. It does not mean a remote refund or message can be retried safely after a lost response.

### Step 4 — break, diagnose and repair the integrated path

| Observed result | First boundary to inspect | Required evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unsupported question gets a policy answer | `process` topic gate and unchanged unknown-topic case | Actual request, status, text and citations |
| Wrong owner reads the draft | Owner predicate in `get_record`, before JSON leaves SQL | Same stored ID, two identities, 200 versus 404 |
| Stale approval succeeds | Version/digest comparison inside the lock | Changed digest gets 409 and no receipt |
| Timeout returns plausible text | Exception classification before saving | Failed record read back under the original ID |
| Recreated API loses the result | Compose database volume and project name | Same ID and payload before/after replacement |

Student variation: add one explicit forbidden operation and its case to `test_core.py` before changing the gate. Preserve the unsupported-topic and opened-item exclusion cases. Run the pure tests, actual HTTP checks, restart readback and fresh restore comparison. Your release evidence must include the failed case and corrected rerun; a successful browser button alone is insufficient.

### Read a failed acceptance report

The HTTP check starts a fresh report before its first request and updates it as checks run. A failed assertion or dependency exception leaves completed=false, the checks observed so far and error_type; it still exits nonzero. A completed=true report means the whole procedure finished. Latency p95 uses nearest rank, ceil(.95*n)-1, over its labeled sample. Do not reuse an older successful report after a new failed run, and do not mistake twelve sequential observations for a capacity benchmark.
<!-- student-depth:end -->

## Build from a fresh folder

Create exactly the files shown in the course with their shown paths. From this directory:

```sh
docker compose -p capstone-boot up -d --build --wait
python3 check.py --base http://127.0.0.1:8211 --kind bootcamp --output observed.json
```

```python
"""A bounded read-only agent with a scripted proposal adapter, never a hidden LLM."""
import re
KIND='bootcamp'
VERSION='support-policy-v1'
POLICIES=[{'id':'refund-v1','text':'Refunds are available within 14 days for unopened items. Opened items are excluded.'}]
def scripted(observation):return {'name':'draft'} if observation else {'name':'search'}
def run(text,mode,decide=scripted,max_steps=2):
 if type(max_steps) is not int or not 1<=max_steps<=5:raise ValueError('step_budget')
 observation=None;trace=['validate']
 for _ in range(max_steps):
  action=decide(dict(observation) if observation else None)
  if type(action) is not dict or set(action)!={'name'}:raise ValueError('action_contract')
  name=action['name'];trace.append(name)
  if name=='search':
   observation=dict(POLICIES[0])
   if len(observation['text'])>512:raise ValueError('context')
  elif name=='draft':
   if not observation:raise ValueError('evidence_required')
   if mode=='timeout':raise TimeoutError('fixture')
   proposal={'text':observation['text'],'citations':[observation['id']]} if mode=='fixture' else {'text':'90 days','citations':['invented']}
   if set(proposal)!={'text','citations'} or proposal['citations']!=[observation['id']] or proposal['text']!=observation['text']:raise ValueError('provider_contract')
   return {'status':'needs_review',**proposal,'context_chars':len(observation['text']),'model':'scripted_fixture','trace':trace+['validated_draft','await_review']}
  else:return {'status':'denied','text':None,'citations':[],'trace':trace}
 return {'status':'failed','error':'step_budget','text':None,'citations':[],'trace':trace}
def process(text,mode,documents):
 terms=set(re.findall(r'[a-z]+',text.lower()))
 if terms & {'send','delete','issue','transfer'}:return {'status':'denied','text':None,'citations':[],'trace':['validate','deny_action']}
 if terms & {'ignore','override'}:return {'status':'abstain','text':None,'citations':[],'trace':['validate','untrusted_instruction']}
 if not terms & {'refund','refunds','opened','unopened'}:return {'status':'abstain','text':None,'citations':[],'trace':['validate','retrieve','no_evidence']}
 return run(text,mode)
if __name__=='__main__':
 assert run('refund','fixture',max_steps=1)['error']=='step_budget'
 assert run('refund','fixture',lambda observation:{'name':'delete'})['status']=='denied'
 try:run('refund','fixture',lambda observation:{'name':'draft'})
 except ValueError:pass
```

Save **`docs/capstone-evidence.md`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **180 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Apply the three engineering pillars

## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to A multi-user AI service deployed from containers

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Load-test offered vs. completed work, p95 and cost per accepted result at stated concurrency. Autoscaling settings are hypotheses until observed against downstream/GPU limits.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Test readiness against the actual database, restart/readback, isolated restore, denied owner access, overload rejection and a dependency outage on the deployed revision.

### Context Management

Budget resident model memory/KV cache and per-request context separately. Keep tenant/revision-aware application caches; never assume a process-local cache is shared across replicas.

## Failure and deployment work

Separate request concurrency, worker capacity and model/GPU capacity. Add admission control, shared quotas, bounded queues, maximum instances and a documented fallback/stop budget.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

exercise.solution:
## Complete guided-practice reference

Save the entire block as solution.py in a new scratch directory. Use Python 3.12 and run `python3 -I solution.py` with assertions enabled. All imports and synthetic data are included. The Python checks use the standard library and no provider account. This reference covers the bounded practice, not the completed integration project.



```python
import sqlite3
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
from pathlib import Path
POLICY = {'id':'returns-v1','text':'Only unopened items within 14 days; opened items excluded.'}
def draft(condition, provider):
    if condition is None: return {'status':'clarify','citations':[]}
    if condition not in {'unopened','opened'}: return {'status':'abstain','citations':[]}
    try: answer = provider(POLICY['text'])
    except TimeoutError: return {'status':'generation_failed','citations':[]}
    return {'status':'needs_review','answer':answer,'citations':[POLICY['id']]}
def offline(text): return text  # Deterministic fake provider, not a trained model.
with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path=Path(folder)/'runs.sqlite'
    db=sqlite3.connect(path)
    db.execute('CREATE TABLE runs(id TEXT,owner TEXT,status TEXT,source TEXT)')
    result=draft('unopened',offline)
    with db: db.execute('INSERT INTO runs VALUES(?,?,?,?)',('r1','acme',result['status'],result['citations'][0]))
    db.close(); db=sqlite3.connect(path)
    assert db.execute('SELECT source FROM runs WHERE id=? AND owner=?',('r1','acme')).fetchone()==('returns-v1',)
    assert db.execute('SELECT source FROM runs WHERE id=? AND owner=?',('r1','other')).fetchone() is None
    assert draft(None,offline)['status']=='clarify'
    assert draft('commercial-contract',offline)['status']=='abstain'
    assert draft('opened',offline)['status']=='needs_review'
    def unavailable(text): raise TimeoutError()
    assert draft('unopened',unavailable)['status']=='generation_failed'
    db.close()
print('offline application slice: draft, clarify, abstain, failure, durable scoped readback')

# Complete guided-practice reference change
import json
with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    db=sqlite3.connect(Path(folder)/'slice.sqlite');db.execute('CREATE TABLE runs(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,question TEXT,result TEXT)')
    inputs=[('normal','unopened',offline),('missing',None,offline),('unsupported','commercial-contract',offline),('outage','unopened',unavailable)]
    for identifier,condition,provider in inputs:
        result=draft(condition,provider)
        with db:db.execute('INSERT INTO runs VALUES(?,?,?)',(identifier,'condition='+str(condition),json.dumps(result)))
    assert db.execute('SELECT count(*) FROM runs').fetchone()[0]==4
    failed=json.loads(db.execute('SELECT result FROM runs WHERE id=?',('outage',)).fetchone()[0])
    assert failed['status']=='generation_failed'
    assert db.execute('SELECT question FROM runs WHERE id=?',('missing',)).fetchone()==('condition=None',)
    db.close()
print('practice: all4 input/result paths retained, including provider failure; HTTP/UI still separate')
```

## Expected reference observation

```text
offline application slice: draft, clarify, abstain, failure, durable scoped readback
practice: all4 input/result paths retained, including provider failure; HTTP/UI still separate
```

chapters.body:
# ai-agent-bootcamp: complete independent student capstone

## Product and prerequisite contract

Ask a supported refund question; an unsupported topic must abstain and a requested write must be denied. The bounded loop permits search and draft only, enforces evidence-before-draft and stops at its step budget. Confirm a stored draft with a reviewer and prove replay creates the same local receipt.

Sessions 4–6 define the model contract and budget; 7–9 teach source identity and grounding; 10–12 teach bounded actions and approval; 13–14 teach HTTP/data ownership; 16–20 teach tests, traces, containers and recovery.

The assembly mechanics below repair the previously missing connection between separate lesson examples. Read them before attempting the final project. Every file follows inline in the course; the optional program download contains the identical capstone/ directory. Python 3.12 and Docker Compose are required. There is no import from another academy program, Workshop checkout or private app database.

## Connect the pieces before changing them

1. Read core.py first. Its process(input, mode, documents) function returns a status, text and evidence IDs. It must never receive the expected test answer. The provider is a named scripted fixture, so a passing run proves control flow, not model quality.
2. Read app.py's exact and identity functions. Reject extra fields and blank input before retrieval. Demo bearer strings resolve to a trusted owner/role at the server; a JSON owner field is rejected. These published fixture tokens are local teaching identities, not production authentication.
3. Trace ask: validate → owner-filter persisted sources → core workflow → save result → return ID. A timeout is a stored failed result, not an empty successful answer. Health runs a real query against the required table.

10. check.py sends real HTTP requests and reads back their actual IDs. It tests changed approvals, wrong owners, malformed input, failures and concurrent duplicate review. import re

```python
VERSION='support-policy-v1'
POLICIES=[{'id':'refund-v1','text':'Refunds are available within 14 days for unopened items. Opened items are excluded.'}]
def scripted(observation):return {'name':'draft'} if observation else {'name':'search'}
def run(text,mode,decide=scripted,max_steps=2):

 observation=None;trace=['validate']

  action=decide(dict(observation) if observation else None)
  if type(action) is not dict or set(action)!={'name'}:raise ValueError('action_contract')
  name=action['name'];trace.append(name)
  if name=='search':

   if len(observation['text'])>512:raise ValueError('context')
  elif name=='draft':
   if not observation:raise ValueError('evidence_required')
   if mode=='timeout':raise TimeoutError('fixture')
   proposal={'text':observation['text'],'citations':[observation['id']]} if mode=='fixture' else {'text':'90 days','citations':['invented']}
   if set(proposal)!={'text','citations'} or proposal['citations']!=[observation['id']] or proposal['text']!=observation['text']:raise ValueError('provider_contract')
   return {'status':'needs_review',**proposal,'context_chars':len(observation['text']),'model':'scripted_fixture','trace':trace+['validated_draft','await_review']}
  else:return {'status':'denied','text':None,'citations':[],'trace':trace}

def process(text,mode,documents):
 terms=set(re.findall(r'[a-z]+',text.lower()))
 if terms & {'send','delete','issue','transfer'}:return {'status':'denied','text':None,'citations':[],'trace':['validate','deny_action']}
 if terms & {'ignore','override'}:return {'status':'abstain','text':None,'citations':[],'trace':['validate','untrusted_instruction']}

 return run(text,mode)
```

```python
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):run('refund','fixture',lambda o:{'name':'draft'})

    def test_proposal_shape_is_not_authority(self):

                run('refund','fixture',lambda o:action)
```

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to A multi-user AI service deployed from containers

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Load-test offered vs. completed work, p95 and cost per accepted result at stated concurrency. Autoscaling settings are hypotheses until observed against downstream/GPU limits.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Test readiness against the actual database, restart/readback, isolated restore, denied owner access, overload rejection and a dependency outage on the deployed revision.

### Context Management

Budget resident model memory/KV cache and per-request context separately. Keep tenant/revision-aware application caches; never assume a process-local cache is shared across replicas.

## Failure and deployment work

Separate request concurrency, worker capacity and model/GPU capacity. Add admission control, shared quotas, bounded queues, maximum instances and a documented fallback/stop budget.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

# Capstone evaluation and peer critique

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Capstone build: support-agent vertical slice**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Capstone build: support-agent vertical slice (`academy-v2:ai-agent-bootcamp:22`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Vertical slice** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: One complete user path through interface, API, application logic, storage and visible result.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **the support-agent release packet**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Package, hand over, and plan the next release**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Capstone evaluation and peer critique

## Before you begin

Complete sessions 1–22 in this bootcamp. Keep your policy fixtures and evaluation labels in your own workspace. The example below runs independently so a prior missing file cannot block understanding.

## Why this decision matters

A final review should challenge the strongest claim you are making. If you claim supported answers, inspect evidence support. If you claim reliable actions, repeat and interrupt them. If you claim useful time savings, measure the human review time as well as generation time. Define a rubric before reviewing the final output.

A peer review is useful because another person will make different assumptions. Give the reviewer setup instructions and an unfamiliar question, then observe where they struggle. Preserve critical feedback and the limitations that remain. Improvement is a traceable change and a rerun of relevant cases, not a rewritten success story.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Peer critique

A reviewer tests the project against explicit criteria and unfamiliar inputs.

### Disposition

A finding is fixed, deferred or rejected with a recorded reason and owner.

### Release evidence

Observed behavior for the exact candidate revision and evaluation set.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Peer critique

Peer critique asks another reviewer to judge a specific output against the same source and rubric. Record the initial disagreement before resolving it; otherwise the final labels hide a source of uncertainty. A delayed independent second pass can serve when no peer is available, but should be labeled as such rather than invented collaboration.

## Step 2 · Disposition

A disposition records what happens to a finding: fix, defer with owner, reject with reason or narrow the claim. Connect the correction to a regression case and rerun it. Editing the report to remove a failure is not fixing the candidate. Fresh untouched cases are required for a new generalization claim after tuning.

## Step 3 · Release evidence

Release evidence binds results to exact candidate and dataset revisions and retains critical failures. Seven supported and two correct abstentions do not cancel one unsupported answer. State the blocking rule before review, preserve the counterexample and make a scoped decision. “Peer reviewed” without the actual judgments and source basis proves very little.

## Worked implementation: Capstone evaluation and peer critique

## Walk through the data and decision

1. Ten reviewed synthetic cases include one critical unsupported answer.

2. That single counterexample blocks the current release despite nine favorable outcomes.

3. Fixes need a recorded disposition, rerun and fresh review rather than deletion of the original finding.

## Predict before running

Read the assertions and predict the output and rejected cases. Save the **entire** following block as `example.py` in a new scratch folder. Use Python 3.12; every import and synthetic fixture required for this example is included. Run `python3 -I example.py`. Assertions must be enabled; do not use `-O`. No model, network, database service or third-party package is required. SQLite examples create a temporary database and clean it up.

```python
review = [('supported',7),('correct_abstention',2),('unsupported_answer',1)]
total = sum(n for _,n in review)
critical = dict(review)['unsupported_answer']
assert total==10 and critical==1
report = {'dataset':'unseen-v1','candidate':'demo-r3','total':total,
          'supported':7,'correct_abstention':2,'critical_false_answers':critical,
          'promotion':'blocked pending review' if critical else 'review gates'}
assert report['promotion']=='blocked pending review'
print(report)
```

## Expected observation

```text
{'dataset': 'unseen-v1', 'candidate': 'demo-r3', 'total': 10, 'supported': 7, 'correct_abstention': 2, 'critical_false_answers': 1, 'promotion': 'blocked pending review'}
```

## Walk through the mechanism and its limits

The 9/10 superficially correct outcomes cannot erase the unsupported answer. Category counts preserve the nature of that failure. Candidate and dataset IDs make the result traceable. These are simulated reviewer labels, not actual measurements of your capstone; copy the report structure, not its scores. Once you tune on these cases, they are development evidence.

## Extend the example

Have a peer label one genuinely unfamiliar case and record disagreement before resolving it against policy text. Fix two findings, rerun the affected cases, and add fresh untouched cases for any new generalization claim.

The assertions demonstrate only the named local behavior. They do not execute your capstone, grade factual judgments, or prove that a real provider or external integration works.

Build a finding-disposition gate that keeps an unresolved critical issue blocking release even when another defect has a successful rerun.

## Build it yourself

1. Freeze a candidate revision and run the held-out evaluation set.
2. Have a reviewer assess setup, support, abstention, ownership, and failure handling using a written rubric.

4. Publish before-and-after results with sample size and remaining failures.

The reviewer submits a case outside the original scope. Record whether it reveals a legitimate gap or a new requirement rather than silently expanding the claimed release.

- Results include failure cases and denominators.

- Claims in the README match the observed evidence.

## Deliverable

## Failure and deployment work

## Evaluation precision

## Module evidence to retain

## Complete guided-practice reference

Save the entire block as solution.py in a new scratch directory. Use Python 3.12 and run `python3 -I solution.py` with assertions enabled. All imports and synthetic data are included. The Python checks use the standard library and no provider account. This reference covers the bounded practice, not the completed integration project.



```python
review = [('supported',7),('correct_abstention',2),('unsupported_answer',1)]
total = sum(n for _,n in review)
critical = dict(review)['unsupported_answer']
assert total==10 and critical==1
report = {'dataset':'unseen-v1','candidate':'demo-r3','total':total,
          'supported':7,'correct_abstention':2,'critical_false_answers':critical,
          'promotion':'blocked pending review' if critical else 'review gates'}
assert report['promotion']=='blocked pending review'

# Complete guided-practice reference change
findings=[{'id':'f1','critical':True,'disposition':'fix','rerun':'passed'},
          {'id':'f2','critical':True,'disposition':'deferred','rerun':'untested'}]
def blockers(rows):return [r['id'] for r in rows if r['critical'] and not(r['disposition']=='fix' and r['rerun']=='passed')]
assert blockers(findings)==['f2']
corrected=[dict(r,disposition='fix',rerun='passed') if r['id']=='f2' else r for r in findings]
assert blockers(corrected)==[] and findings[1]['rerun']=='untested'
print('practice: deferred critical issue blocks; original finding retained beside separately labeled correction')
```

```text
practice: deferred critical issue blocks; original finding retained beside separately labeled correction
```

chapters.body:
## Before you begin

Complete sessions 1–22 in this bootcamp. Keep your policy fixtures and evaluation labels in your own workspace. The example below runs independently so a prior missing file cannot block understanding.

## Why this decision matters

A final review should challenge the strongest claim you are making. If you claim supported answers, inspect evidence support. If you claim reliable actions, repeat and interrupt them. If you claim useful time savings, measure the human review time as well as generation time. Define a rubric before reviewing the final output.

A peer review is useful because another person will make different assumptions. Give the reviewer setup instructions and an unfamiliar question, then observe where they struggle. Preserve critical feedback and the limitations that remain. Improvement is a traceable change and a rerun of relevant cases, not a rewritten success story.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Peer critique

A reviewer tests the project against explicit criteria and unfamiliar inputs.

### Disposition

A finding is fixed, deferred or rejected with a recorded reason and owner.

### Release evidence

Observed behavior for the exact candidate revision and evaluation set.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Peer critique

Peer critique asks another reviewer to judge a specific output against the same source and rubric. Record the initial disagreement before resolving it; otherwise the final labels hide a source of uncertainty. A delayed independent second pass can serve when no peer is available, but should be labeled as such rather than invented collaboration.

## Step 2 · Disposition

A disposition records what happens to a finding: fix, defer with owner, reject with reason or narrow the claim. Connect the correction to a regression case and rerun it. Editing the report to remove a failure is not fixing the candidate. Fresh untouched cases are required for a new generalization claim after tuning.

## Step 3 · Release evidence

Release evidence binds results to exact candidate and dataset revisions and retains critical failures. Seven supported and two correct abstentions do not cancel one unsupported answer. State the blocking rule before review, preserve the counterexample and make a scoped decision. “Peer reviewed” without the actual judgments and source basis proves very little.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to A multi-user AI service deployed from containers

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Load-test offered vs. completed work, p95 and cost per accepted result at stated concurrency. Autoscaling settings are hypotheses until observed against downstream/GPU limits.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Test readiness against the actual database, restart/readback, isolated restore, denied owner access, overload rejection and a dependency outage on the deployed revision.

### Context Management

Budget resident model memory/KV cache and per-request context separately. Keep tenant/revision-aware application caches; never assume a process-local cache is shared across replicas.

## Failure and deployment work

Separate request concurrency, worker capacity and model/GPU capacity. Add admission control, shared quotas, bounded queues, maximum instances and a documented fallback/stop budget.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

- **packaging and recovery** — taught in Containerize the complete application, Failure recovery and release checklists. Evidence: retain those lessons’ successful case and negative check in the project report.

## Assemble, then test

Package the exact candidate evaluated in 22–23. Verify the file manifest, repeat setup in a fresh workspace and retain the recovery transcript. A missing or unresolved critical finding blocks the release decision.

## Feedback when integration fails

Find the first boundary whose actual output differs from its contract. Rerun that lesson’s isolated positive and negative checks. If they pass, inspect the connecting field names, owner/source IDs, units and state transitions; do not weaken the gold labels or bypass a denied path. Record the failing input and unresolved result. Passing a single variation does not establish the whole project.

## Completion boundary

Reopen the evidence packet in a fresh session. A complete program records both successful checks and remaining limits. Choose further study by the missing capability; another academy program is optional, not a hidden graduation prerequisite.

## Understand the decision: Package, hand over, and plan the next release

## Before you begin

Complete sessions 1–23 in this bootcamp. Keep your policy fixtures and evaluation labels in your own workspace. The example below runs independently so a prior missing file cannot block understanding.

## Why this decision matters

A finished learning project is understandable and reproducible without the author narrating every step. Package the problem brief, architecture, setup, evaluation report, threat model, operational runbook, and known limitations. Use fictional or permissioned examples in a portfolio. A model integration is optional; if present, document provider selection, consent, measured usage, and failure behavior.

Prioritize the next release from observed failures and user needs. Separate defects that undermine the current promise from optional extensions such as semantic retrieval, durable jobs, or MCP interoperability. Keep a short decision log so future changes do not undo deliberate constraints. The final artifact is a maintainable system and its evidence, not a claim of mastery.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Handover package

Setup, scope, architecture, evaluation, operations and limitations usable without the author present.

### Scoped claim

A statement of capability limited to the conditions actually tested.

### Evidence-driven backlog

Future work prioritized from observed defects and user needs with acceptance checks.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Handover package

A handover package contains executable setup, fixtures, declared dependencies, configuration names, operating instructions and evidence. A hash manifest identifies exact bytes but does not prove those files are sufficient. Ask a fresh operator to follow only the instructions, recording every intervention rather than quietly supplying missing assumptions.

## Step 2 · Scoped claim

A scoped claim says precisely what was tested: offline prototype, source revision, workload and remaining limitations. Detecting a changed fixture does not establish answer quality or production readiness. Link each user-facing promise to its observation and avoid converting synthetic data into a client success story.

## Step 3 · Evidence-driven backlog

An evidence-driven backlog starts with an observed gap and a falsifiable acceptance check. “Improve AI” cannot be verified; “retain input after API timeout and show failure on reload” can. Give the item a reason, owner and prerequisite. Prioritize missing release evidence and user harm before speculative integrations.

## Worked implementation: Package, hand over, and plan the next release

## Walk through the data and decision

1. The manifest hashes the actual written file bytes.

2. Changing policies.json produces exactly one changed-file result.

3. Hash verification says nothing about whether a fresh operator can run the workflow.

## Predict before running

Read the assertions and predict the output and rejected cases. Save the **entire** following block as `example.py` in a new scratch folder. Use Python 3.12; every import and synthetic fixture required for this example is included. Run `python3 -I example.py`. Assertions must be enabled; do not use `-O`. No model, network, database service or third-party package is required. SQLite examples create a temporary database and clean it up.

```python
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
import hashlib, json
with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    root=Path(folder)
    files={'README.txt':'Run python3 demo.py. Fake provider; no live calls.',
           'demo.py':'print("read-only offline demo")\n','policies.json':'[{"id":"returns-v1"}]'}
    for name,text in files.items(): (root/name).write_text(text,encoding='utf-8')
    manifest={name:hashlib.sha256((root/name).read_bytes()).hexdigest() for name in files}
    (root/'manifest.json').write_text(json.dumps(manifest),encoding='utf-8')
    assert all((root/name).is_file() for name in manifest)
    (root/'policies.json').write_text('[]',encoding='utf-8')
    changed=[name for name,digest in manifest.items() if hashlib.sha256((root/name).read_bytes()).hexdigest()!=digest]
    assert changed==['policies.json']
print('manifest detects changed fixture; hashes identify files, not teaching quality')
```

## Expected observation

```text
manifest detects changed fixture; hashes identify files, not teaching quality
```

## Walk through the mechanism and its limits

The manifest binds a release to exact setup and fixture bytes, helping a recipient detect drift. It cannot show the instructions are understandable or complete; that requires a fresh setup performed by another person. A hash also does not establish trustworthiness. Keep the release scope, failure evidence, access-removal steps and known gaps next to this manifest.

exercise.solution:
## Complete guided-practice reference

Save the entire block as solution.py in a new scratch directory. Use Python 3.12 and run `python3 -I solution.py` with assertions enabled. All imports and synthetic data are included. The Python checks use the standard library and no provider account. This reference covers the bounded practice, not the completed integration project.



```python
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
import hashlib, json
with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    root=Path(folder)
    files={'README.txt':'Run python3 demo.py. Fake provider; no live calls.',
           'demo.py':'print("read-only offline demo")\n','policies.json':'[{"id":"returns-v1"}]'}
    for name,text in files.items(): (root/name).write_text(text,encoding='utf-8')
    manifest={name:hashlib.sha256((root/name).read_bytes()).hexdigest() for name in files}
    (root/'manifest.json').write_text(json.dumps(manifest),encoding='utf-8')
    assert all((root/name).is_file() for name in manifest)
    (root/'policies.json').write_text('[]',encoding='utf-8')
    changed=[name for name,digest in manifest.items() if hashlib.sha256((root/name).read_bytes()).hexdigest()!=digest]
    assert changed==['policies.json']
print('manifest detects changed fixture; hashes identify files, not teaching quality')

# Complete guided-practice reference change
def package_gaps(root,expected):
    missing=[];changed=[]
    for name,fingerprint in expected.items():
        path=root/name
        if not path.is_file():missing.append(name)
        elif hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()!=fingerprint:changed.append(name)
    return {'missing':sorted(missing),'changed':sorted(changed)}
with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    root=Path(folder);(root/'a.txt').write_text('original');expected={'a.txt':hashlib.sha256(b'original').hexdigest(),'README.txt':'synthetic-expected'}
    assert package_gaps(root,expected)=={'missing':['README.txt'],'changed':[]}
    (root/'a.txt').write_text('edited')
    assert package_gaps(root,expected)['changed']==['a.txt']
backlog={'gap':'missing setup instructions','acceptance':'fresh operator runs the offline normal and timeout paths using README only; interventions recorded'}
assert 'timeout' in backlog['acceptance']
print('practice: missing and changed package entries separated; backlog tied to observable fresh-operator behavior')
```

## Expected reference observation

```text
manifest detects changed fixture; hashes identify files, not teaching quality
practice: missing and changed package entries separated; backlog tied to observable fresh-operator behavior
```

## If your result differs

If a missing file crashes verification, handle absence before hashing. Passing the verifier still requires the operator rehearsal; do not substitute an intact archive for a usable handover.

## Explain before continuing

Name the decision or invariant your change protects. Compare the baseline with your result, retain the failed case, and state what remains untested in the larger project.

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Capstone evaluation and peer critique**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Peer critique** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: A reviewer tests the project against explicit criteria and unfamiliar inputs.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **the support-agent release packet**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Taught-to-project evidence map

- **vertical slice and findings** — taught in Capstone build: support-agent vertical slice, Capstone evaluation and peer critique. Evidence: retain those lessons’ successful case and negative check in the project report.
- **packaging and recovery** — taught in Containerize the complete application, Failure recovery and release checklists. Evidence: retain those lessons’ successful case and negative check in the project report.

## Assemble, then test

Package the exact candidate evaluated in 22–23. Verify the file manifest, repeat setup in a fresh workspace and retain the recovery transcript. A missing or unresolved critical finding blocks the release decision.

## Feedback when integration fails

Find the first boundary whose actual output differs from its contract. Rerun that lesson’s isolated positive and negative checks. If they pass, inspect the connecting field names, owner/source IDs, units and state transitions; do not weaken the gold labels or bypass a denied path. Record the failing input and unresolved result. Passing a single variation does not establish the whole project.

## Completion boundary

Reopen the evidence packet in a fresh session. A complete program records both successful checks and remaining limits. Choose further study by the missing capability; another academy program is optional, not a hidden graduation prerequisite.

## Before you begin

Complete sessions 1–23 in this bootcamp. Keep your policy fixtures and evaluation labels in your own workspace. The example below runs independently so a prior missing file cannot block understanding.

## Why this decision matters

A finished learning project is understandable and reproducible without the author narrating every step. Package the problem brief, architecture, setup, evaluation report, threat model, operational runbook, and known limitations. Use fictional or permissioned examples in a portfolio. A model integration is optional; if present, document provider selection, consent, measured usage, and failure behavior.

Prioritize the next release from observed failures and user needs. Separate defects that undermine the current promise from optional extensions such as semantic retrieval, durable jobs, or MCP interoperability. Keep a short decision log so future changes do not undo deliberate constraints. The final artifact is a maintainable system and its evidence, not a claim of mastery.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Handover package

Setup, scope, architecture, evaluation, operations and limitations usable without the author present.

### Scoped claim

A statement of capability limited to the conditions actually tested.

### Evidence-driven backlog

Future work prioritized from observed defects and user needs with acceptance checks.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Handover package

A handover package contains executable setup, fixtures, declared dependencies, configuration names, operating instructions and evidence. A hash manifest identifies exact bytes but does not prove those files are sufficient. Ask a fresh operator to follow only the instructions, recording every intervention rather than quietly supplying missing assumptions.

## Step 2 · Scoped claim

A scoped claim says precisely what was tested: offline prototype, source revision, workload and remaining limitations. Detecting a changed fixture does not establish answer quality or production readiness. Link each user-facing promise to its observation and avoid converting synthetic data into a client success story.

## Step 3 · Evidence-driven backlog

An evidence-driven backlog starts with an observed gap and a falsifiable acceptance check. “Improve AI” cannot be verified; “retain input after API timeout and show failure on reload” can. Give the item a reason, owner and prerequisite. Prioritize missing release evidence and user harm before speculative integrations.

```python

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    root=Path(folder)
    files={'README.txt':'Run python3 demo.py. Fake provider; no live calls.',

    assert all((root/name).is_file() for name in manifest)
    (root/'policies.json').write_text('[]',encoding='utf-8')
```

## Expected observation

```text
manifest detects changed fixture; hashes identify files, not teaching quality
```

## Walk through the mechanism and its limits

The manifest binds a release to exact setup and fixture bytes, helping a recipient detect drift. It cannot show the instructions are understandable or complete; that requires a fresh setup performed by another person. A hash also does not establish trustworthiness. Keep the release scope, failure evidence, access-removal steps and known gaps next to this manifest.

## Extend the example

Have a peer follow only your README from a clean folder. Record every intervention you needed to make. Add a backlog item with an observable acceptance check for each missing assumption.

The assertions demonstrate only the named local behavior. They do not execute your capstone, grade factual judgments, or prove that a real provider or external integration works.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to A multi-user AI service deployed from containers

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Load-test offered vs. completed work, p95 and cost per accepted result at stated concurrency. Autoscaling settings are hypotheses until observed against downstream/GPU limits.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Test readiness against the actual database, restart/readback, isolated restore, denied owner access, overload rejection and a dependency outage on the deployed revision.

### Context Management

Budget resident model memory/KV cache and per-request context separately. Keep tenant/revision-aware application caches; never assume a process-local cache is shared across replicas.

## Failure and deployment work

Separate request concurrency, worker capacity and model/GPU capacity. Add admission control, shared quotas, bounded queues, maximum instances and a documented fallback/stop budget.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.
