lessons.title: Choose a workflow and a buyer
lessons.content:
# Choose a workflow and a buyer

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Describe a business workflow and read a table of inputs, outputs and costs. Python specimens are inspectable decision models: explain the values and expected result before running them. No client, paid model account or prior academy program is required. Coding syntax must be learned before modifying the optional code; business deliverables remain required.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **a buyer/workflow brief with a measured baseline**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Conduct discovery with evidence**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Choose a workflow and a buyer

## Before you begin

Start with one working draft/review workflow. Use the fictional training-provider engagement; no real client or outreach is required.

## Why this decision matters

A service offer connects a specific buyer to a recurring problem you can credibly address. “I build AI agents” describes a method, not a customer outcome. Choose a workflow you understand well enough to observe its inputs, handoffs, exceptions, and cost of mistakes. Identify who experiences the pain, who approves the work, and who will use the result; these may be three different people.

Start with a low-risk read-only or draft workflow. Do not promise autonomous decisions, regulated advice, or operational savings before measuring the process. Your first goal is to establish whether the problem is frequent, costly enough to matter, and accessible with permissioned data. A simulated client is sufficient for the program exercises.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Buyer

The person or role authorized to approve the commercial engagement.

### End user

The person who performs or benefits from the workflow in daily use.

### Problem hypothesis

An unverified claim about recurring pain that discovery must investigate.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Buyer

A buyer owns the decision to fund or authorize a workflow change. The person feeling the pain may lack budget authority. Map the operations lead’s decision, the evidence they need and unresolved authority before writing an offer. A role title is a hypothesis about responsibility, not proof that someone can approve the pilot.

## Step 2 · End user

An end user performs the workflow and experiences its corrections, waiting and exceptions. Here the assistant prepares a draft while the instructor reviews teaching facts. Saving assistant time can increase instructor effort. Observe both roles and ensure review capacity exists; otherwise faster drafting merely moves the bottleneck.

## Step 3 · Problem hypothesis

A problem hypothesis is a testable claim about frequency, effort, consequence and willingness to change. Forty monthly handouts is explicitly unverified in the specimen. Choose a discovery question that could disconfirm the opportunity. If volume falls or review capacity disappears, revisit the workflow instead of forcing an AI service into it.

## Buyer, workflow, and economic unit

### Start with the unit of work
A service becomes specific when it names one repeatable unit: a support ticket, a purchase record, or a participant handout. Write its trigger, input, current operator, output, and completion rule. A department is too large a unit for a first pilot. A single generated sentence is too small if it cannot finish an actual handoff. Use the fictional training provider throughout this course: the unit is one reviewed handout made from approved course notes.

### Separate three customers
The operator feels the friction, the operational owner is accountable for quality, and the budget owner can fund a change. An instructor may like your demo while the operations lead cannot provide source access and finance has not agreed to recurring costs. Draw three columns and put a named role in each. A single person may occupy multiple columns, but never infer authority from enthusiasm. Ask who accepts the deliverable and who maintains it after you leave.

### Score feasibility without hiding uncertainty
Use four gates before scoring attractiveness: permission to use representative inputs, an observable output standard, a reviewer with time, and a reversible fallback. Failure of a gate means investigate or decline. For opportunities that pass, compare monthly volume, minutes of avoidable work, cost of a wrong accepted output, and your familiarity with the workflow. Keep evidence and assumptions in separate fields. A score of four based on an assumption is not stronger evidence than a score of two based on observation.

### Worked opportunity comparison
Suppose course handouts occur 40 times a month, take 20 minutes each, and always receive instructor review. A payroll adjustment occurs 10 times, takes 8 minutes, and can move money. Even if payroll looks easier to automate technically, the first engagement has a more reversible draft boundary. Choose the handout workflow because you can observe review quality and stop before distribution. The decision is about the test you can run, not the most impressive demo.

### Write a falsifiable offer hypothesis
Use: “For [operator], we will test whether [bounded workflow] improves [observable measure], while [guardrail] stays within [limit], using [permitted inputs].” Add what would disprove it. For the training provider, a failed hypothesis might be that source notes are too incomplete for a reviewer to accept drafts without rewriting. That result should trigger source cleanup or a different service, rather than a stronger prompt.

### Practice record
Create rows for unit, operator, owner, authorizer, monthly volume, evidence source, unknown, and next test. Complete three candidate workflows. Select one and explain which missing fact could reverse your decision. Your output is a defensible opportunity choice; it is not evidence that someone will buy it.

## A workflow selection memo

## Walk through the data and decision

1. The candidate table separates volume assumptions from permission and error consequence.

2. The assistant operates, instructor reviews and operations lead owns the pilot decision.

3. No confirmed budget authority or reviewer availability exists yet.

## Completed specimen: A workflow selection memo

| Candidate | Frequency assumption | Permission/access | Consequence of error | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Handout preparation | 40/month, unverified | Approved text notes only | Instructor catches a false teaching claim | Investigate |
| Automatic assessment grading | 200/month, unverified | Learner records not authorized | Incorrect learner outcome | Exclude from first pilot |
| Course announcement drafting | 4/month, unverified | Public fact sheet | Incorrect dates or promises | Possible alternative |

**Selected hypothesis:** the operations lead may value a source-linked handout draft for one course template. The course assistant operates it, the instructor approves teaching facts, and the operations lead owns the pilot decision. Budget authority is unresolved; instructor availability is also unverified.

**Decision:** conduct discovery before offering a saving. The first candidate has enough possible volume to investigate, not enough evidence to sell a fixed outcome. If instructors cannot review outputs, stop or choose a different workflow.

## Critique and transfer

Change handout volume to two per month and review capacity to zero. Re-score all three candidates, explain the trade-off, and identify a different buyer question rather than forcing the original offer.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

## Practice first, then integrate

## Bounded first practice

Reassess the offer when handout volume is two per month and instructor review capacity is zero. Write a stop/rescope decision and the next disconfirming question.

## Practice acceptance

- The completed baseline/specimen is explained using the lesson walkthrough, with fixture assumptions distinguished from observations.
- Reassess the offer when handout volume is two per month and instructor review capacity is zero. Write a stop/rescope decision and the next disconfirming question.
- The decision and counterexample are recorded with evidence and remaining uncertainty; simulated and observed results are labeled.

## Integrate after practice

## Worked example

A fictional training provider spends hours turning approved course notes into participant handouts. The operations lead owns the process; instructors review factual content; finance approves spending. Your offer could be a draft-and-review workflow for one course format, rather than “AI transformation for the whole company.”

## Build it yourself

1. Choose three familiar industries and one recurring workflow in each.
2. Map user, operational owner, budget owner, and reviewer for each workflow.
3. Score frequency, data access, error cost, and your relevant experience using stated assumptions.
4. Select one simulated client and write a narrow problem hypothesis.

## Break it deliberately

The person who likes your demo cannot authorize data access or budget. Revise your discovery plan to involve the missing decision maker.

## Acceptance checks

- The offer names a buyer and an end user.
- The problem is described independently of a tool.
- Important unknowns are labeled as hypotheses.

## Deliverable

Save **`client-01/opportunity-brief.md`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

## Full project sequence

1. Choose three familiar industries and one recurring workflow in each.
2. Map user, operational owner, budget owner, and reviewer for each workflow.
3. Score frequency, data access, error cost, and your relevant experience using stated assumptions.
4. Select one simulated client and write a narrow problem hypothesis.

## Integration acceptance

- The offer names a buyer and an end user.
- The problem is described independently of a tool.
- Important unknowns are labeled as hypotheses.

## Apply the three engineering pillars

## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to a discovery interview and opportunity scorecard

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Estimate response time, reviewer effort and cost of the current workflow; mark interview assumptions separately from observations. Compare at least two opportunities against a minimum accepted-output standard.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Turn interview claims into falsifiable workflow checks: input availability, reviewer authority and a repeated task. Reject an opportunity without usable evidence.

### Context Management

Inventory which approved source notes the workflow actually needs; exclude unrelated personal/client data and record source ownership.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

chapters.title: Understand the decision: Choose a workflow and a buyer
chapters.body:
## Before you begin

Start with one working draft/review workflow. Use the fictional training-provider engagement; no real client or outreach is required.

## Why this decision matters

A service offer connects a specific buyer to a recurring problem you can credibly address. “I build AI agents” describes a method, not a customer outcome. Choose a workflow you understand well enough to observe its inputs, handoffs, exceptions, and cost of mistakes. Identify who experiences the pain, who approves the work, and who will use the result; these may be three different people.

Start with a low-risk read-only or draft workflow. Do not promise autonomous decisions, regulated advice, or operational savings before measuring the process. Your first goal is to establish whether the problem is frequent, costly enough to matter, and accessible with permissioned data. A simulated client is sufficient for the program exercises.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Buyer

The person or role authorized to approve the commercial engagement.

### End user

The person who performs or benefits from the workflow in daily use.

### Problem hypothesis

An unverified claim about recurring pain that discovery must investigate.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Buyer

A buyer owns the decision to fund or authorize a workflow change. The person feeling the pain may lack budget authority. Map the operations lead’s decision, the evidence they need and unresolved authority before writing an offer. A role title is a hypothesis about responsibility, not proof that someone can approve the pilot.

## Step 2 · End user

An end user performs the workflow and experiences its corrections, waiting and exceptions. Here the assistant prepares a draft while the instructor reviews teaching facts. Saving assistant time can increase instructor effort. Observe both roles and ensure review capacity exists; otherwise faster drafting merely moves the bottleneck.

## Step 3 · Problem hypothesis

A problem hypothesis is a testable claim about frequency, effort, consequence and willingness to change. Forty monthly handouts is explicitly unverified in the specimen. Choose a discovery question that could disconfirm the opportunity. If volume falls or review capacity disappears, revisit the workflow instead of forcing an AI service into it.

chapters.title: Buyer, workflow, and economic unit
chapters.body:
### Start with the unit of work
A service becomes specific when it names one repeatable unit: a support ticket, a purchase record, or a participant handout. Write its trigger, input, current operator, output, and completion rule. A department is too large a unit for a first pilot. A single generated sentence is too small if it cannot finish an actual handoff. Use the fictional training provider throughout this course: the unit is one reviewed handout made from approved course notes.

### Separate three customers
The operator feels the friction, the operational owner is accountable for quality, and the budget owner can fund a change. An instructor may like your demo while the operations lead cannot provide source access and finance has not agreed to recurring costs. Draw three columns and put a named role in each. A single person may occupy multiple columns, but never infer authority from enthusiasm. Ask who accepts the deliverable and who maintains it after you leave.

### Score feasibility without hiding uncertainty
Use four gates before scoring attractiveness: permission to use representative inputs, an observable output standard, a reviewer with time, and a reversible fallback. Failure of a gate means investigate or decline. For opportunities that pass, compare monthly volume, minutes of avoidable work, cost of a wrong accepted output, and your familiarity with the workflow. Keep evidence and assumptions in separate fields. A score of four based on an assumption is not stronger evidence than a score of two based on observation.

### Worked opportunity comparison
Suppose course handouts occur 40 times a month, take 20 minutes each, and always receive instructor review. A payroll adjustment occurs 10 times, takes 8 minutes, and can move money. Even if payroll looks easier to automate technically, the first engagement has a more reversible draft boundary. Choose the handout workflow because you can observe review quality and stop before distribution. The decision is about the test you can run, not the most impressive demo.

### Write a falsifiable offer hypothesis
Use: “For [operator], we will test whether [bounded workflow] improves [observable measure], while [guardrail] stays within [limit], using [permitted inputs].” Add what would disprove it. For the training provider, a failed hypothesis might be that source notes are too incomplete for a reviewer to accept drafts without rewriting. That result should trigger source cleanup or a different service, rather than a stronger prompt.

### Practice record
Create rows for unit, operator, owner, authorizer, monthly volume, evidence source, unknown, and next test. Complete three candidate workflows. Select one and explain which missing fact could reverse your decision. Your output is a defensible opportunity choice; it is not evidence that someone will buy it.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to a discovery interview and opportunity scorecard

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Estimate response time, reviewer effort and cost of the current workflow; mark interview assumptions separately from observations. Compare at least two opportunities against a minimum accepted-output standard.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Turn interview claims into falsifiable workflow checks: input availability, reviewer authority and a repeated task. Reject an opportunity without usable evidence.

### Context Management

Inventory which approved source notes the workflow actually needs; exclude unrelated personal/client data and record source ownership.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

# Conduct discovery with evidence

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Choose a workflow and a buyer**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Choose a workflow and a buyer (`academy-v2:freelancing-masterclass:01`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Buyer** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: The person or role authorized to approve the commercial engagement.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **a buyer/workflow brief with a measured baseline**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Measure the baseline and the decision value**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Conduct discovery with evidence

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–1 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

Discovery is an investigation of how work actually happens. Ask for a recent concrete example, the steps performed, exception cases, review effort, and consequences of a mistake. Avoid leading questions that only confirm enthusiasm for AI. Capture what was observed separately from the client’s interpretation and your own assumptions.

If no real client is available, use the supplied fictional engagement scenario and role-play the interview. Do not present invented interview results as customer validation. A useful discovery record includes unanswered questions and a reason the project might not be suitable. Permission to discuss a workflow is not permission to copy or upload its documents.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Observation

Something directly seen or heard in the actual discovery exercise.

### Interpretation

Your explanation of what an observation might mean.

### Disconfirming evidence

An observation that would weaken the proposed problem or solution hypothesis.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Observation

An observation records what was actually seen or said, including source, date, sample and permission. A participant saying “daily” is an observed statement, not an observed daily count. A role-play must remain labeled simulated. Keep the raw statement alongside the sampled files so disagreement stays inspectable.

## Step 2 · Interpretation

An interpretation explains what the observation might mean. Two files could imply low volume or an incomplete folder. Do not average those possibilities into a fabricated monthly estimate. Ask about the unit of work and sample coverage before using numbers in a benefit calculation or commercial promise.

## Step 3 · Disconfirming evidence

Disconfirming evidence would weaken the proposed service: no recurring task, no authorized inputs, no reviewer or corrections costing more than manual preparation. Ask for a recent exception and invite a reason not to automate. Leading questions such as “Would AI save you time?” collect approval language rather than operational evidence.

## Discovery interviews and evidence synthesis

### Observe the work before proposing a solution
A discovery interview should reconstruct a recent completed case. Start with “Show me the last handout you prepared.” Ask which source arrived, how the operator decided what to include, which correction took longest, who approved it, and what happened after approval. Follow the artifact through the workflow. Asking whether AI would help invites a prediction; observing a recent correction gives you evidence.

### Use an interview sequence
Begin with context and permission. Move to a specific recent example. Trace its normal path. Ask for an exception and its consequence. Identify the people and systems involved. Finish by summarizing your understanding and asking what you missed. Keep questions neutral: “What happens when a note is incomplete?” gives more information than “Would automatic completion solve missing notes?” The latter hides the possibility that completing missing information is unacceptable.

### Keep an evidence ledger
Use four columns: observation, interpretation, assumption, and unresolved question. “The instructor corrected three objectives in the example” is an observation. “Objectives are the largest source of rework” is an interpretation requiring more examples. “This happens every week” is an assumption until you inspect records or hear a supported account. Write a source and date beside each observation. Mark role-play data as simulated.

### Resolve disagreement instead of averaging it
An operator says review takes ten minutes; a manager says two. Both can be describing different intervals. Ask each to identify start and end events. One may count source lookup while the other measures only approval clicks. Define a common timing rule, observe a case, and keep the disagreement in the record until resolved. Do not average incompatible measurements into a confident six-minute baseline.

### Handle access as a separate decision
Permission to discuss a document is not permission to upload it. Use a redacted or synthetic sample during initial discovery. Record who can authorize production access, which fields can leave the organization, and whether provider processing is permitted. If those answers are missing, your next deliverable may be a data-access map rather than a prototype.

### Interview exercise
Role-play an operator who wants faster drafts and an instructor whose main problem is factual errors. Ask eight questions without proposing a product. Produce a current-state map, three observations, two contradictions, one disconfirming finding, and a follow-up test. A good discovery summary can recommend no build when the bottleneck is approval ownership rather than text generation.

## A discovery evidence ledger

## Walk through the data and decision

1. D1 is a simulated statement; D2 is a limited simulated sample.

2. D3 times only one walkthrough, not a representative workflow population.

3. D4 remains an assumption until correction effort is compared.

## Completed specimen: A discovery evidence ledger

| ID | Evidence type | Record | Interpretation | Next action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | Role-play statement | “We do handouts daily.” | Volume may be high | Define what counts as one handout |
| D2 | Simulated observed sample | Two handouts in last month’s sample folder | Sample may be incomplete | Ask for the full count, with permission |
| D3 | Role-play walkthrough | 12 min preparing, 8 min reviewing one note | Review is 40% of this example | Time four more examples |
| D4 | Assumption | Faster drafting reduces review | Could be false | Compare correction time in pilot |

**Follow-up:** “Which steps and documents did you include when you said daily? Were those two files representative or just the available sample?” This asks for definitions without accusing the participant of being wrong.

**Finding:** frequency remains unknown. Do not average “daily” and “two” or describe this role-play as a customer interview. A recent example gives a testable workflow, not proof of demand.

## Critique and transfer

Write eight non-leading questions and role-play a recent exception. Produce separate observation, interpretation and assumption columns; include one answer that would make you decline.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

2. Run a role-play or a permissioned interview without recording by default.

exercise.solution:
## Complete guided-practice reference

Attempt the changed case first, then compare your reasoning with this completed response. This is a worked decision under stated assumptions, not evidence of performed client work.

## Completed interview and evidence correction

Ask: (1) Walk me through the last handout. (2) What counted as finished? (3) Which source files did you use? (4) What required correction? (5) Who approved it? (6) Which cases took longer? (7) What work is missing from this folder? (8) What would make you keep the manual process?

**Role-play answer:** “The two files were final exports; we revised each several times.”

| Record | Type | Permitted conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| Participant says two exports had revisions | Simulated statement | Exports may undercount preparation work |
| Revisions might explain “daily” | Interpretation | Need revision history/count definition |
| Revision count and time unknown | Assumption gap | Do not calculate monthly savings yet |

**Decline condition:** required source/revision access cannot be authorized, or no reviewer can verify teaching facts. Next observation: a permissioned walkthrough of one revision chain. No real interview was conducted by this specimen.

## If your result differs

If daily becomes a numeric monthly fact, the evidence gap was concealed. Eight questions are useful only when they resolve concrete uncertainties.

## Explain before continuing

Name the decision or invariant your change protects. Compare the baseline with your result, retain the failed case, and state what remains untested in the larger project.

chapters.title: Understand the decision: Conduct discovery with evidence
chapters.body:
## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–1 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

Discovery is an investigation of how work actually happens. Ask for a recent concrete example, the steps performed, exception cases, review effort, and consequences of a mistake. Avoid leading questions that only confirm enthusiasm for AI. Capture what was observed separately from the client’s interpretation and your own assumptions.

If no real client is available, use the supplied fictional engagement scenario and role-play the interview. Do not present invented interview results as customer validation. A useful discovery record includes unanswered questions and a reason the project might not be suitable. Permission to discuss a workflow is not permission to copy or upload its documents.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Observation

Something directly seen or heard in the actual discovery exercise.

### Interpretation

Your explanation of what an observation might mean.

### Disconfirming evidence

An observation that would weaken the proposed problem or solution hypothesis.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Observation

An observation records what was actually seen or said, including source, date, sample and permission. A participant saying “daily” is an observed statement, not an observed daily count. A role-play must remain labeled simulated. Keep the raw statement alongside the sampled files so disagreement stays inspectable.

## Step 2 · Interpretation

An interpretation explains what the observation might mean. Two files could imply low volume or an incomplete folder. Do not average those possibilities into a fabricated monthly estimate. Ask about the unit of work and sample coverage before using numbers in a benefit calculation or commercial promise.

## Step 3 · Disconfirming evidence

Disconfirming evidence would weaken the proposed service: no recurring task, no authorized inputs, no reviewer or corrections costing more than manual preparation. Ask for a recent exception and invite a reason not to automate. Leading questions such as “Would AI save you time?” collect approval language rather than operational evidence.

chapters.title: Discovery interviews and evidence synthesis
chapters.body:
### Observe the work before proposing a solution
A discovery interview should reconstruct a recent completed case. Start with “Show me the last handout you prepared.” Ask which source arrived, how the operator decided what to include, which correction took longest, who approved it, and what happened after approval. Follow the artifact through the workflow. Asking whether AI would help invites a prediction; observing a recent correction gives you evidence.

### Use an interview sequence
Begin with context and permission. Move to a specific recent example. Trace its normal path. Ask for an exception and its consequence. Identify the people and systems involved. Finish by summarizing your understanding and asking what you missed. Keep questions neutral: “What happens when a note is incomplete?” gives more information than “Would automatic completion solve missing notes?” The latter hides the possibility that completing missing information is unacceptable.

### Keep an evidence ledger
Use four columns: observation, interpretation, assumption, and unresolved question. “The instructor corrected three objectives in the example” is an observation. “Objectives are the largest source of rework” is an interpretation requiring more examples. “This happens every week” is an assumption until you inspect records or hear a supported account. Write a source and date beside each observation. Mark role-play data as simulated.

### Resolve disagreement instead of averaging it
An operator says review takes ten minutes; a manager says two. Both can be describing different intervals. Ask each to identify start and end events. One may count source lookup while the other measures only approval clicks. Define a common timing rule, observe a case, and keep the disagreement in the record until resolved. Do not average incompatible measurements into a confident six-minute baseline.

### Handle access as a separate decision
Permission to discuss a document is not permission to upload it. Use a redacted or synthetic sample during initial discovery. Record who can authorize production access, which fields can leave the organization, and whether provider processing is permitted. If those answers are missing, your next deliverable may be a data-access map rather than a prototype.

### Interview exercise
Role-play an operator who wants faster drafts and an instructor whose main problem is factual errors. Ask eight questions without proposing a product. Produce a current-state map, three observations, two contradictions, one disconfirming finding, and a follow-up test. A good discovery summary can recommend no build when the bottleneck is approval ownership rather than text generation.

## Completed specimen: A discovery evidence ledger

| ID | Evidence type | Record | Interpretation | Next action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | Role-play statement | “We do handouts daily.” | Volume may be high | Define what counts as one handout |
| D2 | Simulated observed sample | Two handouts in last month’s sample folder | Sample may be incomplete | Ask for the full count, with permission |
| D3 | Role-play walkthrough | 12 min preparing, 8 min reviewing one note | Review is 40% of this example | Time four more examples |
| D4 | Assumption | Faster drafting reduces review | Could be false | Compare correction time in pilot |

**Follow-up:** “Which steps and documents did you include when you said daily? Were those two files representative or just the available sample?” This asks for definitions without accusing the participant of being wrong.

**Finding:** frequency remains unknown. Do not average “daily” and “two” or describe this role-play as a customer interview. A recent example gives a testable workflow, not proof of demand.

## Critique and transfer

Write eight non-leading questions and role-play a recent exception. Produce separate observation, interpretation and assumption columns; include one answer that would make you decline.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to a discovery interview and opportunity scorecard

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Estimate response time, reviewer effort and cost of the current workflow; mark interview assumptions separately from observations. Compare at least two opportunities against a minimum accepted-output standard.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Turn interview claims into falsifiable workflow checks: input availability, reviewer authority and a repeated task. Reject an opportunity without usable evidence.

### Context Management

Inventory which approved source notes the workflow actually needs; exclude unrelated personal/client data and record source ownership.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

lessons.content:
# Measure the baseline and the decision value

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Conduct discovery with evidence**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Conduct discovery with evidence (`academy-v2:freelancing-masterclass:02`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Observation** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: Something directly seen or heard in the actual discovery exercise.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **a buyer/workflow brief with a measured baseline**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Package a service with a bounded outcome**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Measure the baseline and the decision value

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–2 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

A business case should count the work that remains after automation. Measure preparation, generation, correction, approval, and exception handling separately. Time saved is only one possible outcome: consistency, turnaround, accessibility, or traceability may matter more. State the denominator and uncertainty in any estimate.

Use a range rather than a single optimistic forecast. Do not assume every generated output is usable or every saved minute becomes cash. A pilot should test the most important uncertain assumption. Choose measures that you can observe in a small engagement and that the buyer agrees are relevant.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Net time benefit

Baseline effort minus assisted processing, review, exception and other required work.

### Scenario range

Conservative, expected and optimistic outcomes based on explicit assumptions.

### Pilot success measure

An observable result agreed to test a material uncertainty.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Net time benefit

Net time benefit subtracts assisted preparation, routine review, incremental exception work and maintenance from the comparable manual workload. Keep task definitions and time units the same. The specimen’s 90 minutes is capacity released under assumptions; it is not cash income and does not guarantee those minutes can be redeployed.

## Step 2 · Scenario range

A scenario range changes uncertain drivers while keeping the model structure fixed. More review and exceptions can make benefit negative even when generation is fast. Distinguish routine review from extra exception time to avoid double counting. Show which assumption flips the sign before offering a fixed saving.

## Step 3 · Pilot success measure

A pilot success measure declares the acceptance rule and observation window before running. Measure all attempts and correction time on comparable inputs, with separate reviewed quality and support thresholds. A small synthetic sample teaches the method; it cannot justify a future client saving without representative workload and authorized observation.

## Baseline measurement and sensitivity analysis

### Specify the measurement contract
Define the unit, start event, stop event, sample selection, and exception policy before timing. For handouts, start when approved notes are available and stop when an instructor accepts a distributable draft. Include source lookup, correction, and rework. Measuring only model response time would omit most of the business workflow. Record individual cases rather than one remembered average.

### Calculate net benefit
Use an illustrative model: net monthly minutes = volume × (manual minutes − assisted preparation − assisted review − exception proportion × exception minutes) − monthly maintenance. The units must agree. If volume is 40, manual work 20, assisted preparation 4, review 10, exception proportion 0.2, exception work 15, and maintenance 30, the result is 40 × (20 − 4 − 10 − 3) − 30 = 90 minutes. It is not the 640 minutes implied by comparing manual work with generation alone.

### Distinguish capacity from cash
Ninety minutes returned to a salaried team is capacity, not automatically money saved. It may support faster response or additional work; it becomes a cash saving only under a separately justified staffing or expense change. Report time and financial assumptions separately. Do not multiply every saved minute by a billable rate and label the result profit.

### Stress the uncertain inputs
Run conservative, expected, and optimistic cases. Change review effort and exception rate first if those were unmeasured. With review at 14 minutes and exceptions at 30%, the same workflow can have negative benefit. That observation is useful: your pilot should measure review and exception cost before you promise scale. Use ranges to choose the next experiment, not to make a weak case look precise.

### Use paired comparisons carefully
Where possible, compare manual and assisted handling on comparable cases, with the same quality rubric. Avoid training the operator on every test case and then claiming general improvement. Keep some unseen cases for the final check. Report sample size, case mix, median time, range, and material failures. A small pilot guides a local decision; it does not establish universal productivity gains.

### Decision exercise
Build a table with ten synthetic cases, observed stages, error types, and acceptance outcomes. Calculate benefit after exceptions and maintenance. Identify the input at which benefit crosses zero. Write a stop rule such as “If more than two of ten drafts require reconstruction, investigate source quality before extending the pilot.” Explain the uncertainty that remains.

## An editable benefit model with a stop decision

## Walk through the data and decision

1. Manual 40×20 is 800 minutes; assisted routine 560 plus exceptions 120 plus maintenance 30 leaves 90.

2. The conservative assumptions produce−130 and optimistic assumptions 230.

3. The sign change makes review/exception measurement decisive.

## Completed specimen: An editable benefit model with a stop decision

All inputs below are illustrative monthly assumptions.

| Item | Calculation | Minutes |
|---|---|---:|
| Manual workflow | 40 × (12 preparation + 8 review) | 800 |
| Assisted routine work | 40 × (4 preparation + 10 review) | 560 |
| Additional exception work | 40 × 0.20 × 15 | 120 |
| Maintenance | fixed monthly allowance | 30 |
| Net benefit | 800 − 560 − 120 − 30 | **90** |

Exception time here is **incremental** beyond routine review. If your measured exception duration already includes normal review, subtract the overlap rather than count it twice. Ninety minutes is capacity released, not automatically cash saved.

Conservative case: review 14 minutes and exception rate 0.30 gives 800 − 720 − 180 − 30 = **−130 minutes**. exercise.solution:
## Complete guided-practice reference

Attempt the changed case first, then compare your reasoning with this completed response. This is a worked decision under stated assumptions, not evidence of performed client work.

## Completed calculation and decision

- Conservative: `40*(20-4-14-0.30*15)-30 = -130 minutes/month`.
- Break-even review at 20% exceptions: `20-4-0.20*15-30/40 = 12.25 minutes/note`.
- Holding the other assumptions fixed, review above 12.25 minutes makes net benefit negative.

**Decision:** do not promise a saving. Run the declared observation window and stop/rescope if measured net benefit is nonpositive or factual-review gates fail. Record sample size and whether exception minutes overlap ordinary review. The values are worked assumptions, not observed client data.

A sheet can use cells B2 volume, B3 manual minutes, B4 assisted preparation, B5 review, B6 exception fraction, B7 incremental exception minutes and B8 maintenance: `=B2*(B3-B4-B5-B6*B7)-B8`.

```python
def net_minutes(volume,manual,prepare,review,exception_fraction,extra_exception,maintenance):
    return volume*(manual-prepare-review-exception_fraction*extra_exception)-maintenance
assert net_minutes(40,20,4,14,.30,15,30)==-130
break_even=20-4-.20*15-30/40
assert break_even==12.25 and net_minutes(40,20,4,break_even,.20,15,30)==0
assert net_minutes(40,20,4,10,.20,15,30)==90
print('conservative=-130 minutes; break_even_review=12.25 minutes; base=90 minutes; all illustrative')
```

## Expected reference observation

```text
conservative=-130 minutes; break_even_review=12.25 minutes; base=90 minutes; all illustrative
```

## If your result differs

If the conservative case stays positive, inspect review and exception subtraction. If the result is called revenue, released time has been mistaken for money.

## Explain before continuing

Name the decision or invariant your change protects. Compare the baseline with your result, retain the failed case, and state what remains untested in the larger project.

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–2 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

A business case should count the work that remains after automation. Measure preparation, generation, correction, approval, and exception handling separately. Time saved is only one possible outcome: consistency, turnaround, accessibility, or traceability may matter more. State the denominator and uncertainty in any estimate.

Use a range rather than a single optimistic forecast. Do not assume every generated output is usable or every saved minute becomes cash. A pilot should test the most important uncertain assumption. Choose measures that you can observe in a small engagement and that the buyer agrees are relevant.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Net time benefit

Baseline effort minus assisted processing, review, exception and other required work.

### Scenario range

Conservative, expected and optimistic outcomes based on explicit assumptions.

### Pilot success measure

An observable result agreed to test a material uncertainty.

chapters.title: Baseline measurement and sensitivity analysis
chapters.body:
### Specify the measurement contract
Define the unit, start event, stop event, sample selection, and exception policy before timing. For handouts, start when approved notes are available and stop when an instructor accepts a distributable draft. Include source lookup, correction, and rework. Measuring only model response time would omit most of the business workflow. Record individual cases rather than one remembered average.

### Calculate net benefit
Use an illustrative model: net monthly minutes = volume × (manual minutes − assisted preparation − assisted review − exception proportion × exception minutes) − monthly maintenance. The units must agree. If volume is 40, manual work 20, assisted preparation 4, review 10, exception proportion 0.2, exception work 15, and maintenance 30, the result is 40 × (20 − 4 − 10 − 3) − 30 = 90 minutes. It is not the 640 minutes implied by comparing manual work with generation alone.

### Distinguish capacity from cash
Ninety minutes returned to a salaried team is capacity, not automatically money saved. It may support faster response or additional work; it becomes a cash saving only under a separately justified staffing or expense change. Report time and financial assumptions separately. Do not multiply every saved minute by a billable rate and label the result profit.

### Stress the uncertain inputs
Run conservative, expected, and optimistic cases. Change review effort and exception rate first if those were unmeasured. With review at 14 minutes and exceptions at 30%, the same workflow can have negative benefit. That observation is useful: your pilot should measure review and exception cost before you promise scale. Use ranges to choose the next experiment, not to make a weak case look precise.

### Use paired comparisons carefully
Where possible, compare manual and assisted handling on comparable cases, with the same quality rubric. Avoid training the operator on every test case and then claiming general improvement. Keep some unseen cases for the final check. Report sample size, case mix, median time, range, and material failures. A small pilot guides a local decision; it does not establish universal productivity gains.

### Decision exercise
Build a table with ten synthetic cases, observed stages, error types, and acceptance outcomes. Calculate benefit after exceptions and maintenance. Identify the input at which benefit crosses zero. Write a stop rule such as “If more than two of ten drafts require reconstruction, investigate source quality before extending the pilot.” Explain the uncertainty that remains.

# Package a service with a bounded outcome

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Measure the baseline and the decision value**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Measure the baseline and the decision value (`academy-v2:freelancing-masterclass:03`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Net time benefit** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: Baseline effort minus assisted processing, review, exception and other required work.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **an offer, statement of work and estimate**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Write a statement of work with acceptance tests**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Package a service with a bounded outcome

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–3 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

A well-scoped service describes deliverables, supported inputs, exclusions, dependencies, and acceptance. It should be understandable without knowing which model or framework you use. Package a diagnostic, a pilot, and a possible expansion separately so the client can make a decision after seeing evidence.

Your offer must align with what you can support. If you have only tested plain English text, do not include arbitrary PDFs, scans, voice notes, and multilingual documents under “document automation.” Make the reviewer’s role and the manual fallback visible. A bounded promise is more credible and easier to price than an open-ended commitment to improve everything.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Service package

A bounded outcome with supported inputs, deliverables, exclusions and review duties.

### Exclusion

A capability or effect that is explicitly outside the engagement.

### Expansion gate

Evidence and a separate decision required before broadening scope.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Service package

A service package defines a bounded decision, inputs, deliverables, reviewer duties and acceptance evidence. “Build AI automation” is too vague to judge or finish. The pilot card offers source-linked drafts for one approved text template, with local reviewed export. The buyer can now understand exactly what the experiment will decide.

## Step 2 · Exclusion

An exclusion prevents an adjacent capability from becoming an implied promise. Export does not mean automatic email; text parsing does not mean OCR. Explain exclusions in the same language the user uses, then ask them to teach back the workflow. A misunderstanding is a specification defect to repair before agreement.

## Step 3 · Expansion gate

An expansion gate requires new evidence before broader work. Diagnostic establishes the problem and fields; pilot tests one bounded workflow; expansion needs reviewed outcomes, operational capacity and updated scope. Completing a demo does not authorize more data destinations or autonomous effects. Keep manual fallback available while the result is uncertain.

## Service packaging and staged commitments

### Package a decision, not an unlimited capability
A diagnostic, a pilot, and production support answer different questions. A diagnostic identifies the workflow and feasibility. A pilot tests a bounded change with named users and representative inputs. Production requires ownership, access controls, monitoring, support, and recovery. Give each stage its own deliverable and decision gate. A successful diagnostic does not silently authorize production use.

### Build a service boundary
Describe supported input formats, volume, roles, output, review duty, and exclusions. For example, the handout pilot accepts approved UTF-8 course notes in one template, produces draft handouts with source IDs, and requires instructor approval. It excludes scanned documents, new curriculum creation, automated distribution, and confidential learner data. Exclusions are useful when they prevent a buyer from inferring a capability you have not tested.

### Make dependencies visible
List what the client must provide: representative samples, a reviewer, access decisions, a test environment, and an acceptance owner. Attach a date and consequence to each dependency. If approved samples arrive late, the evaluation schedule changes. Avoid a fixed delivery date that assumes inputs you do not control. A dependency table makes negotiation about the actual work possible.

### Offer useful alternatives
If the source material is inconsistent, offer a data-readiness diagnostic before implementation. If the buyer cannot assign a reviewer, offer a read-only search tool rather than a drafting workflow that needs review. Alternatives should preserve the desired outcome while changing the operational burden. They should not be arbitrary tiers that differ only in the number of prompts.

### Test the offer with teach-back
Give the one-page service description to a reviewer and ask: What will you receive? What can it do with incomplete notes? Who approves a draft? What costs recur? What happens when it fails? Any mismatch between their answers and your intent is a specification defect. Revise the offer before treating agreement as informed.

### Packaging exercise
Write diagnostic, pilot, and expansion cards. Each needs a decision question, inputs, outputs, exclusions, client duties, acceptance evidence, and stop condition. Use fictional costs if practicing. No card should guarantee an income, accuracy rate, or saving that has not been measured.

## A bounded pilot offer card

## Walk through the data and decision

1. The pilot accepts one text format and requires instructor review.

2. Automatic distribution and learner records are explicitly excluded.

3. Expansion depends on observed pilot results rather than enthusiasm at the demo.

## Completed specimen: A bounded pilot offer card

**Decision to support:** can instructors prepare source-linked handout drafts for one approved text-note template with manageable review?

**Inputs:** up to 20 synthetic English UTF-8 notes, one template, one instructor reviewer. **Output:** editable draft with source references, missing-objective flags and local reviewed export. **Deliverables:** runnable prototype, case-level evaluation, cost assumptions and handover guide.

**Excluded:** scanned PDF/OCR, new curriculum invention, automatic email, public publication, learner records, multilingual output. **Client duties in the simulation:** supply template and reviewer time; name an acceptance owner. **Fallback:** existing manual preparation remains available.

**Gate:** diagnostic first establishes fields and baseline; pilot tests the agreed cases; expansion is a new decision based on results. The offer does not guarantee time savings, income or autonomous accuracy. A teach-back that interprets “export” as “send to students” means the offer needs revision before agreement.

## Critique and transfer

Create diagnostic and expansion cards with different decision questions. Have a peer teach back the pilot deliverables and exclusions; record and correct any misunderstanding.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

## Practice first, then integrate

## Bounded first practice

Write distinct diagnostic and expansion cards, and repair a teach-back that interprets export as automatic sending.

## Practice acceptance

- The completed baseline/specimen is explained using the lesson walkthrough, with fixture assumptions distinguished from observations.
- Write distinct diagnostic and expansion cards, and repair a teach-back that interprets export as automatic sending.
- The decision and counterexample are recorded with evidence and remaining uncertainty; simulated and observed results are labeled.

## Integrate after practice

## Worked example

Pilot: “Draft participant handouts from one approved course template, with source references and instructor review.” Inputs: up to 20 synthetic text notes for testing. Exclusions: public publishing, automatic email, scanned PDFs, and changes to approved curriculum. Deliverables: prototype, evaluation report, and handover instructions.

## Build it yourself

1. Write a one-page service offer for the simulated client.
2. Define supported input formats, volume, users, review step, and output.
3. List at least five exclusions that prevent ambiguous expectations.
4. Describe the evidence required before offering an expanded engagement.

## Break it deliberately

The buyer assumes the pilot includes writing new curriculum and sending it to students. Revise the offer so those effects cannot be mistaken for included work.

## Acceptance checks

- The offer describes an outcome and tangible artifacts.
- Input boundaries and review duties are explicit.
- Expansion requires a separate decision.

## Deliverable

Save **`client-02/service-offer.md`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

## Full project sequence

1. Write a one-page service offer for the simulated client.
2. Define supported input formats, volume, users, review step, and output.
3. List at least five exclusions that prevent ambiguous expectations.
4. Describe the evidence required before offering an expanded engagement.

## Integration acceptance

- The offer describes an outcome and tangible artifacts.
- Input boundaries and review duties are explicit.
- Expansion requires a separate decision.

## Apply the three engineering pillars

## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to a fixed-scope statement of work

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Specify latency/quality limits and an explicit usage allowance in the offer. Price review, retries and maintenance, not just a successful generation.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Write Given/When/Then acceptance examples and critical exclusions into the scope. Link each promise to an observable test and a named decision owner.

### Context Management

Define allowed sources, revisions, retention and context allowance; a source expansion or new tenant changes scope and cache handling.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

exercise.solution:
## Complete guided-practice reference

Attempt the changed case first, then compare your reasoning with this completed response. This is a worked decision under stated assumptions, not evidence of performed client work.

## Completed service-stage cards

| Stage | Decision | Deliverable | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Diagnostic | Is there enough authorized, reviewable work to justify a pilot? | Defined unit, permissioned sample, baseline and risks | Named reviewer and agreed scope; otherwise stop |
| Pilot | Can one text-template review workflow meet the agreed cases? | Prototype, case-level results and handover | Reviewed quality, failure behavior and effort within declared bounds |
| Expansion | Does evidence justify another format or distribution capability? | Updated scope, data flow, estimate and tests | New requirements explicitly accepted before build |

**Teach-back failure:** “The system emails students.” **Correction:** “It creates a local file only after instructor review of that exact revision. A person handles distribution. Sending is excluded.” Recheck with a fresh scenario. This is a worked correction; a real peer teach-back remains unperformed until recorded.

## If your result differs

If every stage promises the same finished automation, the gates are cosmetic. Record the original misunderstanding and actual repeat observation when performing teach-back.

## Explain before continuing

Name the decision or invariant your change protects. Compare the baseline with your result, retain the failed case, and state what remains untested in the larger project.

chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to a fixed-scope statement of work

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Specify latency/quality limits and an explicit usage allowance in the offer. Price review, retries and maintenance, not just a successful generation.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Write Given/When/Then acceptance examples and critical exclusions into the scope. Link each promise to an observable test and a named decision owner.

### Context Management

Define allowed sources, revisions, retention and context allowance; a source expansion or new tenant changes scope and cache handling.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

## Before this session

### Specific preparation

Explain **Service package** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: A bounded outcome with supported inputs, deliverables, exclusions and review duties.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **an offer, statement of work and estimate**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Estimate effort, support, and pricing assumptions**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Write a statement of work with acceptance tests

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–4 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

A statement of work translates a proposal into testable responsibilities. Include scope, deliverables, milestones, required client inputs, review windows, acceptance method, and a change process. This program uses a planning template; actual contractual and legal terms need the appropriate local review before use.

Acceptance should describe observable behavior on a named dataset and environment. “Works well” is not a useful condition. Agree on which failures block acceptance and which are documented limitations. Identify who is authorized to accept the work and what happens when client data or access arrives late.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Statement of work

A planning document defining deliverables, responsibilities, dependencies and acceptance.

### Acceptance condition

An agreed observable behavior on a named dataset and environment.

### Change request

A documented proposal to alter scope with its cost, schedule and test impacts.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Statement of work

A statement of work connects deliverables, duties, exclusions and acceptance to the same bounded outcome. Treat this specimen as project planning, not jurisdiction-specific legal drafting. A missing reviewer or new file format changes what can be accepted, even if implementation effort appears small.

## Step 2 · Acceptance condition

An acceptance condition specifies a known fixture, actor, action, expected observable result, reviewer and evidence. “Good quality” leaves disagreement inevitable. Separate field presence, factual support, owner isolation and recoverable failure. A skipped test is not a pass; preserve failed and not-tested states alongside the candidate revision.

## Step 3 · Change request

A change request captures a new promise and its effect on data, authority, effort, operations and tests. Distinguish it from fixing a defect against an existing promise. A supplied scanned PDF remains outside a UTF-8 text pilot until the change is agreed. Do not silently expand scope or mark an untested format accepted.

## Statements of work as executable acceptance

### Translate outcomes into observable behavior
A scope document should connect every deliverable to an acceptance scenario. “Accurate AI summaries” is not testable. “For each approved note, the draft links every factual objective to a source section; missing objectives are flagged for review” identifies behavior a reviewer can inspect. Add negative cases as well as the normal path. Treat this as a delivery planning exercise; real contractual language requires context-specific review.

### Use given, when, then, evidence
Write: Given a named dataset and role, when an action occurs, then an observable result follows, proven by an artifact. Example: Given note N03 with no objective, when a reviewer creates a draft, then the objective is marked missing and export is blocked until reviewed; evidence is the saved draft revision and review event. Include environment and dataset revisions so the test can be repeated.

### Define status categories
Use passed, failed, not tested, and deferred. A deferred condition needs an owner, reason, risk, and explicit acceptance decision. “We did not see a problem” is not equivalent to passed. A demo using one known good document cannot establish behavior on missing fields or failed provider calls. Keep screenshots as supporting evidence rather than the entire test record.

### Define the change boundary
A request to support scanned PDFs changes ingestion, OCR quality, evaluation data, latency, and probably hosting. It is a scope change even when the interface still shows an upload box. The change process should identify affected requirements, effort, acceptance tests, and decision owner. Preserve the original agreement until the change is explicitly accepted.

### Include operational acceptance
Add client-owned accounts, backup/restore, reviewer permissions, and fallback operation where appropriate. A feature can pass its happy path while remaining impossible for the client to operate. Tie handover and access removal to acceptance, not to an informal promise after the project ends.

### Acceptance exercise
Create eight scenarios: normal note, missing objective, contradictory source, malformed input, duplicate submission, unauthorized reviewer, provider failure, and stale edit. Assign each to an owner and an evidence file. Have a peer challenge one ambiguous condition and rewrite it until both of you would give the same result on the same input.
