### Translate outcomes into observable behavior
A scope document should connect every deliverable to an acceptance scenario. “Accurate AI summaries” is not testable. “For each approved note, the draft links every factual objective to a source section; missing objectives are flagged for review” identifies behavior a reviewer can inspect. Add negative cases as well as the normal path. Treat this as a delivery planning exercise; real contractual language requires context-specific review.

### Use given, when, then, evidence
Write: Given a named dataset and role, when an action occurs, then an observable result follows, proven by an artifact. Example: Given note N03 with no objective, when a reviewer creates a draft, then the objective is marked missing and export is blocked until reviewed; evidence is the saved draft revision and review event. Include environment and dataset revisions so the test can be repeated.

### Define status categories
Use passed, failed, not tested, and deferred. A deferred condition needs an owner, reason, risk, and explicit acceptance decision. “We did not see a problem” is not equivalent to passed. A demo using one known good document cannot establish behavior on missing fields or failed provider calls. Keep screenshots as supporting evidence rather than the entire test record.

### Define the change boundary
A request to support scanned PDFs changes ingestion, OCR quality, evaluation data, latency, and probably hosting. It is a scope change even when the interface still shows an upload box. The change process should identify affected requirements, effort, acceptance tests, and decision owner. Preserve the original agreement until the change is explicitly accepted.

### Include operational acceptance
Add client-owned accounts, backup/restore, reviewer permissions, and fallback operation where appropriate. A feature can pass its happy path while remaining impossible for the client to operate. Tie handover and access removal to acceptance, not to an informal promise after the project ends.

### Acceptance exercise
Create eight scenarios: normal note, missing objective, contradictory source, malformed input, duplicate submission, unauthorized reviewer, provider failure, and stale edit. Assign each to an owner and an evidence file. Have a peer challenge one ambiguous condition and rewrite it until both of you would give the same result on the same input.

chapters.title: An acceptance register linked to scope
chapters.body:
## Walk through the data and decision

1. A1–A5 tie known fixtures to visible outcomes and decision owners.

2. Missing objective and contradictory source have different expected behavior.

3. Malformed input, duplicate submission and stale edits are still missing cases.

## Completed specimen: An acceptance register linked to scope

| ID | Given / when | Then | Evidence | Decision owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | N01-v1 complete; create draft | Required sections and source ID present | saved D01-r1 and review sheet | instructor |
| A2 | N03-v1 missing objective; create draft | Objective stays unknown; review flag visible | D03-r1 plus screenshot | instructor |
| A3 | N04-v1 contradictory sections | Conflict retained; no invented reconciliation | conflict annotation | instructor |
| A4 | Another account requests D01 | Inaccessible; no content disclosed | scoped request/response | operations lead |
| A5 | Fake provider times out | Input retained, failure explicit, no approved export | failure trace and readback | operations lead |

**Milestone condition:** A1–A5 are blocking; a skipped test is not a pass. Add three more cases for malformed input, duplicate submission and stale edit. Pin the fixture and release revisions in the completed record.

If a new scan is supplied at review, the original UTF-8 boundary remains until a change is accepted. This is a project-planning specimen, not a jurisdiction-specific contract.

## Critique and transfer

Complete eight scenarios and assign a reviewer and evidence path to each. Rewrite one ambiguous “good quality” criterion until two peers agree how to judge the same output.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to a fixed-scope statement of work

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Specify latency/quality limits and an explicit usage allowance in the offer. Price review, retries and maintenance, not just a successful generation.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Write Given/When/Then acceptance examples and critical exclusions into the scope. Link each promise to an observable test and a named decision owner.

### Context Management

Define allowed sources, revisions, retention and context allowance; a source expansion or new tenant changes scope and cache handling.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

# Estimate effort, support, and pricing assumptions

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Write a statement of work with acceptance tests**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Write a statement of work with acceptance tests (`academy-v2:freelancing-masterclass:05`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Statement of work** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: A planning document defining deliverables, responsibilities, dependencies and acceptance.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **an offer, statement of work and estimate**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Map data, access, and retention**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Estimate effort, support, and pricing assumptions

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–5 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

An estimate should account for discovery, implementation, testing, review, deployment, handover, and support. Separate one-time work from recurring costs. Include uncertainty and the assumptions that could change the estimate. A price is a commercial decision; a cost model helps you understand what the engagement requires before making a promise.

Use fictional currency units in this exercise so the reasoning is independent of market rates. Model API usage from expected volume and observed calls, not only one successful response. Include retries, failed runs, review effort, and maintenance. Do not present a speculative return on investment as a guaranteed saving.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### One-time effort

Work such as discovery, implementation, testing and initial handover.

### Recurring cost

Ongoing usage, hosting, review or support effort after the initial build.

### Contingency

Explicit planning allowance for uncertainty rather than hidden guaranteed profit.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · One-time effort

One-time effort includes discovery, build, evaluation, review and handover. Break it into packages with assumptions and high-case drivers instead of estimating only coding. Forty-four hours is an estimate, not a time log. A contingency allowance is additional planning capacity; do not quietly use it to promise more scope.

## Step 2 · Recurring cost

Recurring cost includes hosting, all provider attempts, review, maintenance and incident work. Usage cost per accepted draft divides all attempt spend by reviewed accepted outputs. It excludes reviewer time unless explicitly included. Hosting and support do not disappear because the implementation fee was paid once.

## Step 3 · Contingency

Contingency represents uncertainty under named assumptions. Low/high estimates reveal which dependency drives the range. Capacity must also account for existing support: fifteen support hours cannot simultaneously be sold as implementation time. Keep internal labor cost, commercial price and buyer value separate; fictional rates are not market recommendations.

## Effort estimation, unit economics, and support capacity

### Estimate by work package
Break the work into discovery, data preparation, implementation, evaluation, deployment, review, training, and handover. Give each a low, expected, and high effort estimate with the source of uncertainty. “Build app: 40 hours” hides which assumption can change the schedule. A dependency on an unknown document format should appear as a risk or investigation task, not an invisible buffer.

### Separate cost, price, and value
Cost is what delivery consumes. Price is the commercial amount agreed. Value is the outcome the buyer cares about. These quantities are related but not interchangeable. For an illustrative 44-hour pilot at 50 fictional units per hour, direct labor cost is 2,200 units; a 20% effort allowance gives 52.8 hours, or 2,640 units. Hosting, provider usage, and support are separate. These are teaching assumptions, not recommended market rates.

### Model recurring usage from accepted work
Count requests, calls per request, retries, input/output tokens, and failed jobs. Divide total cost by accepted outputs rather than only successful API calls. If 100 attempts produce 70 accepted handouts, your unit denominator is 70. Include a review cost and maintenance reserve. A model that is cheap per call can be expensive per accepted result if it generates more corrections.

### Price a boundary you can explain
Fixed-scope pricing needs clear acceptance and change rules. Time-based work needs reporting and a budget control. Ongoing support needs a coverage window, supported versions, and severity definitions. Do not make a fixed promise against an unbounded input set. Choose a model for the simulated engagement and explain which risks each party retains.

### Check your own capacity
Suppose three supported clients each generate four incidents per month, with 45 minutes of investigation and 30 minutes of follow-up per incident. That is 15 support hours before planned maintenance. Add sales and administration when evaluating how much delivery work you can take on. Revenue alone does not establish a sustainable service.

### Estimation exercise
Produce one-time and recurring sheets, three usage scenarios, a change example, and a support-capacity calculation. Label every input as observed, quoted, or assumed. Change volume and acceptance rate together, then explain which assumption deserves validation before making a commercial commitment.

## An effort and capacity estimate

## Walk through the data and decision

1. Expected packages sum to 44 hours;20% allowance gives 52.8.

2. At 50 fictional units/hour labor allowance is 2640, excluding hosting and usage.

3. Three clients×four incidents×75 minutes consumes 15 monthly support hours.

## Completed specimen: An effort and capacity estimate

| Work package | Expected hours | High-case driver |
|---|---:|---|
| Discovery and data | 8 | incomplete template definitions |
| Build | 16 | revision and review conflicts |
| Evaluation | 10 | source contradictions require labels |
| Review | 6 | reviewer feedback turnaround |
| Handover | 4 | fresh setup defects |
| Total | **44** | estimate, not a time log |

A 20% effort allowance gives **52.8 hours**. At **50 fictional units/hour**, planned labor cost is **2,640 units**. This is an illustrative internal cost model, not a market rate or recommended price. Hosting and provider usage are separate; price and the buyer’s value are different quantities.

Recurring example: 100 attempts costing 14 units with 70 accepted drafts gives 0.20 usage units per accepted draft, before review and maintenance. Three clients × four incidents × (45 investigation + 30 follow-up) minutes gives **15 support hours/month**. Do not sell those hours twice as implementation capacity.

## Critique and transfer

Add low/high estimates by package and three usage scenarios. Show which assumption drives the range. Define support coverage and out-of-scope handling separately from a one-time pilot price.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

- The decision and counterexample are recorded with evidence and remaining uncertainty; simulated and observed results are labeled.

## Integrate after practice

## Worked example

An illustrative pilot requires 8 discovery hours, 16 build hours, 10 testing hours, six review hours, and four handover hours. Adding a 20% contingency to 44 hours produces 52.8 planned hours. Provider and hosting charges are separate assumptions. A fixed scope still needs a policy for changes and recurring support.

## Build it yourself

1. Build an editable effort estimate by work package and uncertainty.
2. Use the completed effort and support estimate in this lesson to calculate delivery capacity; keep the session 3 time-benefit calculation separate from your cost and price assumptions.
3. Create three volume scenarios including provider retries and maintenance.
4. Explain how you would handle work outside scope and who owns ongoing service accounts.

## Break it deliberately

Double usage and increase review effort. Identify whether recurring cost or support capacity becomes the limiting factor.

## Acceptance checks

- One-time and recurring costs are separated.
- The estimate includes non-coding work and uncertainty.
- All numerical examples are labeled as illustrative assumptions.

## Deliverable

Save **`client-02/effort-and-cost-model.csv`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

2. Use the completed effort and support estimate in this lesson to calculate delivery capacity; keep the session 3 time-benefit calculation separate from your cost and price assumptions.
3. Create three volume scenarios including provider retries and maintenance.
4. Explain how you would handle work outside scope and who owns ongoing service accounts.

exercise.solution:
## Complete guided-practice reference

Attempt the changed case first, then compare your reasoning with this completed response. This is a worked decision under stated assumptions, not evidence of performed client work.

## Completed estimate revision

| Package | Low | Expected | High |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Discovery/data | 6 | 8 | 12 |
| Build | 12 | 16 | 24 |
| Evaluation | 8 | 10 | 16 |
| Review | 4 | 6 | 10 |
| Handover | 3 | 4 | 6 |
| Total hours before allowance | 33 | 44 | 68 |

At 20% allowance: 39.6 / 52.8 / 81.6 hours. If monthly available time is an assumed 80 hours, the 15-hour support load leaves 65 for other work before sales/admin. The high implementation case exceeds that capacity; revise dates or scope rather than selling the same hours twice. At 14 usage units and zero accepted outputs, cost per accepted output is undefined, not zero. All figures are illustrative assumptions.

```python
low=[6,12,8,4,3];expected=[8,16,10,6,4];high=[12,24,16,10,6]
assert [sum(x) for x in [low,expected,high]]==[33,44,68]
assert [round(sum(x)*1.2,1) for x in [low,expected,high]]==[39.6,52.8,81.6]
```

chapters.title: Understand the decision: Estimate effort, support, and pricing assumptions
chapters.body:
## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–5 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

An estimate should account for discovery, implementation, testing, review, deployment, handover, and support. Separate one-time work from recurring costs. Include uncertainty and the assumptions that could change the estimate. A price is a commercial decision; a cost model helps you understand what the engagement requires before making a promise.

Use fictional currency units in this exercise so the reasoning is independent of market rates. Model API usage from expected volume and observed calls, not only one successful response. Include retries, failed runs, review effort, and maintenance. Do not present a speculative return on investment as a guaranteed saving.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### One-time effort

Work such as discovery, implementation, testing and initial handover.

### Recurring cost

Ongoing usage, hosting, review or support effort after the initial build.

### Contingency

Explicit planning allowance for uncertainty rather than hidden guaranteed profit.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · One-time effort

One-time effort includes discovery, build, evaluation, review and handover. Break it into packages with assumptions and high-case drivers instead of estimating only coding. Forty-four hours is an estimate, not a time log. A contingency allowance is additional planning capacity; do not quietly use it to promise more scope.

## Step 2 · Recurring cost

Recurring cost includes hosting, all provider attempts, review, maintenance and incident work. Usage cost per accepted draft divides all attempt spend by reviewed accepted outputs. It excludes reviewer time unless explicitly included. Hosting and support do not disappear because the implementation fee was paid once.

## Step 3 · Contingency

Contingency represents uncertainty under named assumptions. Low/high estimates reveal which dependency drives the range. Capacity must also account for existing support: fifteen support hours cannot simultaneously be sold as implementation time. Keep internal labor cost, commercial price and buyer value separate; fictional rates are not market recommendations.

chapters.title: Effort estimation, unit economics, and support capacity
chapters.body:
### Estimate by work package
Break the work into discovery, data preparation, implementation, evaluation, deployment, review, training, and handover. Give each a low, expected, and high effort estimate with the source of uncertainty. “Build app: 40 hours” hides which assumption can change the schedule. A dependency on an unknown document format should appear as a risk or investigation task, not an invisible buffer.

### Separate cost, price, and value
Cost is what delivery consumes. Price is the commercial amount agreed. Value is the outcome the buyer cares about. These quantities are related but not interchangeable. For an illustrative 44-hour pilot at 50 fictional units per hour, direct labor cost is 2,200 units; a 20% effort allowance gives 52.8 hours, or 2,640 units. Hosting, provider usage, and support are separate. These are teaching assumptions, not recommended market rates.

### Model recurring usage from accepted work
Count requests, calls per request, retries, input/output tokens, and failed jobs. Divide total cost by accepted outputs rather than only successful API calls. If 100 attempts produce 70 accepted handouts, your unit denominator is 70. Include a review cost and maintenance reserve. A model that is cheap per call can be expensive per accepted result if it generates more corrections.

### Price a boundary you can explain
Fixed-scope pricing needs clear acceptance and change rules. Time-based work needs reporting and a budget control. Ongoing support needs a coverage window, supported versions, and severity definitions. Do not make a fixed promise against an unbounded input set. Choose a model for the simulated engagement and explain which risks each party retains.

### Check your own capacity
Suppose three supported clients each generate four incidents per month, with 45 minutes of investigation and 30 minutes of follow-up per incident. That is 15 support hours before planned maintenance. Add sales and administration when evaluating how much delivery work you can take on. Revenue alone does not establish a sustainable service.

### Estimation exercise
Produce one-time and recurring sheets, three usage scenarios, a change example, and a support-capacity calculation. Label every input as observed, quoted, or assumed. Change volume and acceptance rate together, then explain which assumption deserves validation before making a commercial commitment.

## Completed specimen: An effort and capacity estimate

| Work package | Expected hours | High-case driver |
|---|---:|---|
| Discovery and data | 8 | incomplete template definitions |

| Evaluation | 10 | source contradictions require labels |
| Review | 6 | reviewer feedback turnaround |

Recurring example: 100 attempts costing 14 units with 70 accepted drafts gives 0.20 usage units per accepted draft, before review and maintenance. Three clients × four incidents × (45 investigation + 30 follow-up) minutes gives **15 support hours/month**. Do not sell those hours twice as implementation capacity.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to a fixed-scope statement of work

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Specify latency/quality limits and an explicit usage allowance in the offer. Price review, retries and maintenance, not just a successful generation.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Write Given/When/Then acceptance examples and critical exclusions into the scope. Link each promise to an observable test and a named decision owner.

### Context Management

Define allowed sources, revisions, retention and context allowance; a source expansion or new tenant changes scope and cache handling.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

lessons.content:
# Map data, access, and retention

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Estimate effort, support, and pricing assumptions**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Estimate effort, support, and pricing assumptions (`academy-v2:freelancing-masterclass:06`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **One-time effort** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: Work such as discovery, implementation, testing and initial handover.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **a data map, thin pilot and scoped feedback log**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Build a thin pilot with visible limitations**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Map data, access, and retention

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–6 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

Data access is a delivery dependency and a trust boundary. Inventory what data the workflow reads, where it is stored, who can see it, whether it is sent to a provider, and when it is deleted. Obtain the client’s authorization for the specific flow before using real information. A client sharing one sample does not authorize uploading the entire archive.

Start with synthetic fixtures and a minimal data schema. Avoid including credentials or personal content in demonstrations, logs, screenshots, or portfolio artifacts. Document the account owner for each external service and how access will be revoked at handover. Use separate client environments rather than mixing data in a personal experiment.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Data-flow map

A record of inputs, destinations, processing, storage, logs and exports.

### Data minimization

Using only the fields needed for the agreed task.

### Access revocation

Removing implementer privileges while preserving client-owned operation.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Data-flow map

A data-flow map follows each field from intake through storage, provider calls, logs, exports and backups. A new hosted model is a new destination even if the interface looks unchanged. Name the role with access and purpose at each stage. Track configuration names rather than secret values in the handover document.

## Step 2 · Data minimization

Data minimization excludes fields unnecessary for the bounded task. Learner names are outside this handout pilot, so reject or remove them before processing. Hiding them in the interface does not remove them from uploaded files or logs. Use a synthetic marker to inspect actual stored/exported payloads at each boundary.

## Step 3 · Access revocation

Access revocation changes who can use data but does not automatically delete every copy. Exports and backups have separate retention/expiry policies and owners. Record those policies as agreements to obtain, not universal defaults. A revoked implementer should lose access without disabling the client’s separate service identity or recovery role.

## Data inventory and least-privilege delivery

### Map data by movement
Inventory the fields needed for each step, where they originate, which component reads them, whether a provider receives them, where outputs are stored, and when they are removed. Include logs, caches, backups, and exports. “We delete the uploaded file” is incomplete if its content remains in traces or generated drafts. Begin with synthetic notes so you can test the data flow without real client information.

### Separate account ownership from implementer access
The client should be able to operate the service after your access is removed. Use client-owned service accounts and narrowly scoped implementer roles for the exercise. Record who can rotate keys, change billing, approve users, and recover backups. Do not put actual keys in a handover document or a screenshot. Document variable names and storage locations instead.

### Apply least privilege to behavior
A drafting service needs read access to approved notes and write access to draft storage. It does not need permission to send email or change the source curriculum. Separate reviewer approval from generation. Log who approved which revision and invalidate approval when the material changes. A model’s instruction cannot substitute for an application permission check.

### Build retention into the design
For each data class, specify purpose, access, retention trigger, and deletion method. Test deletion in primary storage and explain how backup retention affects complete removal. If jurisdiction-specific obligations matter, investigate them before a real engagement; this lesson provides a technical inventory, not a universal legal rule.

### Trace one record
Follow synthetic note N03 through ingestion, draft generation, review, export, logging, and backup. At each boundary, list the minimum fields. Replace full source text in operational logs with IDs and status where possible. Confirm that error messages do not echo credentials or confidential payloads.

### Access exercise
Create an operator, reviewer, administrator, and implementer role. Write an allow/deny matrix and test one allowed and one denied action per role. Remove implementer access and verify routine operation still works. The evidence should describe the actual denial or success, not merely a checkbox saying security was considered.

## A field-level data-flow register

## Walk through the data and decision

1. The register includes logs, exports and backups, not only the input table.

2. Learner names are excluded at intake.

3. Deleting an input leaves exported and backed-up copies to their separately owned lifecycle.

## Completed specimen: A field-level data-flow register

| Data | Destination | Role with access | Retention assumption | Removal test |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Approved note text | local store | instructor | pilot plus 30 days, to agree | delete then read returns absent |
| Draft + source ID | local store/export | assigned instructor | same draft policy | delete draft and inspect export copy |
| Stage/outcome IDs | logs | operator | seven days, to agree | rotate and inspect sample |
| Backups | isolated client-owned store | administrator | two copies, to agree | expire old copy and verify |
| Learner names | none | none | excluded | synthetic canary rejected at intake |

The offline fake provider receives no real client data. A later hosted model adds a destination and must trigger a new data-flow decision. The retention values are planning assumptions, not default policy or compliance claims.

Deleting an input does not delete an already exported handout or every backup. Record those separate lifecycles and the owner responsible for each. A hidden sheet in a supplied workbook must be inspected before intake, not discovered after upload.

## Critique and transfer

Add an access-provision/revoke checklist and a provider boundary row for a hypothetical integration. Follow a synthetic canary through logs, drafts, exports and backups; report exactly which copies remain.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

## Practice first, then integrate

## Bounded first practice

Add a hypothetical hosted-provider row and a revoke/copy check. State exactly which canary copies remain after deleting local input.

## Practice acceptance

- The completed baseline/specimen is explained using the lesson walkthrough, with fixture assumptions distinguished from observations.
- Add a hypothetical hosted-provider row and a revoke/copy check. State exactly which canary copies remain after deleting local input.
- The decision and counterexample are recorded with evidence and remaining uncertainty; simulated and observed results are labeled.

## Integrate after practice

## Worked example

The handout workflow reads approved course notes and outputs drafts for instructors. Learner names are unnecessary and should be excluded. A provider integration would introduce another data destination; the client must understand and approve that choice before real notes leave the agreed environment.

## Build it yourself

1. Create a data-flow diagram covering input, processing, provider boundary, storage, logs, and exports.
2. List data fields, owners, access roles, retention, and deletion behavior.
3. Build synthetic samples that exercise the same structure without private content.
4. Write a checklist for access provisioning and revocation.

## Break it deliberately

A sample contains a hidden sheet with learner names. Your intake process should inspect and minimize the sample before it reaches any provider.

## Acceptance checks

- Every data destination and account owner is listed.
- Only necessary fields appear in the prototype.
- Access removal and deletion are part of the handover plan.

## Deliverable

Save **`client-03/data-access-plan.md`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

## Full project sequence

1. Create a data-flow diagram covering input, processing, provider boundary, storage, logs, and exports.
2. List data fields, owners, access roles, retention, and deletion behavior.
3. Build synthetic samples that exercise the same structure without private content.
4. Write a checklist for access provisioning and revocation.

## Integration acceptance

- Every data destination and account owner is listed.
- Only necessary fields appear in the prototype.
- Access removal and deletion are part of the handover plan.

## Apply the three engineering pillars

## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to a permissioned client-data inventory and prototype

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Compare a manual baseline with the prototype on identical synthetic inputs, reporting elapsed/review time, total attempts and accepted outputs.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Use a reviewed acceptance set with missing data and unsupported-claim cases; no polished demo substitutes for the failure report.

### Context Management

Build a source/permission manifest with digest/revision, token estimate, omitted fields and cache invalidation rules before any provider request.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

chapters.title: Understand the decision: Map data, access, and retention
chapters.body:
## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–6 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

Data access is a delivery dependency and a trust boundary. Inventory what data the workflow reads, where it is stored, who can see it, whether it is sent to a provider, and when it is deleted. Obtain the client’s authorization for the specific flow before using real information. A client sharing one sample does not authorize uploading the entire archive.

Start with synthetic fixtures and a minimal data schema. Avoid including credentials or personal content in demonstrations, logs, screenshots, or portfolio artifacts. Document the account owner for each external service and how access will be revoked at handover. Use separate client environments rather than mixing data in a personal experiment.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Data-flow map

A record of inputs, destinations, processing, storage, logs and exports.

### Data minimization

Using only the fields needed for the agreed task.

### Access revocation

Removing implementer privileges while preserving client-owned operation.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Data-flow map

A data-flow map follows each field from intake through storage, provider calls, logs, exports and backups. A new hosted model is a new destination even if the interface looks unchanged. Name the role with access and purpose at each stage. Track configuration names rather than secret values in the handover document.

## Step 2 · Data minimization

Data minimization excludes fields unnecessary for the bounded task. Learner names are outside this handout pilot, so reject or remove them before processing. Hiding them in the interface does not remove them from uploaded files or logs. Use a synthetic marker to inspect actual stored/exported payloads at each boundary.

## Step 3 · Access revocation

Access revocation changes who can use data but does not automatically delete every copy. Exports and backups have separate retention/expiry policies and owners. Record those policies as agreements to obtain, not universal defaults. A revoked implementer should lose access without disabling the client’s separate service identity or recovery role.

chapters.title: Data inventory and least-privilege delivery
chapters.body:
### Map data by movement
Inventory the fields needed for each step, where they originate, which component reads them, whether a provider receives them, where outputs are stored, and when they are removed. Include logs, caches, backups, and exports. “We delete the uploaded file” is incomplete if its content remains in traces or generated drafts. Begin with synthetic notes so you can test the data flow without real client information.

### Separate account ownership from implementer access
The client should be able to operate the service after your access is removed. Use client-owned service accounts and narrowly scoped implementer roles for the exercise. Record who can rotate keys, change billing, approve users, and recover backups. Do not put actual keys in a handover document or a screenshot. Document variable names and storage locations instead.

### Apply least privilege to behavior
A drafting service needs read access to approved notes and write access to draft storage. It does not need permission to send email or change the source curriculum. Separate reviewer approval from generation. Log who approved which revision and invalidate approval when the material changes. A model’s instruction cannot substitute for an application permission check.

### Build retention into the design
For each data class, specify purpose, access, retention trigger, and deletion method. Test deletion in primary storage and explain how backup retention affects complete removal. If jurisdiction-specific obligations matter, investigate them before a real engagement; this lesson provides a technical inventory, not a universal legal rule.

### Trace one record
Follow synthetic note N03 through ingestion, draft generation, review, export, logging, and backup. At each boundary, list the minimum fields. Replace full source text in operational logs with IDs and status where possible. Confirm that error messages do not echo credentials or confidential payloads.

### Access exercise
Create an operator, reviewer, administrator, and implementer role. Write an allow/deny matrix and test one allowed and one denied action per role. Remove implementer access and verify routine operation still works. The evidence should describe the actual denial or success, not merely a checkbox saying security was considered.

chapters.body:
## Walk through the data and decision

1. The register includes logs, exports and backups, not only the input table.

2. Learner names are excluded at intake.

3. Deleting an input leaves exported and backed-up copies to their separately owned lifecycle.

## Completed specimen: A field-level data-flow register

| Data | Destination | Role with access | Retention assumption | Removal test |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Approved note text | local store | instructor | pilot plus 30 days, to agree | delete then read returns absent |
| Draft + source ID | local store/export | assigned instructor | same draft policy | delete draft and inspect export copy |
| Stage/outcome IDs | logs | operator | seven days, to agree | rotate and inspect sample |
| Backups | isolated client-owned store | administrator | two copies, to agree | expire old copy and verify |
| Learner names | none | none | excluded | synthetic canary rejected at intake |

The offline fake provider receives no real client data. A later hosted model adds a destination and must trigger a new data-flow decision. The retention values are planning assumptions, not default policy or compliance claims.

Deleting an input does not delete an already exported handout or every backup. Record those separate lifecycles and the owner responsible for each. A hidden sheet in a supplied workbook must be inspected before intake, not discovered after upload.

## Critique and transfer

Add an access-provision/revoke checklist and a provider boundary row for a hypothetical integration. Follow a synthetic canary through logs, drafts, exports and backups; report exactly which copies remain.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to a permissioned client-data inventory and prototype

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Compare a manual baseline with the prototype on identical synthetic inputs, reporting elapsed/review time, total attempts and accepted outputs.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Use a reviewed acceptance set with missing data and unsupported-claim cases; no polished demo substitutes for the failure report.

### Context Management

Build a source/permission manifest with digest/revision, token estimate, omitted fields and cache invalidation rules before any provider request.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

lessons.content:
# Build a thin pilot with visible limitations

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Map data, access, and retention**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Map data, access, and retention (`academy-v2:freelancing-masterclass:07`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Data-flow map** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: A record of inputs, destinations, processing, storage, logs and exports.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **a data map, thin pilot and scoped feedback log**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Use client feedback without losing scope**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Build a thin pilot with visible limitations

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–7 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

A pilot tests whether the workflow can meet the agreed outcome within constraints. Implement a narrow end-to-end path rather than a broad collection of mock screens. Use fake adapters to test behavior and a real integration only when it is necessary and authorized. Label each simulated step clearly in the demo.

Build uncertainty handling before polishing presentation. Missing source content, provider failure, and invalid output should produce a reviewable state without losing user work. The pilot should help the client make a go/no-go decision; it should not conceal manual steps behind an “AI automation” label.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Thin pilot

A narrow but complete end-to-end workflow that tests an agreed uncertainty.

### Fake integration

A clearly labeled deterministic substitute for an external dependency.

### Go/no-go evidence

Observed results that support continuing, conditioning or stopping an engagement.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Thin pilot

A thin pilot implements the smallest connected path needed to test the client decision. Read one authorized note, produce a draft, flag missing information, save/reload and review before export. A polished mockup alone cannot show recoverable state or measured review effort. Keep the manual workflow available as fallback.

## Step 2 · Fake integration

A fake integration supplies controlled outputs or failures to isolate orchestration. It is valuable when named honestly. The reference generator below is deterministic, not an AI model; it tests missing-objective and timeout handling. It cannot establish the quality or safety of a future model’s teaching content.

## Step 3 · Go/no-go evidence

Go/no-go evidence comes from the declared scenarios and thresholds. Keep normal, missing-objective and timeout results, including original input and status. A demo viewer should identify every fake/manual component without coaching. Do not infer time savings, readiness or permission for automatic distribution from a successful synthetic path.

## Prototype, pilot, and production evidence

### Match the build to the question
A prototype can test whether users understand a review screen using fake data. A pilot tests a bounded workflow with representative inputs and real operating constraints. Production serves ongoing work with assigned ownership and recovery. Label the stage clearly. A polished interface does not turn a prototype into production, and a local demo does not establish reliable multi-user operation.

### Build one vertical slice
For the handout service, implement source input → draft creation → instructor review → saved approved revision → export. A collection of disconnected screens cannot test the end-to-end handoff. Keep the slice small: one input template, one reviewer role, one output format. Preserve the manual fallback so the team can finish work if the pilot stops.

### Show uncertainty in the interface
Missing source information should appear as unresolved, not a confident completion. Display draft status, source revision, review state, and provider failure separately. A disabled export with a clear reason is more useful than silently producing an incomplete file. The interface should help a reviewer understand what requires judgment.

### Define what each evidence type proves
A screenshot proves appearance at a moment. An API response proves one request returned a value. A reload check can show persistence. A second-user denial shows one access boundary. A restore rehearsal demonstrates a recovery procedure in the tested environment. Combine evidence to support the claim you actually make; do not use a screenshot to claim database isolation.

### Add a stop rule
Choose a condition that pauses expansion: missing source ownership, unacceptable false acceptance, review time above the baseline, or no one available to operate the service. Agree on the rule before looking at favorable outputs. A failed pilot can still be a useful engagement when it prevents an expensive unsupported rollout.

### Pilot exercise
Write the decision question, smallest complete flow, representative cases, success measure, guardrail, fallback, and expansion gate. Implement the slice with synthetic data. Ask a reviewer to handle one unseen normal case and one failure without coaching. Record where the design failed to communicate its limits.

## A pilot demonstration record with honest boundaries

## Walk through the data and decision

1. The completed pilot record separates real local save from fake generation.

2. Missing-objective review is distinct from a provider timeout.

exercise.solution:
## Complete guided-practice reference

Attempt the changed case first, then compare your reasoning with this completed response. This is a worked decision under stated assumptions, not evidence of performed client work.

## Complete bounded pilot reference

The following Python example includes its data, fake generator and temporary SQLite store. Save as solution.py and run `python3 -I solution.py`. It performs no provider calls. Its assertions test lifecycle and readback, not semantic teaching quality.

**Decision after this run:** the mechanical paths can be inspected; instructor review, usability, timing and real-model behavior remain untested. Continue only as a reviewed synthetic pilot. Do not fill the specimen’s client-result column from expected outputs.

```python
import json,sqlite3,tempfile
from pathlib import Path
def fake_generate(note):
    if note['id']=='N03':raise TimeoutError()
    return {'outline':'Draft: '+note['title'],'review_reasons':[] if note.get('objective') else ['objective_missing']}
notes=[{'id':'N01','title':'Returns','objective':'Explain unopened eligibility'},
       {'id':'N02','title':'Shipping','objective':None},{'id':'N03','title':'Access','objective':'Request reset'}]
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path=Path(folder)/'pilot.sqlite';db=sqlite3.connect(path)
    db.execute('CREATE TABLE drafts(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,input TEXT,result TEXT)')
    for note in notes:
        try:result={**fake_generate(note),'status':'needs_instructor_review','approved':False}
        except TimeoutError:result={'status':'generation_failed','approved':False}
        with db:db.execute('INSERT INTO drafts VALUES(?,?,?)',(note['id'],json.dumps(note),json.dumps(result)))
    db.close();db=sqlite3.connect(path)
    rows={identifier:(json.loads(raw),json.loads(result)) for identifier,raw,result in db.execute('SELECT * FROM drafts')}
    assert len(rows)==3 and rows['N02'][1]['review_reasons']==['objective_missing']
    assert rows['N03'][0]['title']=='Access' and rows['N03'][1]['status']=='generation_failed'
    assert not any(result['approved'] for raw,result in rows.values());db.close()
print('3 inputs/results survived reopen; missing objective flagged; timeout retained; no approved export')
```

## Expected reference observation

```text
3 inputs/results survived reopen; missing objective flagged; timeout retained; no approved export
```

## If your result differs

If only successful drafts survive, failure evidence is lost. If every row says approved, generation was mistaken for instructor acceptance.

## Explain before continuing

Name the decision or invariant your change protects. Compare the baseline with your result, retain the failed case, and state what remains untested in the larger project.

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–7 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

A pilot tests whether the workflow can meet the agreed outcome within constraints. Implement a narrow end-to-end path rather than a broad collection of mock screens. Use fake adapters to test behavior and a real integration only when it is necessary and authorized. Label each simulated step clearly in the demo.

Build uncertainty handling before polishing presentation. Missing source content, provider failure, and invalid output should produce a reviewable state without losing user work. The pilot should help the client make a go/no-go decision; it should not conceal manual steps behind an “AI automation” label.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Thin pilot

A narrow but complete end-to-end workflow that tests an agreed uncertainty.

### Fake integration

A clearly labeled deterministic substitute for an external dependency.

### Go/no-go evidence

Observed results that support continuing, conditioning or stopping an engagement.

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Thin pilot

A thin pilot implements the smallest connected path needed to test the client decision. Read one authorized note, produce a draft, flag missing information, save/reload and review before export. A polished mockup alone cannot show recoverable state or measured review effort. Keep the manual workflow available as fallback.

## Step 2 · Fake integration

A fake integration supplies controlled outputs or failures to isolate orchestration. It is valuable when named honestly. The reference generator below is deterministic, not an AI model; it tests missing-objective and timeout handling. It cannot establish the quality or safety of a future model’s teaching content.

## Step 3 · Go/no-go evidence

Go/no-go evidence comes from the declared scenarios and thresholds. Keep normal, missing-objective and timeout results, including original input and status. A demo viewer should identify every fake/manual component without coaching. Do not infer time savings, readiness or permission for automatic distribution from a successful synthetic path.

chapters.title: Prototype, pilot, and production evidence
chapters.body:
### Match the build to the question
A prototype can test whether users understand a review screen using fake data. A pilot tests a bounded workflow with representative inputs and real operating constraints. Production serves ongoing work with assigned ownership and recovery. Label the stage clearly. A polished interface does not turn a prototype into production, and a local demo does not establish reliable multi-user operation.

### Build one vertical slice
For the handout service, implement source input → draft creation → instructor review → saved approved revision → export. A collection of disconnected screens cannot test the end-to-end handoff. Keep the slice small: one input template, one reviewer role, one output format. Preserve the manual fallback so the team can finish work if the pilot stops.

### Show uncertainty in the interface
Missing source information should appear as unresolved, not a confident completion. Display draft status, source revision, review state, and provider failure separately. A disabled export with a clear reason is more useful than silently producing an incomplete file. The interface should help a reviewer understand what requires judgment.

### Define what each evidence type proves
A screenshot proves appearance at a moment. An API response proves one request returned a value. A reload check can show persistence. A second-user denial shows one access boundary. A restore rehearsal demonstrates a recovery procedure in the tested environment. Combine evidence to support the claim you actually make; do not use a screenshot to claim database isolation.

### Add a stop rule
Choose a condition that pauses expansion: missing source ownership, unacceptable false acceptance, review time above the baseline, or no one available to operate the service. Agree on the rule before looking at favorable outputs. A failed pilot can still be a useful engagement when it prevents an expensive unsupported rollout.

### Pilot exercise
Write the decision question, smallest complete flow, representative cases, success measure, guardrail, fallback, and expansion gate. Implement the slice with synthetic data. Ask a reviewer to handle one unseen normal case and one failure without coaching. Record where the design failed to communicate its limits.

# Use client feedback without losing scope

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Build a thin pilot with visible limitations**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Build a thin pilot with visible limitations (`academy-v2:freelancing-masterclass:08`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Thin pilot** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: A narrow but complete end-to-end workflow that tests an agreed uncertainty.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **a data map, thin pilot and scoped feedback log**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Create a client-readable evaluation report**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Use client feedback without losing scope

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–8 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

Feedback contains bugs, preferences, new requirements, and misunderstandings. Classify it before acting. A bug violates an agreed acceptance condition; a preference changes presentation; a new requirement adds behavior or constraints. Record each item with an example and its effect on the user task.

Do not defend every design choice or accept every request immediately. Reproduce the issue, identify the responsible layer, and compare it with the scope. A change decision should include an impact on quality, effort, schedule, and tests. Maintain an evidence trail so review conversations refer to a specific version rather than different memories of a demo.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Defect

A behavior that violates an agreed acceptance condition.

### Preference

A requested presentation change judged against the audience and rubric.

### New requirement

Additional behavior or constraints outside the agreed scope.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Defect

A defect violates an existing acceptance condition. Reproduce it on the named release and fixture before estimating a fix. Losing an approved objective on export is a defect against the promised template; restoring it does not require inventing a new service package. Preserve failing and corrected observations.

## Step 2 · Preference

A preference changes presentation within the agreed task and still needs an audience reason. “Too formal” is not automatically a bug or an excuse to ignore the user. Compare two revisions on the instructor’s task and rubric, then record a decision. Avoid endless tone changes with no stopping criterion.

## Step 3 · New requirement

A new requirement changes capability, authority, input format or operational scope. Translation adds datasets and review needs; allowing assistants to approve changes permissions even if it is one dropdown. Classify by the promise and consequence rather than implementation size. Keep deferred work with an owner and reconsideration condition.

## Feedback triage and bounded iteration

### Treat feedback as evidence about a layer
Separate a source defect, model error, interface confusion, missing capability, and changed business objective. Each has a different owner and remedy. “The draft is wrong” might come from contradictory approved notes; a prompt tweak could hide the problem. Ask for the input, observed output, expected behavior, and consequence before choosing a fix.

### Use a triage record
Store ID, case revision, reporter role, observation, expected behavior, severity, owning layer, proposed action, and closure evidence. Link the record to an acceptance scenario if one exists. If the requested behavior falls outside the agreed scope, record it as a change candidate rather than silently absorbing it into defect work.

### Prioritize using consequence and reproducibility
A reproducible source-citation failure can block the pilot even if it appears rarely. A cosmetic request may be frequent but have little effect on acceptance. Use severity, exposure, and reversibility, and keep uncertainty visible. Avoid multiplying arbitrary scores into a false impression of precision.

### Close the learning loop
For each accepted fix, add a regression case, update the owning rule or component, and define when to recheck it. A fix is not closed merely because the developer changed something. The original reporter or an authorized reviewer should be able to repeat the case and observe the intended behavior.

### Retire stale controls
If a workaround no longer applies after a source or product change, give someone responsibility for removing it. Accumulated prompt instructions can conflict and become impossible to audit. Keep a reason and review date for temporary controls. Prefer a small testable rule over an ever-growing prompt warning.

### Feedback exercise
Create five feedback records covering source error, unclear review label, unsupported scan, duplicate job, and a new email feature. Classify defect versus change, assign an owner, and write the evidence needed for closure. Implement one simulated correction and rerun its failing case plus the existing representative set.

## A feedback triage and disposition log

## Walk through the data and decision

1. FB1 restores A1; FB2 needs audience-based review.

2. FB3 adds language scope, while FB4 changes authority.

3. Each disposition needs verification rather than a label alone.

## Completed specimen: A feedback triage and disposition log

| ID | Feedback and revision | Classification | Decision | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FB1 | D01-r2 export loses approved objective | Defect against A1 | Fix serialization | exported objective matches saved revision |
| FB2 | D01-r2 “tone too formal” | Preference | Test against instructor audience rubric | paired reviewer task |
| FB3 | “Translate into three languages” | New requirement | Prepare separate change; do not include now | new datasets/tests if accepted |
| FB4 | “Assistants should approve for instructors” | Permission change | Hold pending authority decision | allowed/denied-role cases |

Fixing FB1 restores the current promise; accepting FB3 changes it. FB2 needs a task-based reason rather than implementer taste. FB4 affects authority even if implemented as a dropdown.

For conflicting requests, quote the prior requirement and show alternatives, effort and acceptance impact. Keep a local decision note for this exercise; preparing a recommendation is not authorization to send a proposal.

## Critique and transfer

Classify ten role-play items, reproduce two defects, and write a change request for one expansion. Record a deferred item with owner and a condition for revisiting it.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

## Practice first, then integrate

## Bounded first practice

Classify four new feedback items against the current promise and write a disposition with observable verification for each.

## Practice acceptance

- The completed baseline/specimen is explained using the lesson walkthrough, with fixture assumptions distinguished from observations.
- Classify four new feedback items against the current promise and write a disposition with observable verification for each.
- The decision and counterexample are recorded with evidence and remaining uncertainty; simulated and observed results are labeled.

## Integrate after practice

## Worked example

“The export is missing the approved learning objectives” is a defect if the statement of work requires them. “Also translate all handouts into three languages” is a new requirement. “This paragraph is too formal” is a preference to test against the agreed audience and rubric.

## Build it yourself

1. Collect ten role-play feedback items and classify each.
2. Reproduce two defects with fixtures and add regression tests.
3. Write one change request for a genuine expansion.
4. Send no external messages; prepare a local decision log and revised milestone plan for review.

## Break it deliberately

A late preference conflicts with an earlier approved requirement. Document the conflict and obtain a scope decision before implementing it in the simulated engagement.

## Acceptance checks

- Feedback refers to examples and a version.
- Defects and new scope have different handling.
- Each accepted change updates relevant acceptance checks.

## Deliverable

Save **`client-03/feedback-decision-log.md`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

## Full project sequence

1. Collect ten role-play feedback items and classify each.
2. Reproduce two defects with fixtures and add regression tests.
3. Write one change request for a genuine expansion.
4. Send no external messages; prepare a local decision log and revised milestone plan for review.

## Integration acceptance

- Feedback refers to examples and a version.
- Defects and new scope have different handling.
- Each accepted change updates relevant acceptance checks.

## Apply the three engineering pillars

## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to a permissioned client-data inventory and prototype

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Compare a manual baseline with the prototype on identical synthetic inputs, reporting elapsed/review time, total attempts and accepted outputs.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Use a reviewed acceptance set with missing data and unsupported-claim cases; no polished demo substitutes for the failure report.

### Context Management

Build a source/permission manifest with digest/revision, token estimate, omitted fields and cache invalidation rules before any provider request.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to a permissioned client-data inventory and prototype

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Compare a manual baseline with the prototype on identical synthetic inputs, reporting elapsed/review time, total attempts and accepted outputs.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Use a reviewed acceptance set with missing data and unsupported-claim cases; no polished demo substitutes for the failure report.

### Context Management

Build a source/permission manifest with digest/revision, token estimate, omitted fields and cache invalidation rules before any provider request.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.
