# Create a client-readable evaluation report

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Use client feedback without losing scope**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Use client feedback without losing scope (`academy-v2:freelancing-masterclass:09`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Defect** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: A behavior that violates an agreed acceptance condition.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **an evaluation report, milestone plan and change ledger**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

## Understand the decision: Create a client-readable evaluation report

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–9 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

The client needs evidence relevant to the business task, not only technical test counts. Report whether outputs are supported, reviewable, complete, and appropriately escalated. Explain sample size and which input types remain untested. A small pilot can establish feasibility for its scope without demonstrating reliability at arbitrary volume.

Use the agreed dataset and preserve raw results. Separate contract failures, factual errors, review burden, and infrastructure problems. If the same examples shaped every iteration, state that limitation and test a small fresh set before the final decision. Never replace a failed example without explaining why it was excluded.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Client-readable evaluation

Results explained in terms of the agreed business task and limitations.

### Fresh review set

Representative examples not used to tune the current candidate.

### Conditional acceptance

Proceeding only with explicit unresolved conditions, owners and limits.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Client-readable evaluation

A client-readable evaluation explains inputs, rubric, candidate and outcomes without hiding behind one accuracy number. Sixteen complete cases, three clarifications and one unsupported statement describe different behaviors. Clarification can be correct yet impose review work. Preserve all twenty attempted cases and the strongest counterexample.

## Step 2 · Fresh review set

A fresh review set has not already guided prompt or implementation changes. Once a case is used to fix a defect it becomes regression evidence, not untouched evaluation. Retain its history and obtain genuinely new cases before claiming improved generalization. Record reviewer agreement and label uncertainties rather than inventing consensus.

## Step 3 · Conditional acceptance

Conditional acceptance states what can continue, under which controls and what remains blocking. One unsupported teaching claim may permit further reviewed pilot work but block unattended distribution. Separate format completeness, factual support, cost and correction effort. A favorable average cannot override a declared critical gate.

## Client-readable evaluation and decision reports

### Start with the decision
A useful report tells the buyer what was tested, what happened, and what decision the evidence supports. Put the scope and recommendation before tool names. A result such as “18 of 20 drafts preserved every required objective on dataset v2” is interpretable. “The AI scored 90%” lacks a denominator, a rubric, and consequences.

### Separate quality dimensions
For handouts, measure objective coverage, unsupported claims, source traceability, false acceptance, reviewer effort, and turnaround. A fluent output may still invent a requirement. An answer can cite an existing source ID while misrepresenting its text. Keep mechanical reference validation separate from factual entailment review.

### Classify results honestly
Report passed, failed, deferred, and not tested. Include raw counts and the most consequential failure. A small synthetic sample does not demonstrate performance on real client data, unseen languages, or scans. State those limits near the result, not only in an appendix. Label all fictional or role-play results as simulated.

### Explain the trade-off
Suppose version A accepts 9 of 10 drafts and includes one unsupported objective; version B accepts 7 and sends 3 to review with no unsupported accepted draft in the sample. The buyer must weigh review capacity against the cost of a wrong accepted output. Present both measures and recommend the next test, rather than declaring the version with a larger acceptance percentage the winner.

### Make the report reproducible
Include dataset revision, input selection rule, rubric, configuration revision, environment, and observed outputs. Preserve a small audit trail from claim to case record. Do not paste secret-bearing logs. A future maintainer should be able to rerun the evaluation and explain a changed score.

### Reporting exercise
Write a one-page decision memo and an evidence appendix. Include one accepted case, one rejection, one ambiguous case, a before/after comparison, and a recommendation with a condition that would reverse it. Ask a peer to identify what you did not test; revise any claim that overstates the evidence.

## A client-readable result and recommendation

## Walk through the data and decision

1. The specimen’s categories total 20 and include a factual blocker.

2. 16/20 is 80%, not a 95% accuracy claim.

3. The recommendation narrows use to reviewed pilot work while requiring a cause fix and fresh review.

## Completed specimen: A client-readable result and recommendation

**Candidate:** demo-r3; dataset: synthetic-notes-v2; 20 cases, all retained. This is an illustrative report, not a measured client result.

| Primary outcome | Count | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| Required sections present; no flagged issue in review | 16 | Passed these rubric checks |
| Source clarification required | 3 | Not ready for unattended distribution |
| Unsupported teaching statement | 1 | Blocking factual defect |
| Total | **20** | No cases excluded |

“16/20 complete without a flagged issue” describes this sample. It does not mean 95% accurate, nor does it establish that every sentence is correct. Report factual review and format completeness as separate dimensions when collecting real results. Include individual correction times; a synthetic average is not observed saving.

**Recommendation:** continue only as a reviewed pilot; block unattended release. Inspect the unsupported statement, identify its source/version, fix the cause, rerun affected cases and obtain fresh review before expansion. Three clarification outcomes may be correct system behavior but still consume reviewer capacity.

Replace the specimen with actual per-case results and review minutes from your pilot. Write a scoped recommendation and one condition that would change it; preserve the strongest counterexample.

4. Write a go, conditional-go, or stop recommendation supported by actual results.

An answer can cite an existing source ID while misrepresenting its text. Keep mechanical reference validation separate from factual entailment review.

### Classify results honestly
Report passed, failed, deferred, and not tested. Include raw counts and the most consequential failure. A small synthetic sample does not demonstrate performance on real client data, unseen languages, or scans. State those limits near the result, not only in an appendix. Label all fictional or role-play results as simulated.

### Explain the trade-off
Suppose version A accepts 9 of 10 drafts and includes one unsupported objective; version B accepts 7 and sends 3 to review with no unsupported accepted draft in the sample. The buyer must weigh review capacity against the cost of a wrong accepted output. Present both measures and recommend the next test, rather than declaring the version with a larger acceptance percentage the winner.

### Make the report reproducible
Include dataset revision, input selection rule, rubric, configuration revision, environment, and observed outputs. Preserve a small audit trail from claim to case record. Do not paste secret-bearing logs. A future maintainer should be able to rerun the evaluation and explain a changed score.

### Reporting exercise
Write a one-page decision memo and an evidence appendix. Include one accepted case, one rejection, one ambiguous case, a before/after comparison, and a recommendation with a condition that would reverse it. Ask a peer to identify what you did not test; revise any claim that overstates the evidence.

chapters.body:
## Walk through the data and decision

1. The specimen’s categories total 20 and include a factual blocker.

2. 16/20 is 80%, not a 95% accuracy claim.

3. The recommendation narrows use to reviewed pilot work while requiring a cause fix and fresh review.

## Completed specimen: A client-readable result and recommendation

**Candidate:** demo-r3; dataset: synthetic-notes-v2; 20 cases, all retained. This is an illustrative report, not a measured client result.

| Primary outcome | Count | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| Required sections present; no flagged issue in review | 16 | Passed these rubric checks |
| Source clarification required | 3 | Not ready for unattended distribution |
| Unsupported teaching statement | 1 | Blocking factual defect |
| Total | **20** | No cases excluded |

“16/20 complete without a flagged issue” describes this sample. It does not mean 95% accurate, nor does it establish that every sentence is correct. Report factual review and format completeness as separate dimensions when collecting real results. Include individual correction times; a synthetic average is not observed saving.

**Recommendation:** continue only as a reviewed pilot; block unattended release. Inspect the unsupported statement, identify its source/version, fix the cause, rerun affected cases and obtain fresh review before expansion. Three clarification outcomes may be correct system behavior but still consume reviewer capacity.

## Critique and transfer

Replace the specimen with actual per-case results and review minutes from your pilot. Write a scoped recommendation and one condition that would change it; preserve the strongest counterexample.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to a client acceptance report and change request

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Report per-accepted-output spend, p95 and reviewer corrections for the exact delivery candidate; keep failed and unavailable attempts visible.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Automate structural checks and attach authorized claim-level review. Block delivery when a mandatory gate fails even if averages improve.

### Context Management

Freeze source/prompt/model/context versions with the delivery manifest. Reevaluate after a change instead of silently expanding context.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

# Plan delivery milestones and manage risk

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Create a client-readable evaluation report**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Create a client-readable evaluation report (`academy-v2:freelancing-masterclass:10`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Client-readable evaluation** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: Results explained in terms of the agreed business task and limitations.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **an evaluation report, milestone plan and change ledger**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Manage change requests and commercial boundaries**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Plan delivery milestones and manage risk

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–10 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

A delivery plan should make dependencies and uncertainty visible early. Break work into milestones with an artifact, an acceptance check, a responsible person, and prerequisites. A milestone that only says “backend finished” tells the client little about usable progress. Prefer demonstrable slices such as “reviewed draft saved and reloaded.”

Maintain a risk register with likelihood assumptions, impact, mitigation, owner, and a trigger for action. The purpose is to decide what to do when conditions change, not to produce a long document nobody uses. Plan feedback windows and avoid scheduling all review at the end.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Milestone

A reviewable artifact with acceptance, an owner and prerequisites.

### Dependency

Something another activity needs before its claim can be completed.

### Risk trigger

An observable condition that prompts a planned mitigation or escalation.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Milestone

A milestone is an accepted artifact, not merely a calendar date or a percentage done. Define what observation closes it and who can accept it. M3 needs both a working M2 and reviewer availability; a developer finishing code alone cannot mark case-level factual acceptance complete.

## Step 2 · Dependency

A dependency is something another activity needs: approved templates, access, labels or a reviewer. A delay can leave useful independent work possible while still blocking acceptance. Separate implementation effort from elapsed waiting time. Keep synthetic progress labeled synthetic when real samples are unavailable.

## Step 3 · Risk trigger

A risk trigger tells an owner when to take a concrete action. “Reviewer unavailable before M3” can trigger a reschedule or authorized alternate; “monitor risk” does not change anything. Preserve quality and authority gates when revising dates instead of quietly deleting the task that caused the delay.

## Milestones, dependency risk, and delivery forecasting

### Make milestones observable
A milestone is a decision supported by an artifact: source readiness approved, vertical slice observed, evaluation reviewed, or handover rehearsed. “Backend complete” is difficult for a buyer to interpret. Connect each milestone to inputs, owner, acceptance evidence, and the next decision it unlocks.

### Plan around dependencies
Create a dependency graph for representative data, reviewer availability, access approval, implementation, evaluation, and acceptance. Work that depends on unknown source formats should not start with a promise of final quality. Schedule a short feasibility task first. Parallelize only work that can genuinely proceed without those answers.

### Maintain a risk register
For each risk record cause, possible event, consequence, likelihood evidence, mitigation, owner, trigger, and contingency. “AI may fail” is too vague. “Scanned notes may lose objective numbering; run a five-scan feasibility test before offering OCR support” gives you an action and a decision date. Track assumptions separately from problems already observed.

### Use ranges and update them
An estimate is a forecast based on current knowledge. Keep original and revised assumptions visible. When access is delayed, explain which milestone moves and what can still proceed. Do not silently reduce evaluation time to preserve a calendar date; that transfers risk into the deliverable without an explicit decision.

### Report progress through evidence
A useful status note contains completed evidence, current uncertainty, next decision, and help needed from the client. It should not be a list of hours spent. If the prototype works only on known good cases, say so. A blocker with a proposed smaller alternative is more actionable than a generic red status.

### Planning exercise
Build four milestones with owners and evidence, a dependency map, and five risks. Simulate a two-day delay in approved data and a reviewer absence. Reforecast the plan, identify a safe parallel task, and write a concise update that explains the impact without promising untested work.

## A milestone and risk decision sheet

## Walk through the data and decision

1. M1 stabilizes fields before M2; M3 needs reviewer and evaluation evidence.

2. Missing real notes permits synthetic build work, not real-data claims.

3. An unavailable instructor leaves acceptance pending until a named authorized reviewer can act.

## Completed specimen: A milestone and risk decision sheet

| Milestone | Artifact and acceptance | Dependency | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | labeled notes-v1 + agreed A1–A8 | template and instructor review | instructor |
| M2 | normal + timeout draft saved/reloaded | M1 fields stable | implementer |
| M3 | case-level evaluation + handover rehearsal | reviewer availability and M2 | operations lead |

| Risk | Trigger | Action | Consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reviewer unavailable | no slot before M3 | request new date or named alternate | acceptance pending, not passed |
| Real notes delayed | agreed intake date missed | continue synthetic implementation | real-data claims deferred |
| Source contradiction | two active objectives disagree | preserve conflict, request owner decision | draft review blocked |

A dependency delay may leave useful implementation work possible without making acceptance possible. Separate elapsed calendar time from effort. A risk owner must have an action they can take; “monitor closely” alone does not change the plan.

## Critique and transfer

Add two risks and simulate the instructor being absent for the last week. Revise milestone dates, labels and remaining claims without silently removing the factual-review gate.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

## Practice first, then integrate

## Bounded first practice

Replan a final-week reviewer absence without dropping factual review. Distinguish work that can continue from acceptance that must wait.

## Practice acceptance

- The completed baseline/specimen is explained using the lesson walkthrough, with fixture assumptions distinguished from observations.
- Replan a final-week reviewer absence without dropping factual review. Distinguish work that can continue from acceptance that must wait.
- The decision and counterexample are recorded with evidence and remaining uncertainty; simulated and observed results are labeled.

## Integrate after practice

## Worked example

Milestone 1 validates synthetic data and the acceptance dataset. Milestone 2 demonstrates draft-and-review persistence. Milestone 3 passes the scoped evaluation and handover rehearsal. If source access is delayed, the plan continues with fixtures but cannot claim real-data validation.

## Build it yourself

1. Create three delivery milestones with observable acceptance.
2. Map client access, reviewer availability, and provider setup as dependencies.
3. Write five risks with concrete triggers and mitigation owners.
4. Simulate a delayed dependency and revise the plan without hiding what remains unverified.

## Break it deliberately

The client reviewer is unavailable during the final week. Show which work can proceed and which acceptance decisions must remain pending.

## Acceptance checks

- Every milestone produces a reviewable artifact.
- Dependency delays do not become false completion claims.
- The risk plan includes actions triggered by observed conditions.

## Deliverable

Save **`client-04/delivery-plan.md`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

## Full project sequence

1. Create three delivery milestones with observable acceptance.
2. Map client access, reviewer availability, and provider setup as dependencies.
3. Write five risks with concrete triggers and mitigation owners.
4. Simulate a delayed dependency and revise the plan without hiding what remains unverified.

## Integration acceptance

- Every milestone produces a reviewable artifact.
- Dependency delays do not become false completion claims.
- The risk plan includes actions triggered by observed conditions.

## Apply the three engineering pillars

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

### Context Management

Freeze source/prompt/model/context versions with the delivery manifest. Reevaluate after a change instead of silently expanding context.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

chapters.title: Understand the decision: Plan delivery milestones and manage risk
chapters.body:
## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–10 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

A delivery plan should make dependencies and uncertainty visible early. Break work into milestones with an artifact, an acceptance check, a responsible person, and prerequisites. A milestone that only says “backend finished” tells the client little about usable progress. Prefer demonstrable slices such as “reviewed draft saved and reloaded.”

Maintain a risk register with likelihood assumptions, impact, mitigation, owner, and a trigger for action. The purpose is to decide what to do when conditions change, not to produce a long document nobody uses. Plan feedback windows and avoid scheduling all review at the end.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Milestone

A reviewable artifact with acceptance, an owner and prerequisites.

### Dependency

Something another activity needs before its claim can be completed.

### Risk trigger

An observable condition that prompts a planned mitigation or escalation.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Milestone

A milestone is an accepted artifact, not merely a calendar date or a percentage done. Define what observation closes it and who can accept it. M3 needs both a working M2 and reviewer availability; a developer finishing code alone cannot mark case-level factual acceptance complete.

## Step 2 · Dependency

A dependency is something another activity needs: approved templates, access, labels or a reviewer. A delay can leave useful independent work possible while still blocking acceptance. Separate implementation effort from elapsed waiting time. Keep synthetic progress labeled synthetic when real samples are unavailable.

## Step 3 · Risk trigger

A risk trigger tells an owner when to take a concrete action. “Reviewer unavailable before M3” can trigger a reschedule or authorized alternate; “monitor risk” does not change anything. Preserve quality and authority gates when revising dates instead of quietly deleting the task that caused the delay.

chapters.title: Milestones, dependency risk, and delivery forecasting
chapters.body:
### Make milestones observable
A milestone is a decision supported by an artifact: source readiness approved, vertical slice observed, evaluation reviewed, or handover rehearsed. “Backend complete” is difficult for a buyer to interpret. Connect each milestone to inputs, owner, acceptance evidence, and the next decision it unlocks.

### Plan around dependencies
Create a dependency graph for representative data, reviewer availability, access approval, implementation, evaluation, and acceptance. Work that depends on unknown source formats should not start with a promise of final quality. Schedule a short feasibility task first. Parallelize only work that can genuinely proceed without those answers.

### Maintain a risk register
For each risk record cause, possible event, consequence, likelihood evidence, mitigation, owner, trigger, and contingency. “AI may fail” is too vague. “Scanned notes may lose objective numbering; run a five-scan feasibility test before offering OCR support” gives you an action and a decision date. Track assumptions separately from problems already observed.

### Use ranges and update them
An estimate is a forecast based on current knowledge. Keep original and revised assumptions visible. When access is delayed, explain which milestone moves and what can still proceed. Do not silently reduce evaluation time to preserve a calendar date; that transfers risk into the deliverable without an explicit decision.

### Report progress through evidence
A useful status note contains completed evidence, current uncertainty, next decision, and help needed from the client. It should not be a list of hours spent. If the prototype works only on known good cases, say so. A blocker with a proposed smaller alternative is more actionable than a generic red status.

### Planning exercise
Build four milestones with owners and evidence, a dependency map, and five risks. Simulate a two-day delay in approved data and a reviewer absence. Reforecast the plan, identify a safe parallel task, and write a concise update that explains the impact without promising untested work.

chapters.title: A milestone and risk decision sheet
chapters.body:
## Walk through the data and decision

1. M1 stabilizes fields before M2; M3 needs reviewer and evaluation evidence.

2. Missing real notes permits synthetic build work, not real-data claims.

3. An unavailable instructor leaves acceptance pending until a named authorized reviewer can act.

## Completed specimen: A milestone and risk decision sheet

| Milestone | Artifact and acceptance | Dependency | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | labeled notes-v1 + agreed A1–A8 | template and instructor review | instructor |
| M2 | normal + timeout draft saved/reloaded | M1 fields stable | implementer |
| M3 | case-level evaluation + handover rehearsal | reviewer availability and M2 | operations lead |

| Risk | Trigger | Action | Consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reviewer unavailable | no slot before M3 | request new date or named alternate | acceptance pending, not passed |
| Real notes delayed | agreed intake date missed | continue synthetic implementation | real-data claims deferred |
| Source contradiction | two active objectives disagree | preserve conflict, request owner decision | draft review blocked |

A dependency delay may leave useful implementation work possible without making acceptance possible. Separate elapsed calendar time from effort. A risk owner must have an action they can take; “monitor closely” alone does not change the plan.

## Critique and transfer

Add two risks and simulate the instructor being absent for the last week. Revise milestone dates, labels and remaining claims without silently removing the factual-review gate.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to a client acceptance report and change request

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Report per-accepted-output spend, p95 and reviewer corrections for the exact delivery candidate; keep failed and unavailable attempts visible.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Automate structural checks and attach authorized claim-level review. Block delivery when a mandatory gate fails even if averages improve.

### Context Management

Freeze source/prompt/model/context versions with the delivery manifest. Reevaluate after a change instead of silently expanding context.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

## Understand the decision: Manage change requests and commercial boundaries

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–11 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

Scope control protects both the client outcome and your ability to deliver it. A change request should describe the requested behavior, why it matters, alternatives, and impacts on data, tests, cost, and schedule. Small interface changes can have large implications if they introduce new roles or external actions.

In the simulated engagement, prepare changes locally for review rather than sending proposals or making commitments. Actual commercial and contractual decisions require agreement between the parties. The useful skill is making the trade-off concrete enough that the buyer can choose knowingly.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Scope impact

How a request changes behavior, data flows, tests, duties or schedule.

### Operational effect

A change in external state such as sending messages or publishing content.

### Alternative option

A smaller route to the buyer’s objective with explicitly different trade-offs.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Scope impact

Scope impact identifies the new input, output, user authority and acceptance promise behind a requested change. Automatic email is not just one extra button: it adds recipients, sending credentials and an irreversible external effect. Start from the current local-export boundary and enumerate what must change before estimating effort.

## Step 2 · Operational effect

Operational effect includes retries, uncertain results, duplicate prevention, monitoring and incident ownership. A timeout after remote acceptance cannot safely be retried under a new key. Exact recipient/content approval must survive dispatch and reconciliation. The exercise uses fake effects and plans; no message is sent.

## Step 3 · Alternative option

An alternative option lets the buyer choose a smaller workflow that still addresses the need. A local dispatch manifest for a human sender may avoid hosted sending while retaining review. Present consequences and unresolved estimates honestly. Accepting a change requires consistent scope, data-flow, milestone and test revisions rather than a verbal yes to a feature.

## Change control and commercial conversations

### Identify a change by behavior
A request is a change when it alters supported inputs, roles, effects, scale, quality criteria, operating duties, or agreed outputs. “Just send the handout automatically” introduces recipient selection, authorization, duplicate-send prevention, audit history, and recovery. Its size cannot be judged by the number of interface fields.

### Write an impact assessment
Record requested outcome, current boundary, proposed behavior, affected data, permissions, tests, dependencies, effort range, operating cost, and schedule impact. Offer at least one smaller alternative. For automated distribution, an export-ready draft with explicit manual send may meet the immediate need while avoiding a new external-action surface.

### Separate defect from changed expectation
If the app fails an agreed supported case, investigate a defect. If the buyer introduces a new format that was excluded, assess a change. If the original document was ambiguous, acknowledge and resolve the ambiguity rather than using scope as an excuse. Preserve the evidence and update the shared specification once a decision is made.

### Make the decision traceable
Use approved, rejected, deferred, or needs investigation. Record the authorized decision maker and the revision of scope, estimate, and acceptance affected by an approved change. Do not implement new consequential actions on informal enthusiasm alone. In this course, prepare local simulated decisions; no message or contract is sent.

### Protect the relationship through clarity
Explain the goal you share, the new work it entails, the alternatives, and the decision needed. Avoid defensive phrases or unexplained surcharges. The aim is for both sides to understand cost, time, and risk before work starts. A precise smaller option is often more useful than a binary yes or no.

### Change exercise
Assess a new input format, a reviewer-role change, and automatic email. For each identify five affected tests or operating duties, provide an estimate range, and propose an alternative. Update your simulated delivery plan for one accepted change and rerun its acceptance scenarios.

## A change request for automatic email

## Walk through the data and decision

1. CR-03 names new authority and data destinations before discussing implementation.

2. The uncertain-send case needs reconciliation, not automatic fresh retry.

3. The current simulated pilot defers sending and retains reviewed local export.

## Completed specimen: A change request for automatic email

**CR-03, proposed only:** send approved handouts to participants. **Reason:** reduce manual distribution work. **Current scope:** local reviewed export; no external sends.

**New requirements:** client-owned sending account, approved recipient source, sender permission, exact content/recipient approval, durable idempotency key, send-outcome ledger, retry/reconciliation behavior, opt-in test environment and incident owner. A lost send response is uncertain; repeating with a new key can duplicate delivery.

**Acceptance additions:** stale approval blocked; unauthorized sender denied; duplicate submission produces one fake effect; timeout after fake acceptance reconciled; wrong recipient never silently repaired. **Data-flow impact:** recipient addresses and provider logs become new data destinations.

**Alternatives:** retain reviewed local export; or create a local dispatch manifest for a human sender. **Estimate:** investigate provider and test environment before quoting effort. **Decision:** defer CR-03 in the simulated pilot and finish A1–A8. No email is sent by this exercise.

Prepare one cosmetic and one permission change in the same format. For an accepted hypothetical change, update milestones, estimate, data register and tests; demonstrate all four affected artifacts agree.

chapters.body:
## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–11 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

Scope control protects both the client outcome and your ability to deliver it. A change request should describe the requested behavior, why it matters, alternatives, and impacts on data, tests, cost, and schedule. Small interface changes can have large implications if they introduce new roles or external actions.

In the simulated engagement, prepare changes locally for review rather than sending proposals or making commitments. Actual commercial and contractual decisions require agreement between the parties. The useful skill is making the trade-off concrete enough that the buyer can choose knowingly.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Scope impact

How a request changes behavior, data flows, tests, duties or schedule.

### Operational effect

A change in external state such as sending messages or publishing content.

### Alternative option

A smaller route to the buyer’s objective with explicitly different trade-offs.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Scope impact

Scope impact identifies the new input, output, user authority and acceptance promise behind a requested change. Automatic email is not just one extra button: it adds recipients, sending credentials and an irreversible external effect. Start from the current local-export boundary and enumerate what must change before estimating effort.

## Step 2 · Operational effect

Operational effect includes retries, uncertain results, duplicate prevention, monitoring and incident ownership. A timeout after remote acceptance cannot safely be retried under a new key. Exact recipient/content approval must survive dispatch and reconciliation. The exercise uses fake effects and plans; no message is sent.

## Step 3 · Alternative option

An alternative option lets the buyer choose a smaller workflow that still addresses the need. A local dispatch manifest for a human sender may avoid hosted sending while retaining review. Present consequences and unresolved estimates honestly. Accepting a change requires consistent scope, data-flow, milestone and test revisions rather than a verbal yes to a feature.

chapters.title: Change control and commercial conversations
chapters.body:
### Identify a change by behavior
A request is a change when it alters supported inputs, roles, effects, scale, quality criteria, operating duties, or agreed outputs. “Just send the handout automatically” introduces recipient selection, authorization, duplicate-send prevention, audit history, and recovery. Its size cannot be judged by the number of interface fields.

### Write an impact assessment
Record requested outcome, current boundary, proposed behavior, affected data, permissions, tests, dependencies, effort range, operating cost, and schedule impact. Offer at least one smaller alternative. For automated distribution, an export-ready draft with explicit manual send may meet the immediate need while avoiding a new external-action surface.

### Separate defect from changed expectation
If the app fails an agreed supported case, investigate a defect. If the buyer introduces a new format that was excluded, assess a change. If the original document was ambiguous, acknowledge and resolve the ambiguity rather than using scope as an excuse. Preserve the evidence and update the shared specification once a decision is made.

### Make the decision traceable
Use approved, rejected, deferred, or needs investigation. Record the authorized decision maker and the revision of scope, estimate, and acceptance affected by an approved change. Do not implement new consequential actions on informal enthusiasm alone. In this course, prepare local simulated decisions; no message or contract is sent.

### Protect the relationship through clarity
Explain the goal you share, the new work it entails, the alternatives, and the decision needed. Avoid defensive phrases or unexplained surcharges. The aim is for both sides to understand cost, time, and risk before work starts. A precise smaller option is often more useful than a binary yes or no.

### Change exercise
Assess a new input format, a reviewer-role change, and automatic email. For each identify five affected tests or operating duties, provide an estimate range, and propose an alternative. Update your simulated delivery plan for one accepted change and rerun its acceptance scenarios.

## Completed specimen: A change request for automatic email

**CR-03, proposed only:** send approved handouts to participants. **Reason:** reduce manual distribution work. **Current scope:** local reviewed export; no external sends.

**New requirements:** client-owned sending account, approved recipient source, sender permission, exact content/recipient approval, durable idempotency key, send-outcome ledger, retry/reconciliation behavior, opt-in test environment and incident owner. A lost send response is uncertain; repeating with a new key can duplicate delivery.

**Acceptance additions:** stale approval blocked; unauthorized sender denied; duplicate submission produces one fake effect; timeout after fake acceptance reconciled; wrong recipient never silently repaired. **Data-flow impact:** recipient addresses and provider logs become new data destinations.

**Alternatives:** retain reviewed local export; or create a local dispatch manifest for a human sender. **Estimate:** investigate provider and test environment before quoting effort. **Decision:** defer CR-03 in the simulated pilot and finish A1–A8. No email is sent by this exercise.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to a client acceptance report and change request

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Report per-accepted-output spend, p95 and reviewer corrections for the exact delivery candidate; keep failed and unavailable attempts visible.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Automate structural checks and attach authorized claim-level review. Block delivery when a mandatory gate fails even if averages improve.

### Context Management

Freeze source/prompt/model/context versions with the delivery manifest. Reevaluate after a change instead of silently expanding context.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

# Deploy with client-owned access and a recovery path

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Manage change requests and commercial boundaries**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Manage change requests and commercial boundaries (`academy-v2:freelancing-masterclass:12`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Scope impact** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: How a request changes behavior, data flows, tests, duties or schedule.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **a recovery runbook, acceptance record and support agreement**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Train users and run acceptance testing**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Deploy with client-owned access and a recovery path

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–12 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

A deployment is a transfer of operational responsibility. Decide who owns hosting, domains, provider accounts, billing, backups, and incident response. Do not create a dependency on your private account unless the arrangement is explicit and appropriate. For the program, use a local isolated environment and simulate the ownership handoff.

A runbook must cover routine use and failure handling. Document health checks, configuration names, log locations, restore steps, and escalation. Keep secret values outside the document. Verify a backup restore into an isolated database. A deployment checklist is evidence of work only when its steps have actually been performed and recorded.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Operational ownership

The party responsible for service accounts, data, recurring charges and incident response.

### Recovery evidence

An observed restart or restore result rather than an unchecked backup file.

### Credential separation

Client operation does not depend on an implementer’s private personal key.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Operational ownership

Operational ownership identifies who can administer hosting, data, billing, review and incidents after handover. The client’s service identity must be separate from the implementer’s temporary role. A named account in a table is not proof the client can operate it; require a fresh-operator action and actual readback.

## Step 2 · Recovery evidence

Recovery evidence ties restart and restore observations to a release, snapshot and representative records. Restoring into an isolated target protects the source during rehearsal. An intact backup file is not enough. Show which data point was recovered and which post-snapshot work would be absent; keep recovery limits explicit.

## Step 3 · Credential separation

Credential separation removes the implementer without destroying runtime or administrator access. List configuration names and the agreed secret-store procedure, never secret values in the runbook. A local role simulation teaches the access rule; it does not prove a real cloud IAM policy or production disaster-recovery plan.

## Operational ownership, rollout, and recovery

### Transfer capability, not just files
Handover succeeds when the client can run, administer, pay for, and recover the service without your private accounts. Create an ownership matrix for hosting, domain, provider account, database, backups, user administration, and incident decisions. Include a named fallback owner where possible.

### Rehearse the deployment path
Record configuration names, supported runtime, migration command, health check, and a simple smoke case. Keep secret values in the agreed secret store. Deploy into an isolated environment first and record the version actually running. “Works on my laptop” does not prove the client environment has its dependencies or network access.

### Roll out in stages
Use a limited group or shadow output before wider use. Choose promotion and rollback criteria in advance: quality, review burden, latency, error rate, and cost. Shadow generation must not create external effects. A rollback needs a known previous version and compatible data, not merely an old container image.

### Restore data as a test
A backup file is not evidence of recoverability. Restore into a separate database, verify a known record and access boundaries, and record time and errors. Understand which data would be lost between backups and how long restoration takes. Those observations inform recovery objectives; they do not guarantee every future incident will match the rehearsal.

### Remove implementer access
Use a simulated implementer role and revoke it after handover. Verify the client administrator and routine operator still work. Rotate shared development credentials where necessary. Check deployment automation does not depend on your personal token.

### Handover exercise
Create the ownership matrix, deploy the pilot locally, save a record, restart, restore into isolation, and remove implementer access. Have a peer follow the runbook without coaching. Record any undocumented assumption and repair the instructions before acceptance.

## An ownership and recovery handover matrix

## Walk through the data and decision

1. The matrix gives administrator, runtime and reviewer distinct responsibilities.

2. Revoke implementer should preserve service and administrator operation.

3. Restart/restore claims need observed content, not checked boxes.

## Completed specimen: An ownership and recovery handover matrix

| Asset | Accountable owner | Implementer access | Handover observation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hosting/service | client administrator | temporary limited role | client restarts service after revoke |
| Database and backups | client administrator | scoped deployment role | isolated restore content checked |
| Content review | instructor | no approval authority by default | instructor reviews fresh draft |
| Provider account, if added | client billing owner | restricted runtime credential | revoke implementer without stopping service |
| Recurring charges | operations lead | read-only cost visibility if agreed | cost owner identified |

The runbook lists configuration **names**, never secret values. State how the administrator finds the agreed secret store and rotates access. Record exact release and backup IDs, observed restore content and limitations. A checked box without an observation is not a handover test.

For the local simulation, use distinct roles and synthetic records. Revoking an implementer role must not remove the application’s separate service identity or the client administrator’s recovery access.

## Critique and transfer

Perform local restart/readback and an isolated restore. Give a peer the runbook, remove your simulated operator role and record what they can still operate without your credentials.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

## Practice first, then integrate

## Bounded first practice

Run a self-contained local role/recovery rehearsal: revoke the implementer, retain administrator/runtime readback and verify an isolated backup restore.

## Practice acceptance

- The completed baseline/specimen is explained using the lesson walkthrough, with fixture assumptions distinguished from observations.

- The decision and counterexample are recorded with evidence and remaining uncertainty; simulated and observed results are labeled.

## Integrate after practice

## Worked example

The client owns the service account; the implementer receives a limited role. At handover, the role can be removed without stopping the application. The runbook lists variable names, while credentials remain in the agreed secret store. A synthetic restore test confirms data recovery before acceptance.

## Build it yourself

1. Create an ownership matrix for infrastructure, data, credentials, and recurring charges.
2. Deploy the pilot locally with runtime configuration and persistent storage.
3. Restart it and verify a saved record survives.
4. Perform an isolated restore and document how implementer access is revoked.

## Break it deliberately

Remove the implementer’s simulated account. The application and client administrator should still work without borrowing the implementer’s credentials.

## Acceptance checks

- Service ownership is independent of personal credentials.
- Persistence and restoration are observed.
- The runbook contains no secret values.

## Deliverable

Save **`client-05/operations-handover.md`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **180 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

## Full project sequence

1. Create an ownership matrix for infrastructure, data, credentials, and recurring charges.
2. Deploy the pilot locally with runtime configuration and persistent storage.
3. Restart it and verify a saved record survives.
4. Perform an isolated restore and document how implementer access is revoked.

## Integration acceptance

- Service ownership is independent of personal credentials.
- Persistence and restoration are observed.
- The runbook contains no secret values.

## Apply the three engineering pillars

## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to an operator runbook and incident drill

### Deterministic Evaluation

Have a fresh operator restart, read back, deny wrong-owner access and restore isolated synthetic records; attach transcripts and unresolved failures.

### Context Management

Define who can refresh data, revoke access, invalidate caches and prune logs. A handover needs lifecycle ownership, not a folder of prompts.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

exercise.solution:
## Complete guided-practice reference

Attempt the changed case first, then compare your reasoning with this completed response. This is a worked decision under stated assumptions, not evidence of performed client work.

## Completed local rehearsal reference

Save/run the Python below in a new scratch folder. It uses synthetic roles and a temporary SQLite database. It tests local access policy and representative restored content only.

**Runbook record:** release synthetic-r1; record d1; expected restored body reviewed draft; implementer role removed; administrator/runtime retained. Replace these expected observations with your actual output. Cloud IAM, encrypted backup custody, live service restart and recovery-time targets remain untested. No real credentials or accounts are changed.

```python
import sqlite3,tempfile
from pathlib import Path
roles={'implementer','administrator','runtime'}
def read_as(actor,db):
    if actor not in roles:return None
    return db.execute('SELECT id,body FROM drafts').fetchall()
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    root=Path(folder);source=sqlite3.connect(root/'source.sqlite');backup=sqlite3.connect(root/'backup.sqlite')
    source.execute('CREATE TABLE drafts(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,body TEXT)')
    with source:source.execute('INSERT INTO drafts VALUES(?,?)',('d1','reviewed draft'))
    source.backup(backup);roles.remove('implementer')
    assert read_as('implementer',source) is None
    assert read_as('runtime',source)==[('d1','reviewed draft')]
    restore=sqlite3.connect(root/'restore.sqlite');backup.backup(restore)
    assert read_as('administrator',restore)==[('d1','reviewed draft')]
    for db in [source,backup,restore]:db.close()
print('local implementer denied; runtime retained; administrator read isolated restored d1; cloud roles untested')
```

## Expected reference observation

```text
local implementer denied; runtime retained; administrator read isolated restored d1; cloud roles untested
```

## If your result differs

If revocation removes the runtime identity too, roles were conflated. A local policy dictionary cannot certify actual cloud permissions.

## Explain before continuing

Name the decision or invariant your change protects. Compare the baseline with your result, retain the failed case, and state what remains untested in the larger project.

chapters.body:
## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–12 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

A deployment is a transfer of operational responsibility. Decide who owns hosting, domains, provider accounts, billing, backups, and incident response. Do not create a dependency on your private account unless the arrangement is explicit and appropriate. For the program, use a local isolated environment and simulate the ownership handoff.

A runbook must cover routine use and failure handling. Document health checks, configuration names, log locations, restore steps, and escalation. Keep secret values outside the document. Verify a backup restore into an isolated database. A deployment checklist is evidence of work only when its steps have actually been performed and recorded.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Operational ownership

The party responsible for service accounts, data, recurring charges and incident response.

### Recovery evidence

An observed restart or restore result rather than an unchecked backup file.

### Credential separation

Client operation does not depend on an implementer’s private personal key.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Operational ownership

Operational ownership identifies who can administer hosting, data, billing, review and incidents after handover. The client’s service identity must be separate from the implementer’s temporary role. A named account in a table is not proof the client can operate it; require a fresh-operator action and actual readback.

## Step 2 · Recovery evidence

Recovery evidence ties restart and restore observations to a release, snapshot and representative records. Restoring into an isolated target protects the source during rehearsal. An intact backup file is not enough. Show which data point was recovered and which post-snapshot work would be absent; keep recovery limits explicit.

## Step 3 · Credential separation

Credential separation removes the implementer without destroying runtime or administrator access. List configuration names and the agreed secret-store procedure, never secret values in the runbook. A local role simulation teaches the access rule; it does not prove a real cloud IAM policy or production disaster-recovery plan.

chapters.title: Operational ownership, rollout, and recovery
chapters.body:
### Transfer capability, not just files
Handover succeeds when the client can run, administer, pay for, and recover the service without your private accounts. Create an ownership matrix for hosting, domain, provider account, database, backups, user administration, and incident decisions. Include a named fallback owner where possible.

### Rehearse the deployment path
Record configuration names, supported runtime, migration command, health check, and a simple smoke case. Keep secret values in the agreed secret store. Deploy into an isolated environment first and record the version actually running. “Works on my laptop” does not prove the client environment has its dependencies or network access.

### Roll out in stages
Use a limited group or shadow output before wider use. Choose promotion and rollback criteria in advance: quality, review burden, latency, error rate, and cost. Shadow generation must not create external effects. A rollback needs a known previous version and compatible data, not merely an old container image.

### Restore data as a test
A backup file is not evidence of recoverability. Restore into a separate database, verify a known record and access boundaries, and record time and errors. Understand which data would be lost between backups and how long restoration takes. Those observations inform recovery objectives; they do not guarantee every future incident will match the rehearsal.

### Remove implementer access
Use a simulated implementer role and revoke it after handover. Verify the client administrator and routine operator still work. Rotate shared development credentials where necessary. Check deployment automation does not depend on your personal token.

### Handover exercise
Create the ownership matrix, deploy the pilot locally, save a record, restart, restore into isolation, and remove implementer access. Have a peer follow the runbook without coaching. Record any undocumented assumption and repair the instructions before acceptance.

chapters.title: An ownership and recovery handover matrix
chapters.body:
## Walk through the data and decision

1. The matrix gives administrator, runtime and reviewer distinct responsibilities.

2. Revoke implementer should preserve service and administrator operation.

3. Restart/restore claims need observed content, not checked boxes.

## Completed specimen: An ownership and recovery handover matrix

| Asset | Accountable owner | Implementer access | Handover observation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hosting/service | client administrator | temporary limited role | client restarts service after revoke |
| Database and backups | client administrator | scoped deployment role | isolated restore content checked |
| Content review | instructor | no approval authority by default | instructor reviews fresh draft |
| Provider account, if added | client billing owner | restricted runtime credential | revoke implementer without stopping service |
| Recurring charges | operations lead | read-only cost visibility if agreed | cost owner identified |

The runbook lists configuration **names**, never secret values. State how the administrator finds the agreed secret store and rotates access. Record exact release and backup IDs, observed restore content and limitations. A checked box without an observation is not a handover test.

For the local simulation, use distinct roles and synthetic records. Revoking an implementer role must not remove the application’s separate service identity or the client administrator’s recovery access.

## Critique and transfer

Perform local restart/readback and an isolated restore. Give a peer the runbook, remove your simulated operator role and record what they can still operate without your credentials.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to an operator runbook and incident drill

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Include routine usage, alert response, fallback and restore labor in the ongoing service budget. Compare capacity assumptions with actual drill observations.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Have a fresh operator restart, read back, deny wrong-owner access and restore isolated synthetic records; attach transcripts and unresolved failures.

### Context Management

Define who can refresh data, revoke access, invalidate caches and prune logs. A handover needs lifecycle ownership, not a folder of prompts.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.
