# Train users and run acceptance testing

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Deploy with client-owned access and a recovery path**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Deploy with client-owned access and a recovery path (`academy-v2:freelancing-masterclass:13`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Operational ownership** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: The party responsible for service accounts, data, recurring charges and incident response.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **a recovery runbook, acceptance record and support agreement**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Support boundaries, maintenance, and incident review**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Train users and run acceptance testing

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–13 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

Training should teach the workflow, review responsibilities, and failure response rather than only where to click. Users need to know when to trust a draft, how to inspect evidence, when to escalate, and how to recover from an unavailable service. Give them realistic cases they have not seen before.

Acceptance testing belongs to the authorized reviewer using the agreed scenarios. Record passed, failed, deferred, and not-tested separately. A user attending a demo does not establish acceptance. A useful handover rehearsal observes someone else operating the system without the implementer correcting every step.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Acceptance session

An authorized reviewer checks agreed scenarios and records their actual outcomes.

### Not tested

No observation establishes whether a condition passes or fails.

### Handover rehearsal

Another person uses the guide and system without continual author intervention.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Acceptance session

An acceptance session asks an authorized user to perform defined tasks on a candidate revision. Demonstrating a feature for them measures attendance, not independent use. Include missing information and failure cases, preserve any assistance you give and ask the trainee to explain why a draft cannot yet be distributed.

## Step 2 · Not tested

Not tested is a distinct status from passed, failed and out of scope. A missing instructor makes factual acceptance untested; an optional PDF outside the agreed input boundary is deferred. Mixing those categories produces false green reports. Keep failed first attempts after a correction so the reason for changed teaching remains visible.

## Step 3 · Handover rehearsal

A handover rehearsal checks whether instructions and system labels support independent operation. “Draft complete” can mislead a trainee into bypassing review. Change the label and instructions, then observe a fresh input without coaching. Repeating the same coached case to success does not establish the new instruction works independently.

## Training design and user acceptance rehearsal

### Teach decisions before clicks
Users need to know what is a draft, how to inspect source evidence, what makes an output unacceptable, and when to escalate. A click tour on a perfect example does not teach those decisions. Design training around a normal case, an incomplete source, a contradiction, an unavailable provider, and a stale edit.

### Define role-specific tasks
An operator creates a draft; a reviewer accepts or rejects a revision; an administrator manages access. Teach each role its own responsibility and boundary. Do not imply that a green generation status means approval. Give the reviewer a short rubric and show how corrections affect the saved artifact.

### Observe teach-back
Ask the trainee to complete an unseen case and explain why they accepted or rejected it. Avoid taking over the mouse or supplying the answer at every hesitation. Record confusion, source lookups, mistakes, and time. Those observations evaluate both the guide and the interface.

### Run acceptance separately from training
Acceptance belongs to the authorized owner using agreed scenarios and evidence. Attending training is not acceptance. Keep passed, failed, deferred, and not tested distinct. A failed recovery scenario cannot be hidden behind a successful generation demo. Update the acceptance record when a defect is repaired and retested.

### Build a usable quick-start guide
Include purpose, supported inputs, normal steps, review rubric, common failure symptoms, fallback procedure, and escalation owner. Use synthetic examples. Include version and review date so a changed interface does not leave users following stale instructions.

### Training exercise

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–13 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

Training should teach the workflow, review responsibilities, and failure response rather than only where to click. Users need to know when to trust a draft, how to inspect evidence, when to escalate, and how to recover from an unavailable service. Give them realistic cases they have not seen before.

Acceptance testing belongs to the authorized reviewer using the agreed scenarios. Record passed, failed, deferred, and not-tested separately. A user attending a demo does not establish acceptance. A useful handover rehearsal observes someone else operating the system without the implementer correcting every step.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Acceptance session

An authorized reviewer checks agreed scenarios and records their actual outcomes.

### Not tested

No observation establishes whether a condition passes or fails.

### Handover rehearsal

Another person uses the guide and system without continual author intervention.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Acceptance session

An acceptance session asks an authorized user to perform defined tasks on a candidate revision. Demonstrating a feature for them measures attendance, not independent use. Include missing information and failure cases, preserve any assistance you give and ask the trainee to explain why a draft cannot yet be distributed.

## Step 2 · Not tested

Not tested is a distinct status from passed, failed and out of scope. A missing instructor makes factual acceptance untested; an optional PDF outside the agreed input boundary is deferred. Mixing those categories produces false green reports. Keep failed first attempts after a correction so the reason for changed teaching remains visible.

## Step 3 · Handover rehearsal

A handover rehearsal checks whether instructions and system labels support independent operation. “Draft complete” can mislead a trainee into bypassing review. Change the label and instructions, then observe a fresh input without coaching. Repeating the same coached case to success does not establish the new instruction works independently.

chapters.title: Training design and user acceptance rehearsal
chapters.body:
### Teach decisions before clicks
Users need to know what is a draft, how to inspect source evidence, what makes an output unacceptable, and when to escalate. A click tour on a perfect example does not teach those decisions. Design training around a normal case, an incomplete source, a contradiction, an unavailable provider, and a stale edit.

### Define role-specific tasks
An operator creates a draft; a reviewer accepts or rejects a revision; an administrator manages access. Teach each role its own responsibility and boundary. Do not imply that a green generation status means approval. Give the reviewer a short rubric and show how corrections affect the saved artifact.

### Observe teach-back
Ask the trainee to complete an unseen case and explain why they accepted or rejected it. Avoid taking over the mouse or supplying the answer at every hesitation. Record confusion, source lookups, mistakes, and time. Those observations evaluate both the guide and the interface.

### Run acceptance separately from training
Acceptance belongs to the authorized owner using agreed scenarios and evidence. Attending training is not acceptance. Keep passed, failed, deferred, and not tested distinct. A failed recovery scenario cannot be hidden behind a successful generation demo. Update the acceptance record when a defect is repaired and retested.

### Build a usable quick-start guide
Include purpose, supported inputs, normal steps, review rubric, common failure symptoms, fallback procedure, and escalation owner. Use synthetic examples. Include version and review date so a changed interface does not leave users following stale instructions.

### Training exercise
Write a five-case rehearsal. Have another person or a clearly labeled role-play operator use your guide. Capture the observed result and one improvement per failure. End with an acceptance record that identifies unresolved conditions and who can decide whether they block handover.

## Understand the decision: Support boundaries, maintenance, and incident review

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–14 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

Support is a defined service, not an indefinite promise to fix everything immediately. Specify the supported environment, reporting channel, coverage assumptions, severity definitions, and responsibility for third-party changes. Distinguish response targets from resolution guarantees. For a simulated engagement, use illustrative assumptions rather than a commitment to real clients.

Plan maintenance around dependencies that change: model behavior, provider availability, source documents, and application versions. A model or prompt revision can change quality even when the UI code is unchanged. Rerun representative evaluations before promotion and keep a recovery path. Incident review should identify contributing conditions and corrective checks rather than assign blame.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Support scope

Defined coverage, environment, responsibilities and escalation assumptions.

### Response target

A planned time to acknowledge or begin handling a report, distinct from guaranteed resolution.

### Incident review

A record of observations, recovery and contributing conditions with testable corrective actions.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Support scope

Support scope states covered versions, environments, hours and responsibilities. Separate operational troubleshooting from new features and factual approval duties. A service must say who can pause exports and who resolves source contradictions. Support capacity is recurring effort that belongs in the estimate, not an unlimited promise bundled with a pilot.

## Step 2 · Response target

A response target is time to acknowledge or triage under an agreed coverage assumption; it is not a guaranteed resolution time. Severity depends on impact and available fallback. Preserve uncertainty about a provider outage rather than promising a fix outside your control. Escalate to the named owner with evidence and a safe manual path.

## Step 3 · Incident review

An incident review reconstructs timeline, affected source/release IDs, contributing conditions, containment, recovery and prevention checks. Restarting a service cannot repair stale policy selection. Keep original drafts and supersession history, then require new exact-revision review. A blameless review still needs concrete owners and testable corrective actions.

## Support design and incident learning

### Specify the supported service
Name the environment, versions, features, reporting route, coverage window, and excluded changes. Distinguish response target from resolution guarantee. An incident caused by a third-party outage may be outside your repair control while still requiring diagnosis and a fallback. Use illustrative assumptions in this course rather than making real service commitments.

### Classify incidents by consequence
Define examples: unavailable drafting, unauthorized access, unsupported accepted content, slow response, and cosmetic defects. A low error count does not make an authorization failure low severity. Record affected users, exposure period, workaround, and the decision owner. Avoid including private content in broadly shared incident notes.

### Contain, recover, then investigate
Pause external effects or promotion when needed. Preserve enough evidence to understand the incident without copying secrets. Restore a safe operating path, including manual operation if appropriate. After recovery, reconstruct the timeline, contributing conditions, detection gap, and corrective actions.

### Treat model and source changes as releases
A prompt, model, retrieval setting, or policy revision can change behavior without a frontend code change. Keep their revisions and rerun representative evaluations before promotion. Maintain a rollback or source-deactivation path. A restart does not fix a stale policy index.

### Close actions with evidence
Assign each corrective action an owner, due condition, and verification case. “Be more careful” is not a control. “The index activation step rejects a source revision without a completed evaluation record” is testable. Review whether temporary controls should be retired after the underlying fix.

### Incident exercise
Simulate a source-policy update that makes an accepted handout stale. Identify affected outputs, disable the stale revision, prepare a local reviewer note, restore the correct source, and add a regression case. Write a short incident review with facts separated from hypotheses.

## Completed specimen: An incident tabletop with concrete corrective checks

**Scenario:** yesterday’s handout cites returns-v1 after returns-v2 became active. **Impact in simulation:** three drafts may contain stale teaching conditions; no automatic distribution exists.

**Timeline:** 09:00 instructor detects mismatch; 09:05 operator pauses affected exports; 09:15 source owner confirms effective revision; 09:30 affected drafts identified by source ID; 10:00 corrected drafts await review. These times are fictional tabletop events, not an actual incident.

**Contributing conditions:** active pointer changed without evaluation; drafts did not show source age. **Recovery:** preserve original drafts, record supersession, regenerate against confirmed v2 and obtain new review. Restarting the API alone does not change source selection.

**Corrective checks:** current query uses v2; historical-date query still retrieves v1 when appropriate; edited draft invalidates approval; source revision is visible in the review screen. Assign one owner and due date to each. A support response target is time to acknowledge/triage, not a guarantee of resolution.

3. Read data-policy.json and requests.csv from lessons 7–9. Only id, source and text are approved. policy-v1 permits a verbatim source draft. An empty source or unapproved revision routes to needs_source; no model fills the gap.

## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. ## Completed specimen: An incident tabletop with concrete corrective checks

**Scenario:** yesterday’s handout cites returns-v1 after returns-v2 became active. **Impact in simulation:** three drafts may contain stale teaching conditions; no automatic distribution exists.

**Timeline:** 09:00 instructor detects mismatch; 09:05 operator pauses affected exports; 09:15 source owner confirms effective revision; 09:30 affected drafts identified by source ID; 10:00 corrected drafts await review. These times are fictional tabletop events, not an actual incident.

**Contributing conditions:** active pointer changed without evaluation; drafts did not show source age. **Recovery:** preserve original drafts, record supersession, regenerate against confirmed v2 and obtain new review. Restarting the API alone does not change source selection.

**Corrective checks:** current query uses v2; historical-date query still retrieves v1 when appropriate; edited draft invalidates approval; source revision is visible in the review screen. Assign one owner and due date to each. A support response target is time to acknowledge/triage, not a guarantee of resolution.

## Critique and transfer

Write coverage, severity and escalation assumptions for a small service. Run a provider-format-change tabletop and record retained data, manual fallback, recovery checks and one prevention test.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

chapters.title: Connect the taught pieces before the capstone
chapters.body:
# Complete simulated client engagement

The capstone is a coherent client delivery, not a claim that a real client signed off. Use Python 3.12; no third-party package, model account or another program is needed. The client/ files are complete synthetic artifacts, and engagement.py actually runs their pilot and recovery checks.

## Build the engagement in order

1. Read baseline.json: 40 items × (8−5) minutes − 30 maintenance minutes = 90 projected minutes/week. These are fictional assumptions; they are not observed ROI. Match the buyer and workflow to the discovery and baseline lessons 1–3.
2. Compare offer.json and scope.json from lessons 4–6. Every promise must be in scope and have an acceptance ID. Automatic publication, real hosting and factual client acceptance are explicitly excluded. A fixed estimate is not permission to expand scope.
3. Read data-policy.json and requests.csv from lessons 7–9. Only id, source and text are approved. policy-v1 permits a verbatim source draft. An empty source or unapproved revision routes to needs_source; no model fills the gap.
4. acceptance.json fixes expected outcomes before the pilot runs. engagement.py opens a fresh SQLite file, writes drafts, closes it and reads back independently. It compares actual statuses and text with those unchanged cases. A passed schema or exact string is mechanical evidence, not general semantic review.
5. changes.json and support.json carry lessons 10–15 forward: reject an automatic-publication scope change, name manual fallback and assign maintenance/retention responsibility. The script creates a real backup, restores into a distinct file and compares rows through fresh connections. It does not simply trust a supplied recovery=true flag.
6. The report, client-email.md and case-study.md carry lessons 16–18 into the same client identity. They distinguish local checks, illustrative projections and unperformed human acceptance. Do not replace untested fields with passed to make the handover look complete. The generated email is a local file; nothing is sent.

## Run the delivered pilot and its counterexamples

From this directory:

```sh
python3 engagement.py --inputs client --output my-delivery
python3 check.py
```

Use a fresh output folder for each run; existing pilot databases are preserved rather than overwritten. Expected: scoped_local_handover true, client_acceptance not_performed; check.py prints actual pilot/acceptance/restore success and blocks four changed inputs. Inspect my-delivery/acceptance-report.json, client-email.md, case-study.md and restored.sqlite3. The source artifact hashes bind the report to the files you actually ran.

## Transfer and useful feedback

Change the buyer, source and baseline consistently across the client packet. Write the new acceptance cases before running the pilot. Deliberately add an unsupported promise and confirm it blocks handover; then restore the scoped offer. A failing expected label means the candidate disagrees with the fixed contract; it is not permission to rewrite labels after observing output. A human still needs to review factual usefulness, client authority and real deployment acceptance before any real engagement. Submit both the failed output and the scoped correction. Latency/restore duration are measured locally, costs stay unknown, and source/retention boundaries are explicit.


The final project chapter in this program provides every file, exact commands and the failure checks. Explain the storage, ownership and observed-result boundaries above before proceeding. No code from another program is required.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to an operator runbook and incident drill

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Include routine usage, alert response, fallback and restore labor in the ongoing service budget. Compare capacity assumptions with actual drill observations.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Have a fresh operator restart, read back, deny wrong-owner access and restore isolated synthetic records; attach transcripts and unresolved failures.

### Context Management

Define who can refresh data, revoke access, invalidate caches and prune logs. A handover needs lifecycle ownership, not a folder of prompts.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

lessons.title: Write an evidence-based case study
lessons.content:
# Write an evidence-based case study

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Support boundaries, maintenance, and incident review**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Support boundaries, maintenance, and incident review (`academy-v2:freelancing-masterclass:15`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Support scope** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: Defined coverage, environment, responsibilities and escalation assumptions.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **a consent-aware case study and consistent final client packet**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Prepare outreach and qualification responsibly**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Understand the decision: Write an evidence-based case study

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–15 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

A credible case study explains the client context, constraints, decisions, implementation, observed results, and remaining limitations. Ask for permission before using real client names, logos, quotes, or data. A self-directed project is valid when labeled accurately. Do not invent testimonials or imply a simulated buyer is a paying customer.

Use the same baseline and evaluation definitions from discovery. If the pilot improved one measure but worsened another, include the trade-off. Screenshots can illustrate a workflow, but they do not replace evidence of persistence, access control, or factual support. Show the artifact that substantiates each technical claim.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Permissioned case study

A portfolio uses client identity or data only with appropriate permission.

### Simulated engagement

A self-directed scenario accurately labeled rather than represented as a paying client.

### Claim-evidence map

Each result statement points to its baseline, evaluation or implementation artifact.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Permissioned case study

A permissioned case study uses only authorized client identity, artifacts, quotations and data. A self-directed simulation can still show valuable engineering decisions without inventing a customer endorsement. Keep permission to publish separate from access to build or test; the latter does not grant rights to a logo or confidential screenshot.

## Step 2 · Simulated engagement

A simulated engagement must be labeled wherever an outcome could be mistaken for commercial evidence. Ten synthetic notes and a role-play buyer are not ten customer projects. Describe the setup, your work, the failed attempt and its correction. Do not turn illustrative numbers in the specimen into measured results in a portfolio.

## Step 3 · Claim-evidence map

A claim-evidence map connects each sentence to the observation supporting its population and revision. A two-minute difference over ten notes supports twenty minutes on that sample if actually measured, not future monthly saving. Narrow broad “secure” or “production-ready” claims to the exact ownership, recovery or load cases observed.

## Portfolio claims and evidence-backed case studies

### Make one claim per evidence trail
A case study should connect context, constraint, decision, implementation, measured result, and limitation. For each result, identify the dataset, baseline, metric, sample size, and artifact. “Built an AI assistant” is a capability description. “Saved drafts persisted after restart on the local test stack” is a scoped technical observation.

### Label simulated work accurately
A self-directed project can demonstrate useful engineering. Call the training provider fictional and the engagement simulated. Do not turn role-play feedback into a testimonial or say a paying client used the service. Accuracy about provenance makes the technical evidence easier to trust.

### Show a consequential failure
Include an example that changed your design: a missing objective produced invented text, a stale edit overwrote approval, or an export included an unreviewed draft. Explain how you reproduced the failure, what changed, and which test now catches it. A polished screenshot without this reasoning does not show how you handle delivery risk.

### Separate local results from general claims
A ten-document synthetic evaluation can support a statement about those cases and settings. It cannot establish performance on every client document or predict business savings. Show the remaining uncertainty and the next validation step. Avoid a percentage without a denominator or a comparison without a common rubric.

### Protect others' information
Use synthetic artifacts or explicit permission for names, data, quotes, and logos. Redact credentials, internal URLs, and private records from logs and images. A public repository is not automatically a suitable place for a client's operational details.

### Case-study exercise
Write a one-page narrative and a claim-to-evidence table. Include one architecture sketch, a workflow example, a before/after comparison, an important failure, and an operational limitation. Ask a peer to challenge your strongest claim and narrow it until every word is supported.

## A case-study claim audit

## Walk through the data and decision

1. The audit replaces broad claims with scoped evidence requirements.

2. Two minutes across ten observations totals 20 minutes only for that sample.

3. Permission for logos/quotes and actual client attribution remains absent in the simulation.

## Completed specimen: A case-study claim audit

| Draft claim | Supporting evidence required | Defensible wording |
|---|---|---|
| “Saved a client hours” | actual client baseline and comparable timed work | “Simulated engagement; ten synthetic notes” until measured |
| “Review fell from 8 to 6 minutes” | same task definition, case-level times and sample | “In a ten-note synthetic comparison, mean review was 8 versus 6 minutes” if actually observed |
| “Secure app” | much broader evidence than this pilot | “Cross-account read denied in the recorded ownership cases” |
| “Production-ready” | operations, load, recovery and organizational acceptance | “Offline reviewed prototype with stated limits” |

If the two-minute difference is observed over ten notes, that is 20 minutes on that sample, not proof of future monthly savings. Include differences in errors or reviewer workload. Describe one failed attempt, its cause and the test that motivated the correction.

No customer quote, logo or simulated buyer is presented as a real endorsement. Specific evidence preserves the value of a self-directed project without inventing a commercial history.

## Critique and transfer

Audit five statements in your own case study. Link each to a real evidence file or narrow/remove it. Include a failure and clearly label every simulated result.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

## Practice first, then integrate

## Bounded first practice

Audit five portfolio claims and narrow/remove each one according to the available synthetic evidence.

## Practice acceptance

- The completed baseline/specimen is explained using the lesson walkthrough, with fixture assumptions distinguished from observations.
- Audit five portfolio claims and narrow/remove each one according to the available synthetic evidence.
- The decision and counterexample are recorded with evidence and remaining uncertainty; simulated and observed results are labeled.

## Integrate after practice

## Worked example

“Simulated engagement for a training provider: draft review time fell from eight to six minutes on ten synthetic notes, while two outputs required source clarification.” This is a scoped observation. It does not establish market demand or predict a client’s future savings.

## Build it yourself

1. Write a case study using only synthetic or permissioned artifacts.
2. Map each result claim to a baseline, evaluation record, or test.
3. Include one failed attempt and the decision it changed.
4. Review all labels for simulated versus actual work.

## Break it deliberately

A portfolio draft says “helped a client” when the engagement was fictional. Correct it and preserve the value through specific implementation evidence.

## Acceptance checks

- No invented customer, result, or testimonial appears.
- Claims include sample size and scope.
- A failure and its correction are explained.

## Deliverable

Save **`client-06/case-study.md`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

## Full project sequence

1. Write a case study using only synthetic or permissioned artifacts.
2. Map each result claim to a baseline, evaluation record, or test.
3. Include one failed attempt and the decision it changed.
4. Review all labels for simulated versus actual work.

## Integration acceptance

- No invented customer, result, or testimonial appears.
- Claims include sample size and scope.
- A failure and its correction are explained.

## Apply the three engineering pillars

## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to an evidence-backed case study and reusable service package

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Publish only observed latency, costs and accepted outcomes with workload caveats; do not turn a one-client result into a universal ROI promise.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Link each public claim to dataset/release and acceptance evidence. Test the reusable package with a different synthetic client and retain failures.

### Context Management

Remove client data from reusable templates, reset owner/source IDs and test cross-client isolation and stale-cache rejection.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

chapters.body:
## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–15 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

A credible case study explains the client context, constraints, decisions, implementation, observed results, and remaining limitations. Ask for permission before using real client names, logos, quotes, or data. A self-directed project is valid when labeled accurately. Do not invent testimonials or imply a simulated buyer is a paying customer.

Use the same baseline and evaluation definitions from discovery. If the pilot improved one measure but worsened another, include the trade-off. Screenshots can illustrate a workflow, but they do not replace evidence of persistence, access control, or factual support. Show the artifact that substantiates each technical claim.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Permissioned case study

A portfolio uses client identity or data only with appropriate permission.

### Simulated engagement

A self-directed scenario accurately labeled rather than represented as a paying client.

### Claim-evidence map

Each result statement points to its baseline, evaluation or implementation artifact.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Permissioned case study

A permissioned case study uses only authorized client identity, artifacts, quotations and data. A self-directed simulation can still show valuable engineering decisions without inventing a customer endorsement. Keep permission to publish separate from access to build or test; the latter does not grant rights to a logo or confidential screenshot.

## Step 2 · Simulated engagement

A simulated engagement must be labeled wherever an outcome could be mistaken for commercial evidence. Ten synthetic notes and a role-play buyer are not ten customer projects. Describe the setup, your work, the failed attempt and its correction. Do not turn illustrative numbers in the specimen into measured results in a portfolio.

## Step 3 · Claim-evidence map

A claim-evidence map connects each sentence to the observation supporting its population and revision. A two-minute difference over ten notes supports twenty minutes on that sample if actually measured, not future monthly saving. Narrow broad “secure” or “production-ready” claims to the exact ownership, recovery or load cases observed.

chapters.title: Portfolio claims and evidence-backed case studies
chapters.body:
### Make one claim per evidence trail
A case study should connect context, constraint, decision, implementation, measured result, and limitation. For each result, identify the dataset, baseline, metric, sample size, and artifact. “Built an AI assistant” is a capability description. “Saved drafts persisted after restart on the local test stack” is a scoped technical observation.

### Label simulated work accurately
A self-directed project can demonstrate useful engineering. Call the training provider fictional and the engagement simulated. Do not turn role-play feedback into a testimonial or say a paying client used the service. Accuracy about provenance makes the technical evidence easier to trust.

### Show a consequential failure
Include an example that changed your design: a missing objective produced invented text, a stale edit overwrote approval, or an export included an unreviewed draft. Explain how you reproduced the failure, what changed, and which test now catches it. A polished screenshot without this reasoning does not show how you handle delivery risk.

### Separate local results from general claims
A ten-document synthetic evaluation can support a statement about those cases and settings. It cannot establish performance on every client document or predict business savings. Show the remaining uncertainty and the next validation step. Avoid a percentage without a denominator or a comparison without a common rubric.

### Protect others' information
Use synthetic artifacts or explicit permission for names, data, quotes, and logos. Redact credentials, internal URLs, and private records from logs and images. A public repository is not automatically a suitable place for a client's operational details.

### Case-study exercise
Write a one-page narrative and a claim-to-evidence table. Include one architecture sketch, a workflow example, a before/after comparison, an important failure, and an operational limitation. Ask a peer to challenge your strongest claim and narrow it until every word is supported.

chapters.title: A case-study claim audit
chapters.body:
## Walk through the data and decision

1. The audit replaces broad claims with scoped evidence requirements.

2. Two minutes across ten observations totals 20 minutes only for that sample.

3. Permission for logos/quotes and actual client attribution remains absent in the simulation.

## Completed specimen: A case-study claim audit

| Draft claim | Supporting evidence required | Defensible wording |
|---|---|---|
| “Saved a client hours” | actual client baseline and comparable timed work | “Simulated engagement; ten synthetic notes” until measured |
| “Review fell from 8 to 6 minutes” | same task definition, case-level times and sample | “In a ten-note synthetic comparison, mean review was 8 versus 6 minutes” if actually observed |
| “Secure app” | much broader evidence than this pilot | “Cross-account read denied in the recorded ownership cases” |
| “Production-ready” | operations, load, recovery and organizational acceptance | “Offline reviewed prototype with stated limits” |

If the two-minute difference is observed over ten notes, that is 20 minutes on that sample, not proof of future monthly savings. Include differences in errors or reviewer workload. Describe one failed attempt, its cause and the test that motivated the correction.

No customer quote, logo or simulated buyer is presented as a real endorsement. Specific evidence preserves the value of a self-directed project without inventing a commercial history.

## Critique and transfer

Audit five statements in your own case study. Link each to a real evidence file or narrow/remove it. Include a failure and clearly label every simulated result.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to an evidence-backed case study and reusable service package

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Publish only observed latency, costs and accepted outcomes with workload caveats; do not turn a one-client result into a universal ROI promise.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Link each public claim to dataset/release and acceptance evidence. Test the reusable package with a different synthetic client and retain failures.

### Context Management

Remove client data from reusable templates, reset owner/source IDs and test cross-client isolation and stale-cache rejection.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

## Next checkpoint

## Understand the decision: Prepare outreach and qualification responsibly

## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–16 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

Outreach should connect a plausible workflow problem to relevant evidence, not promise generic AI transformation. Research an organization’s published business information and distinguish what you know from what you infer. A useful first conversation asks permission to explore a specific problem and makes it easy to decline.

This lesson prepares drafts only; it does not send messages or scrape private contacts. Use fictional prospects for practice or published business channels with the proper authorization in a real engagement. Qualification checks whether the buyer has a relevant problem, authority, feasible data access, timing, and a realistic review process. Declining a poor fit protects both sides.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Qualification

Checking problem fit, authority, data feasibility, timing and review capacity.

### Published fact

Information actually available from an identifiable public business source.

### Outreach assumption

An unverified inference that should be phrased as a question, not an asserted problem.

## Learn each concept step by step

Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Qualification

Qualification asks whether a workflow, authority, permitted data, review capacity, timing and resources fit the bounded service. Interest in AI is not enough. Ask for a recent task and a reason the workflow may not fit. A decline can be the correct outcome when the required review or permission is absent.

## Step 2 · Published fact

A published fact is a sourced statement about a prospect; it is not evidence of an internal pain point. A profile listing four cohorts supports the cohort count only. Keep the source/date and separate the hypothesis that handout preparation is costly. This exercise uses fictional profiles, so it performs no prospect research or real outreach.

## Step 3 · Outreach assumption

An outreach assumption should be posed as a question, not asserted as a diagnosed problem. Describe the synthetic prototype honestly, invite a discussion only if relevant and avoid guaranteed savings. Preparing local drafts is separate from sending messages. No message, access request or proposal is sent by this learning exercise.

## Qualification and problem-specific outreach preparation

### Research a plausible workflow, then ask
Published information can suggest an operating context; it rarely proves an internal problem. A business running many courses may prepare handouts, but you cannot infer that its current process is broken. Write the public fact, your inference, and the question you would ask in separate fields.

### Qualify fit before proposing delivery
Check problem relevance, owner authority, access feasibility, review capacity, timing, and the ability to measure an outcome. A buyer who wants fully autonomous publication but cannot assign a reviewer may not fit your current service. A respectful decline or a diagnostic is preferable to an unsupported promise.

### Draft a concise introduction
Use a relevant public observation, a specific workflow hypothesis, one accurately labeled piece of evidence, and an invitation to discuss the current process. Do not invent urgency, savings, or a relationship. For the exercise, use fictional organizations and keep messages as local drafts.

### Prepare useful follow-up questions
Ask for a recent example, the current completion rule, what causes rework, who reviews results, and which data can be used in a pilot. Avoid requesting confidential files before access is agreed. If someone declines, record the outcome and do not turn follow-up into pressure.

### Evaluate your own readiness
Before offering a capability, confirm you can demonstrate its normal behavior, a failure, evidence of persistence, the review boundary, and a recovery path. A demo built on hand-picked examples may be suitable for learning but insufficient for a real engagement. Qualify yourself as carefully as the prospect.

### Qualification exercise
Create three fictional prospect records, separate observations from assumptions, draft an introduction, and write five discovery questions. Define three decline conditions. Have a peer role-play an enthusiastic but unsuitable buyer and explain a bounded alternative without promising results you have not observed.

## A local outreach draft and qualification decision

## Walk through the data and decision

1. The fictional cohort count remains a fact about the supplied profile only.

2. Preparation pain and budget authority remain hypotheses.

3. Reviewer absence or unauthorized data are explicit decline/rescope conditions.

## Completed specimen: A local outreach draft and qualification decision

**Fictional prospect fact:** the training provider’s public-style profile lists four live cohorts. **Hypothesis:** instructors may spend time preparing handouts; this has not been observed.

**Unsent draft:** “Your course profile lists several live cohorts. I built a synthetic handout-review prototype that may be relevant to preparation work. If this is a current priority, would a short discussion of your existing process be useful? The example is a reviewed draft workflow, not automatic teaching or distribution.”

**Qualification agenda:** who owns the workflow and budget; recent concrete example; volume and correction work; authority to use samples; reviewer availability; timing; acceptable fallback. Ask for access only after its scope is agreed.

**Decline/rescope conditions:** no reviewer for factual teaching, no permission to use the input, or demand for guaranteed unsupported outcomes. A polite response or interest in AI is not a qualified buying decision. This exercise prepares local drafts only and sends nothing.

## Critique and transfer

Create three fictional profiles with facts and hypotheses separate. Prepare one introduction and one disconfirming question for each. Role-play a request for confidential autonomous processing and record your scope response.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

## Bounded first practice

## Practice acceptance

- The decision and counterexample are recorded with evidence and remaining uncertainty; simulated and observed results are labeled.

## Integrate after practice

A local draft says “Your public course page mentions several live cohorts. I built a synthetic handout-review prototype that may be relevant to preparation work. If that workflow is a priority, I’d be interested in understanding your current process.” It avoids claiming the organization has a problem you have not observed.

## Build it yourself

1. Create three fictional prospect profiles with evidence and assumptions separated.
2. Draft a short problem-specific introduction and a follow-up question for each.
3. Write a qualification checklist and three reasons to decline.
4. Prepare a discovery agenda that requests no sensitive documents before access is agreed.

## Break it deliberately

A prospect wants a fully autonomous workflow involving confidential records with no review. Explain the scope or evidence conditions needed before proceeding.

## Acceptance checks

- Drafts distinguish published facts from assumptions.
- No message is sent as part of the exercise.
- Qualification includes authority, data, and review feasibility.

## Deliverable

Save **`client-06/outreach-drafts.md`** in your separate program workspace. Include your inputs, actual outputs, decisions, and unresolved limitations. Budget about **120 minutes** for reading, implementation and review; this is an estimate, not a timed requirement.

## Explain your judgment

Which acceptance check would change your decision if it failed? Explain what your artifact demonstrates and what it cannot establish. Completion in this academy records your own report; the platform does not execute your work or certify it.

1. Create three fictional prospect profiles with evidence and assumptions separated.
2. Draft a short problem-specific introduction and a follow-up question for each.
3. Write a qualification checklist and three reasons to decline.
4. Prepare a discovery agenda that requests no sensitive documents before access is agreed.

- Drafts distinguish published facts from assumptions.
- No message is sent as part of the exercise.
- Qualification includes authority, data, and review feasibility.

exercise.solution:
## Complete guided-practice reference

Attempt the changed case first, then compare your reasoning with this completed response. This is a worked decision under stated assumptions, not evidence of performed client work.

## Completed qualification cards

| Fictional profile fact | Hypothesis | Disconfirming question |
|---|---|---|
| Four live cohorts listed | Repeated handout preparation might be costly | How many handouts need revision, and who reviews them? |
| One annual workshop listed | Volume may be too low for a pilot | Is there recurring work outside that event? |
| Public course templates listed | A bounded text workflow may be possible | Are those templates authorized inputs and is an instructor available? |

**Unsent introduction:** “I built a synthetic, instructor-reviewed handout prototype. If preparation is a current priority, would discussing one recent workflow be useful?” Adapt the fact sentence only to the supplied fictional card; never claim an unobserved saving.

**Role-play response to confidential autonomous processing:** decline that scope; offer only an explicitly authorized input/review boundary if feasible. Qualification remains unresolved until actual permission, task evidence and decision authority are established.

## If your result differs

If every profile is marked qualified, the process lacks a disconfirming gate. Do not present fictional people or published facts as customer consent.

## Explain before continuing

Name the decision or invariant your change protects. Compare the baseline with your result, retain the failed case, and state what remains untested in the larger project.

chapters.title: Understand the decision: Prepare outreach and qualification responsibly
chapters.body:
## Before you begin

Bring your artifacts from sessions 1–16 of this program. Continue the same fictional training-provider engagement and keep assumption labels and revision IDs intact.

## Why this decision matters

Outreach should connect a plausible workflow problem to relevant evidence, not promise generic AI transformation. Research an organization’s published business information and distinguish what you know from what you infer. A useful first conversation asks permission to explore a specific problem and makes it easy to decline.

This lesson prepares drafts only; it does not send messages or scrape private contacts. Use fictional prospects for practice or published business channels with the proper authorization in a real engagement. Qualification checks whether the buyer has a relevant problem, authority, feasible data access, timing, and a realistic review process. Declining a poor fit protects both sides.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Qualification

Checking problem fit, authority, data feasibility, timing and review capacity.

### Published fact

Information actually available from an identifiable public business source.

### Outreach assumption

An unverified inference that should be phrased as a question, not an asserted problem.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Work through these explanations before the completed example or exercise. Follow the inputs, mechanism and decision boundary rather than memorizing the definitions.

## Step 1 · Qualification

Qualification asks whether a workflow, authority, permitted data, review capacity, timing and resources fit the bounded service. Interest in AI is not enough. Ask for a recent task and a reason the workflow may not fit. A decline can be the correct outcome when the required review or permission is absent.

## Step 2 · Published fact

A published fact is a sourced statement about a prospect; it is not evidence of an internal pain point. A profile listing four cohorts supports the cohort count only. Keep the source/date and separate the hypothesis that handout preparation is costly. This exercise uses fictional profiles, so it performs no prospect research or real outreach.

## Step 3 · Outreach assumption

An outreach assumption should be posed as a question, not asserted as a diagnosed problem. Describe the synthetic prototype honestly, invite a discussion only if relevant and avoid guaranteed savings. Preparing local drafts is separate from sending messages. No message, access request or proposal is sent by this learning exercise.

chapters.title: Qualification and problem-specific outreach preparation
chapters.body:
### Research a plausible workflow, then ask
Published information can suggest an operating context; it rarely proves an internal problem. A business running many courses may prepare handouts, but you cannot infer that its current process is broken. Write the public fact, your inference, and the question you would ask in separate fields.

### Qualify fit before proposing delivery
Check problem relevance, owner authority, access feasibility, review capacity, timing, and the ability to measure an outcome. A buyer who wants fully autonomous publication but cannot assign a reviewer may not fit your current service. A respectful decline or a diagnostic is preferable to an unsupported promise.

### Draft a concise introduction
Use a relevant public observation, a specific workflow hypothesis, one accurately labeled piece of evidence, and an invitation to discuss the current process. Do not invent urgency, savings, or a relationship. For the exercise, use fictional organizations and keep messages as local drafts.

### Prepare useful follow-up questions
Ask for a recent example, the current completion rule, what causes rework, who reviews results, and which data can be used in a pilot. Avoid requesting confidential files before access is agreed. If someone declines, record the outcome and do not turn follow-up into pressure.

### Evaluate your own readiness
Before offering a capability, confirm you can demonstrate its normal behavior, a failure, evidence of persistence, the review boundary, and a recovery path. A demo built on hand-picked examples may be suitable for learning but insufficient for a real engagement. Qualify yourself as carefully as the prospect.

### Qualification exercise
Create three fictional prospect records, separate observations from assumptions, draft an introduction, and write five discovery questions. Define three decline conditions. Have a peer role-play an enthusiastic but unsuitable buyer and explain a bounded alternative without promising results you have not observed.

chapters.title: A local outreach draft and qualification decision
chapters.body:
## Walk through the data and decision

1. The fictional cohort count remains a fact about the supplied profile only.

2. Preparation pain and budget authority remain hypotheses.

3. Reviewer absence or unauthorized data are explicit decline/rescope conditions.

## Completed specimen: A local outreach draft and qualification decision

**Fictional prospect fact:** the training provider’s public-style profile lists four live cohorts. **Hypothesis:** instructors may spend time preparing handouts; this has not been observed.

**Unsent draft:** “Your course profile lists several live cohorts. I built a synthetic handout-review prototype that may be relevant to preparation work. If this is a current priority, would a short discussion of your existing process be useful? The example is a reviewed draft workflow, not automatic teaching or distribution.”

**Qualification agenda:** who owns the workflow and budget; recent concrete example; volume and correction work; authority to use samples; reviewer availability; timing; acceptable fallback. Ask for access only after its scope is agreed.

**Decline/rescope conditions:** no reviewer for factual teaching, no permission to use the input, or demand for guaranteed unsupported outcomes. A polite response or interest in AI is not a qualified buying decision. This exercise prepares local drafts only and sends nothing.

## Critique and transfer

Create three fictional profiles with facts and hypotheses separate. Prepare one introduction and one disconfirming question for each. Role-play a request for confidential autonomous processing and record your scope response.

Treat the completed specimen as a model of reasoning, not a result to copy into your own evidence. Your submission must replace its assumptions and statuses with your own observations, or remain explicitly simulated.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to an evidence-backed case study and reusable service package

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Publish only observed latency, costs and accepted outcomes with workload caveats; do not turn a one-client result into a universal ROI promise.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Link each public claim to dataset/release and acceptance evidence. Test the reusable package with a different synthetic client and retain failures.

### Context Management

Remove client data from reusable templates, reset owner/source IDs and test cross-client isolation and stale-cache rejection.

## Failure and deployment work

Assign rate/budget caps, failure/manual fallback, hosting ownership, review duties, restore evidence and escalation before expanding the service.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.
