chapters.title: Carry rule-and-exception units into the actual retriever
chapters.body:
## Before this studio

Sessions 7–8: immutable document identities, source locators and chunk budgets. Inputs here are already owner-filtered; the final HTTP adapter performs that filter in SQL.

## Step 1 · Choose a boundary that has an explicit meaning

This corpus treats a blank-line-separated paragraph as one reviewed evidence unit. Splitting every 350 characters can leave a refund rule in one chunk and its exclusion in the next. The query may match only the rule, silently dropping the exclusion. Paragraphs are not universally semantic: the source author or ingestion review must ensure dependent conditions stay together. The example deliberately makes its exception appear beyond the old 350-character cut.

## Step 2 · Rank without losing provenance

Each candidate retains document ID, paragraph position and immutable revision alongside its text. A regex produces lowercase word sets; overlap supplies a transparent lexical score. Stable ID tie-breaking makes repeated fixture runs reproducible. This is not an embedding model or an applicability classifier. Owner filtering must happen before private text reaches this function; adding a scope check after answer construction is too late.

## Step 3 · Refuse a split you have not taught the system to make safely

The 700-character allowance is an explicit evidence budget, not a token limit. A relevant paragraph larger than the allowance raises a reviewed-split error. The final service translates that into needs_correction with no answer or citations. It conservatively refuses even if another smaller passage fits, because silently dropping a relevant exception could mislead. Review the unit or change a measured model-specific budget; do not slice its first 700 characters to make the check pass.

## Step 4 · Keep context selection distinct from answer quality

Whole units are admitted until the character allowance is exhausted. The return value includes selected IDs/text/revisions and actual selected character count. This protects the chosen boundary but cannot prove the selected policy applies to the user. The final extractive fixture labels its model and leaves token usage unknown. Its candidate cache key serializes query, pipeline, route and evidence revisions canonically; no cache is implemented and cache_hit remains false.

## Complete worked example

Save this entire block as example.py in a fresh directory. Run `python3.12 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. All imports are included; no account, provider call or other course is required.

```python
import re
def select_context(text,documents,budget=700):
 """Owner filtering is the caller's responsibility, before passing documents."""
 terms=set(re.findall(r'[a-z]+',text.lower()))
 ranked=[]
 for document in documents:
  # A blank-line-delimited evidence unit must retain its rule and exceptions.
  # Oversized relevant units require a reviewed split, never silent truncation.
  for position,unit in enumerate(document['text'].split('\n\n')):
   unit=unit.strip()
   score=len(terms & set(re.findall(r'[a-z]+',unit.lower())))
   if score:ranked.append((score,document['id']+':'+str(position),unit,document['revision']))
 ranked.sort(key=lambda row:(-row[0],row[1]));selected=[];used=0
 if any(len(row[2])>budget for row in ranked):
  raise ValueError('relevant evidence unit needs a reviewed split')
 for score,id,chunk,revision in ranked:
  if used+len(chunk)<=budget:selected.append((id,chunk,revision));used+=len(chunk)
 return selected,used

text='Refunds within 14 days. '+'Policy detail. '*23+'Opened items are excluded.'
document={'id':'one:policy','revision':'r1','text':text}
selected,used=select_context('refunds',[document])
assert len(text)>350 and selected[0][1].endswith('Opened items are excluded.')
assert used==len(text)
print('rule and exception preserved together; budget counts complete evidence units')
```

## Expected observation

```text
rule and exception preserved together; budget counts complete evidence units
```

## Try the aligned variation

Add a 701-plus-character relevant paragraph and require a reviewed-split failure. Add a separate irrelevant oversized paragraph and prove it does not displace the supported evidence.

Keep the demonstrated assertions and record your prediction, actual result and one failing case before revealing the reference.

## Staged hints

1. Apply relevance before testing a unit against the context budget.

2. A relevant oversized unit must fail, rather than return a truncated success.

3. Compare selected IDs and exact text; a passing character count alone can hide lost exceptions.

## Complete variation reference

After your own attempt, save this complete block as solution.py and run `python3.12 -I solution.py`. It contains the original example as well as the variation.

```python
print('rule and exception preserved together; budget counts complete evidence units')

# Complete exercise variation
oversized={'id':'one:large','revision':'r1','text':'Refunds '+'x'*700}
try:select_context('refunds',[oversized])
except ValueError:pass
else:raise AssertionError('relevant evidence silently truncated')
irrelevant={**oversized,'text':'wallpaper '+'x'*700}
again,count=select_context('refunds',[document,irrelevant])

print('variation: oversized relevant unit refused; irrelevant unit excluded before packing')
```

## Expected variation observation

```text

```

## Diagnose and explain

If the exception disappears, inspect the splitting boundary before tuning ranking. If an irrelevant large paragraph triggers a split failure, budget validation occurred before relevance filtering. chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to A tenant-scoped source-grounded knowledge base

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Compare lexical, dense, hybrid and reranked retrieval on the same labeled queries. Report retrieval latency, reranking spend and answer quality separately.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Assert document scope and revision before retrieval. Measure recall@k/MRR on versioned relevance labels, including no-answer and conflicting-source cases.

### Context Management

Use token-aware chunks retaining page/time provenance and exceptions. Version embedding dimensions/indexes and invalidate retrieval/answer caches on source or permission changes.

## Failure and deployment work

Quarantine failed parsing, bound upload size and worker queues, activate revisions only after indexing checks, and preserve a working previous revision.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

lessons.content:
# Embedding APIs and index version migrations

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Token-aware and semantic chunking**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Token-aware and semantic chunking (`academy-v2:ai-engineering-12-week:08`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Meaning boundary** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: A section retaining the conditions needed to interpret a rule.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **a source-grounded knowledge-base evidence pack**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **pgvector search, metadata filters and ANN recall**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Embedding APIs and index version migrations · concepts and decision

## Before you begin

Sessions 7–8: source revisions and bounded chunks. A vector is a list of numbers; training an embedding model is not required. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

A replacement embedding model returns the same vector length as the previous one.

## Reason through the decision

Do not mix spaces; build, evaluate and activate a separately versioned index.

Vectors from different embedding models are not interchangeable even if their lengths happen to match. Store model/version, dimension and normalization policy with the index manifest. Re-embedding should build a new searchable revision, evaluate it and switch an active pointer; silently mixing vectors can produce plausible but meaningless nearest neighbors. The fixture does not simulate semantic embedding quality.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Embedding space

A model/version/dimension-specific representation contract.

### Parallel index

A new revision evaluated without overwriting the active search state.

### Activation gate

A checked decision to switch current queries to a ready revision.

## Learn each concept step by step

Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Embedding space

An embedding API maps text to coordinates in a particular learned space. Distance is meaningful only within a compatible model/version, dimension and normalization policy. Two models can both return three numbers with unrelated meanings. Reject incompatible records before insertion rather than padding vectors or mixing them behind a shared model name.

## Step 2 · Parallel index

Build a parallel index for a migration: leave v1 searchable, ingest the same approved corpus through the replacement model into v2, evaluate v2 on held-out labels, then switch an active pointer. This costs temporary storage and ingestion work but makes rollback possible. A successful embedding response does not establish retrieval quality.

## Step 3 · Activation gate

Activation is a state transition with conditions: expected model, numeric finite vectors, completed ingestion, scope checks and evaluation evidence. NaN is a floating-point value but has no valid distance ordering; booleans should not count as coordinates. For the cosine-distance index used here, a zero vector has no direction and is also rejected. Validate these before index activation, and preserve v1 when v2 fails.

## Read, run and explain the complete implementation

## Walk through the data and state

1. accept rejects a different vector length.

2. The same length under different-model is also rejected.

3. Only the declared fixture model/dimension is accepted; no semantic quality was measured.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
index={'model':'fixture-embedding-v1','dimensions':3,'revision':'index-1'}
def accept(vector,model):
    if model!=index['model'] or len(vector)!=index['dimensions']:
        raise ValueError('embedding space mismatch')
    if not all(type(x) in (int,float) for x in vector): raise ValueError('numeric vector required')
    return True
assert accept([1.,0.,0.],'fixture-embedding-v1')
for vector,model in [([1.,0.],'fixture-embedding-v1'),([1.,0.,0.],'different-model')]:
    try: accept(vector,model)
    except ValueError: continue
    raise AssertionError('must not mix spaces')
print('embedding model and dimension gates passed')
```

## Observed output

```text
embedding model and dimension gates passed
```

## Transfer beyond the fixture

Vectors from different embedding models are not interchangeable even if their lengths happen to match. Store model/version, dimension and normalization policy with the index manifest. Re-embedding should build a new searchable revision, evaluate it and switch an active pointer; silently mixing vectors can produce plausible but meaningless nearest neighbors. The fixture does not simulate semantic embedding quality.

Use a documented embedding API or installed local model, record measured usage and vector dimension, and implement finite-number validation. Rebuild an isolated index under a different model and prove the old active revision remains available until promotion.

## Complete integration: implementation and test boundaries

## Save and run the complete integration files

These files are part of this lesson, not a download assignment. Save each under the shown name in an isolated workspace. Use Python 3.12 and `python3 -m venv .venv`, then activate that environment. Only install packages for the integration you are running. Record resolved dependency versions with `python -m pip freeze > tested-dependencies.txt`; a version range is not a tested lock file. The standard-library experiment in the previous chapter needs none of these dependencies. Use synthetic data and your own authorized test accounts. Provider calls may incur charges; free academy enrollment does not include provider credits.

First install httpx and select an installed local embedding model in Ollama. Set LOCAL_EMBEDDING_MODEL and EXPECTED_EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS for its documented index contract, then run `python embedding_adapter.py`. The complete adapter sends bounded batches to /api/embed with truncation disabled, validates model/batch/dimension/finite vectors and preserves input order. A model-name mismatch is a deliberate hard error requiring operator inspection rather than silent index mixing. This opt-in run can download/use local model resources; no request is made by importing the file.

Use an isolated pgvector PostgreSQL database. Run `psql "$VECTOR_LAB_DSN" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f vector_lab.sql` after setting the DSN for that disposable database. This schema deliberately uses three-dimensional synthetic vectors to expose owner filtering and score order; it is not a real semantic embedding. Inspect exact-search output before the HNSW index. Replace it with a documented embedding adapter and a matching parallel index before evaluating semantic retrieval. Parameterize application queries and derive owner from authenticated identity, never from model output.

### embedding_adapter.py

```python
"""Explicit opt-in local embedding adapter; install httpx and an embedding model.
Set LOCAL_EMBEDDING_MODEL and EXPECTED_EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS after selecting and
inspecting your model. Importing performs no request. Never mix model indexes.
"""
import asyncio,math,os
import httpx
async def embed(texts,model,dimensions,endpoint='http://127.0.0.1:11434',transport=None):
    if not 1<=len(texts)<=32 or any(not isinstance(t,str) or not t.strip() or len(t)>20000 for t in texts):
        raise ValueError('1–32 nonempty bounded text chunks required')
    if not model or type(dimensions) is not int or dimensions<1:raise ValueError('model/index contract required')
    async with asyncio.timeout(30):
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=20,transport=transport) as client:
            response=await client.post(endpoint.rstrip('/')+'/api/embed',json={'model':model,'input':texts,'truncate':False})
            response.raise_for_status();data=response.json()
    vectors=data.get('embeddings')
    if data.get('model')!=model or not isinstance(vectors,list) or len(vectors)!=len(texts):raise ValueError('model or batch mismatch')
    for vector in vectors:
        if not isinstance(vector,list) or len(vector)!=dimensions:raise ValueError('embedding dimension mismatch')
        if not all(type(v) in (int,float) and math.isfinite(v) for v in vector):raise ValueError('non-finite embedding')
        if not any(v!=0 for v in vector):raise ValueError('zero vector has no cosine direction')
    # Preserve ordering: vectors[i] belongs to texts[i]. Count is real provider usage if supplied.
    return {'model':model,'dimensions':dimensions,'vectors':vectors,'input_tokens':data.get('prompt_eval_count')}
async def main():
    result=await embed(['Unopened items: 30 days. Personalized items excluded.','Shipping takes five days.'],
       os.environ['LOCAL_EMBEDDING_MODEL'],int(os.environ['EXPECTED_EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS']))
    print({'model':result['model'],'dimensions':result['dimensions'],'rows':len(result['vectors']),'input_tokens':result['input_tokens']})
if __name__=='__main__':asyncio.run(main())
```

### vector_lab.sql

```sql
-- Dedicated synthetic lab database only. 3D vectors are labeled fixtures,
-- not real text embeddings. Change the schema/dimension for your chosen model.
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;
```

chapters.body:
## Before you begin

Sessions 7–8: source revisions and bounded chunks. A vector is a list of numbers; training an embedding model is not required. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

A replacement embedding model returns the same vector length as the previous one.

## Reason through the decision

Do not mix spaces; build, evaluate and activate a separately versioned index.

Vectors from different embedding models are not interchangeable even if their lengths happen to match. Store model/version, dimension and normalization policy with the index manifest. Re-embedding should build a new searchable revision, evaluate it and switch an active pointer; silently mixing vectors can produce plausible but meaningless nearest neighbors. The fixture does not simulate semantic embedding quality.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Embedding space

A model/version/dimension-specific representation contract.

### Parallel index

A new revision evaluated without overwriting the active search state.

### Activation gate

A checked decision to switch current queries to a ready revision.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Embedding space

An embedding API maps text to coordinates in a particular learned space. Distance is meaningful only within a compatible model/version, dimension and normalization policy. Two models can both return three numbers with unrelated meanings. Reject incompatible records before insertion rather than padding vectors or mixing them behind a shared model name.

## Step 2 · Parallel index

Build a parallel index for a migration: leave v1 searchable, ingest the same approved corpus through the replacement model into v2, evaluate v2 on held-out labels, then switch an active pointer. This costs temporary storage and ingestion work but makes rollback possible. A successful embedding response does not establish retrieval quality.

## Step 3 · Activation gate

Activation is a state transition with conditions: expected model, numeric finite vectors, completed ingestion, scope checks and evaluation evidence. NaN is a floating-point value but has no valid distance ordering; booleans should not count as coordinates. For the cosine-distance index used here, a zero vector has no direction and is also rejected. Validate these before index activation, and preserve v1 when v2 fails.

chapters.body:
## Walk through the data and state

1. accept rejects a different vector length.

2. The same length under different-model is also rejected.

3. Only the declared fixture model/dimension is accepted; no semantic quality was measured.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
index={'model':'fixture-embedding-v1','dimensions':3,'revision':'index-1'}
def accept(vector,model):
    if model!=index['model'] or len(vector)!=index['dimensions']:
        raise ValueError('embedding space mismatch')
    if not all(type(x) in (int,float) for x in vector): raise ValueError('numeric vector required')
    return True
assert accept([1.,0.,0.],'fixture-embedding-v1')
for vector,model in [([1.,0.],'fixture-embedding-v1'),([1.,0.,0.],'different-model')]:
    try: accept(vector,model)
    except ValueError: continue
    raise AssertionError('must not mix spaces')
print('embedding model and dimension gates passed')
```

## Observed output

```text
embedding model and dimension gates passed
```

## Transfer beyond the fixture

Vectors from different embedding models are not interchangeable even if their lengths happen to match. Store model/version, dimension and normalization policy with the index manifest. Re-embedding should build a new searchable revision, evaluate it and switch an active pointer; silently mixing vectors can produce plausible but meaningless nearest neighbors. The fixture does not simulate semantic embedding quality.

exercise.solution:
## Complete guided-practice reference

Save the entire following block as solution.py and run `python3 -I solution.py` in a new scratch directory. No prior files or provider account are needed. This is one reference implementation of the bounded practice, not a completed live capstone.

```python
index={'model':'fixture-embedding-v1','dimensions':3,'revision':'index-1'}
def accept(vector,model):
    if model!=index['model'] or len(vector)!=index['dimensions']:
        raise ValueError('embedding space mismatch')
    if not all(type(x) in (int,float) for x in vector): raise ValueError('numeric vector required')
    return True
assert accept([1.,0.,0.],'fixture-embedding-v1')
for vector,model in [([1.,0.],'fixture-embedding-v1'),([1.,0.,0.],'different-model')]:
    try: accept(vector,model)
    except ValueError: continue
    raise AssertionError('must not mix spaces')
print('embedding model and dimension gates passed')

# Guided practice reference implementation
import math
def valid_vector(vector,dimensions):
    return len(vector)==dimensions and all(type(v) in (int,float) and math.isfinite(v) for v in vector) and any(v!=0 for v in vector)
assert valid_vector([1.,0.,0.],3)
assert not valid_vector([0.,0.,0.],3)
assert not valid_vector([float('nan'),0.,0.],3) and not valid_vector([True,0.,0.],3)
active_index='v1'
def activate(candidate,parsed,indexed,evaluated):
    global active_index
    if not (parsed and indexed and evaluated):return False
    active_index=candidate;return True
assert not activate('v2',True,True,False) and active_index=='v1'
assert activate('v2',True,True,True) and active_index=='v2'
print('practice: non-finite/bool coordinates rejected; failed migration retained v1; checked v2 activated')
```

```text
embedding model and dimension gates passed
practice: non-finite/bool coordinates rejected; failed migration retained v1; checked v2 activated
```

Exact search considers all eligible vectors and gives a comparison baseline. Approximate nearest-neighbor search such as HNSW avoids some comparisons for speed, which can miss neighbors. ## Complete guided-practice reference

Save the entire following block as solution.py and run `python3 -I solution.py` in a new scratch directory. No prior files or provider account are needed. This is one reference implementation of the bounded practice, not a completed live capstone.

```python

# Guided practice reference implementation
def ann_recall(exact_ids,approximate_ids,authorized_ids):
    if not set(approximate_ids)<=set(authorized_ids):raise PermissionError('scope leak')
    return len(set(exact_ids)&set(approximate_ids))/len(set(exact_ids)) if exact_ids else None
assert ann_recall(['r1','r2'],['r1'],['r1','r2'])==.5
assert ann_recall([],[],[]) is None
try:ann_recall(['r1'],['private'],['r1'])
except PermissionError:pass
else:raise AssertionError('unauthorized ANN output scored as ordinary miss')
print('practice: approximation recall 0.5; empty baseline undefined; leaked owner rejected')
```

## The case

## Reason through the decision

Fuse scoped candidate lists, deduplicate IDs and compare recall/MRR against each baseline.

Lexical and vector scores have different scales; adding raw values makes an undocumented calibration assumption. Reciprocal-rank fusion combines rank positions without claiming those scores are comparable probabilities. Deduplication prevents repeated IDs in one list from receiving extra votes. Fusion cannot recover a passage absent from both candidate sets, and two weak retrievers do not automatically improve quality.

### Lexical retrieval

Matching terms useful for exact names, identifiers and vocabulary.

### Dense retrieval

### Rank fusion

Combining rank positions without assuming raw scores share a scale.

Lexical matching is valuable for exact product codes, names and rare terms. Dense retrieval can find paraphrases that share meaning without words. Neither method authorizes a record or guarantees relevant evidence. Keep both lists in the same owner/revision scope before combining them.

## Step 2 · Dense retrieval

Dense retrieval returns similarity-ranked IDs from an embedding space, not calibrated truth probabilities. Lexical and dense score ranges may differ, so a raw sum can let one scale dominate. ## Step 3 · Rank fusion

## Complete guided-practice reference

Save the entire following block as solution.py and run `python3 -I solution.py` in a new scratch directory. No prior files or provider account are needed. This is one reference implementation of the bounded practice, not a completed live capstone.

```python
def rrf(rankings,k=60):
    scores={}
    for ranking in rankings:
        for rank,identifier in enumerate(dict.fromkeys(ranking),1):
            scores[identifier]=scores.get(identifier,0)+1/(k+rank)
    return sorted(scores,key=lambda identifier:(-scores[identifier],identifier))
lexical=['a','b','c'];dense=['b','d','a']
combined=rrf([lexical,dense])
assert combined[:2]==['b','a']
assert len(combined)==len(set(combined))==4
print({'hybrid_rank':combined,'method':'reciprocal-rank fusion'})

# Guided practice reference implementation
def reciprocal_rank(ranked,relevant):
    return next((1/rank for rank,item in enumerate(ranked,1) if item in relevant),0)
assert rrf([['a','a','b'],dense])==rrf([['a','b'],dense])
assert reciprocal_rank(lexical,{'b'})==.5
assert reciprocal_rank(combined,{'b'})==1
assert reciprocal_rank(combined,{'missing'})==0
print('practice: duplicate vote removed; relevant b reciprocal rank improved from 0.5 to 1 on this fixture')
```

```text
{'hybrid_rank': ['b', 'a', 'd', 'c'], 'method': 'reciprocal-rank fusion'}
```

## Reranking under a latency and spend budget · concepts and decision

## Before you begin

Session 11: immutable candidate IDs and ranked lists. The optional adapter is separate from the deterministic fixture. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

The reranker returns position 1 after the application reordered the candidate list.

## Reason through the decision

Map against the original submitted list; reject invalid/duplicate indexes and preserve a bounded no-rerank fallback.

A reranker scores only the candidates it receives. Map the provider’s original candidate index back to your immutable chunk ID, not to a reordered list. Relevance scores are not calibrated answer confidence. Reranking adds a network call, token processing and latency; skip or fall back under a documented remaining-time budget, then measure the quality effect rather than silently changing behavior.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Candidate ceiling

Maximum evidence set sent to a reranker within budget.

### Index mapping

Provider result positions mapped back to immutable candidate IDs.

### Fallback policy

An explicit measured behavior when reranking exceeds its budget.

## Learn each concept step by step

Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Candidate ceiling

A candidate ceiling bounds how many texts are sent to the reranker. Reranking cannot recover missing evidence, so first evaluate candidate recall. Sending a larger set increases text processing, latency and possibly spend; the right ceiling depends on observed quality gain and a remaining request deadline.

## Step 2 · Index mapping

The provider returns positions into the exact candidate array it received. Position 1 in [c3,c1,c2] means c1. Sorting that array before mapping changes identity even if every index is in range. Save the immutable submitted list and reject negative, out-of-range or duplicate indexes before using the output.

## Step 3 · Fallback policy

A fallback policy defines what happens when reranking is unavailable or would consume the remaining deadline. Returning the authorized original ranking can be acceptable if it is labeled and evaluated; fabricating reranker scores is not. Decide the fallback before failure and retain the failure in cost/quality reports.

## Read, run and explain the complete implementation

## Walk through the data and state

1. Response index 1 maps to c1 in the original three-item array.

2. Index 2 maps to c2, preserving candidate identity.

3. Index 99 raises instead of inventing a document ID.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
# A deterministic fake reranker lets us test identity mapping and budget behavior.

provider_response=[{'index':1,'relevance_score':.9},{'index':2,'relevance_score':.4}]
def map_results(response):
    if any(type(r['index']) is not int or not 0<=r['index']<len(candidates) for r in response):
        raise ValueError('unknown candidate index')
    return [candidates[r['index']]['id'] for r in response]
assert map_results(provider_response)==['c1','c2']
try:map_results([{'index':99}])
except ValueError:print('rerank candidate identity checked; top result c1')
else:raise AssertionError()
```

Install `httpx` and `cohere`. Import `cohere_rerank` from provider_adapters.py and pass your bounded authorized candidate list and query. Configure `COHERE_API_KEY` and `COHERE_RERANK_MODEL` for a supported model. Keep the candidate IDs before calling; returned indexes map into that exact list. ### provider_adapters.py

```python
"""Opt-in async external adapters. No call is made merely by importing this file.
Choose endpoints/models explicitly and run only with authorized synthetic data.
"""
import asyncio
import json
import os

async def ollama_stream(messages,endpoint='http://127.0.0.1:11434',model=None):
    import httpx
    model=model or os.environ['LOCAL_MODEL']
    payload={'model':model,'messages':messages,'stream':True}
    completed=False
    async with asyncio.timeout(60):
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=httpx.Timeout(30,connect=5)) as client:
            async with client.stream('POST',endpoint.rstrip('/')+'/api/chat',json=payload) as response:
                response.raise_for_status()
                async for line in response.aiter_lines():
                    if not line:continue
                    item=json.loads(line)
                    if 'error' in item:raise RuntimeError('local model error')
                    if item.get('message',{}).get('content'):
                        yield {'event':'draft_delta','text':item['message']['content']}
                    if item.get('done'):
                        completed=True
                        yield {'event':'draft_complete','input_tokens':item.get('prompt_eval_count'),
                               'output_tokens':item.get('eval_count'),'model':model}
    if not completed:raise RuntimeError('stream ended before completion; do not cache as a full answer')

async def cohere_rerank(query,candidates):
    import cohere
    if not query.strip() or not 1<=len(candidates)<=30:raise ValueError('query and 1–30 candidates required')
    client=cohere.AsyncClientV2(api_key=os.environ['COHERE_API_KEY'])
    async with asyncio.timeout(15):
        result=await client.rerank(model=os.environ['COHERE_RERANK_MODEL'],query=query,
                                  documents=[c['text'] for c in candidates],top_n=min(5,len(candidates)))
    ids=[]
    for row in result.results:
        if type(row.index) is not int or not 0<=row.index<len(candidates):raise ValueError('invalid rerank index')
        identifier=candidates[row.index]['id']
        if identifier in ids:raise ValueError('duplicate rerank result')
        ids.append(identifier)
    return ids

async def main():
    async for event in ollama_stream([{'role':'user','content':'Explain why a draft needs review in one sentence.'}]):
        print(json.dumps(event))
if __name__=='__main__':asyncio.run(main())
```

## 1. Inspect the input and predict the outcome

```python
assert map_results(provider_response)==['c1','c2']
try:map_results([{'index':99}])
```

```text
rerank candidate identity checked; top result c1
```

## Grounded claims, citations and abstention · concepts and decision

## Before you begin

## The case

A real cited source says only unopened items qualify, but the draft approves an opened item.

## Reason through the decision

Fail factual review despite valid identity; clarify missing conditions or abstain when support is unavailable.

The source exists but contradicts the claim. Separating identity from entailment avoids a common false certificate: valid citations can accompany an unsupported answer. Claim support here is a manual fixture label; semantic judgments need a rubric and evidence, not a confidence string. Applicability also matters: a correct rule for another account or date may still be the wrong answer.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Citation identity

Referenced IDs exist in the selected authorized evidence.

### Entailment

The actual claim follows from the evidence under its scope.

### Applicability

A rule governs the user, date and conditions of this question.

## Learn each concept step by step

Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Citation identity

Citation identity checks whether each cited ID belongs to the selected authorized evidence. It is a useful mechanical gate, but it only proves a reference can be resolved. An answer can cite a real page and say the opposite of that page. Keep citation ID and immutable locator/revision together for inspection.

## Step 2 · Entailment

Entailment asks whether a claim actually follows from the cited evidence. The baseline source permits unopened items; the claim permits opened items, so a reviewer labels it unsupported. Keyword overlap would be high even though meaning is reversed. Break long answers into claims and attach a support decision and evidence for each.

## Step 3 · Applicability

Applicability asks whether a true rule governs this user, date and situation. If the item condition is missing, clarify; if evidence is absent or conflicting, abstain or review. These outcomes differ from answering. An old policy may support a sentence literally while being inapplicable to the active revision.

```python
supported=sum(c['human_support'] for c in claims)
assert identity and supported==0
print({'citation_identity':identity,'reviewed_supported_claims':supported,'claims':len(claims),'ready':False})
```

```text
{'citation_identity': True, 'reviewed_supported_claims': 0, 'claims': 1, 'ready': False}
```

## Complete guided-practice reference

```python
retrieved={'p1':'Only unopened items within 14 days qualify.'}
claims=[{'text':'Opened items qualify.','source':'p1','human_support':False}]
identity=all(c['source'] in retrieved for c in claims)
supported=sum(c['human_support'] for c in claims)
assert identity and supported==0
print({'citation_identity':identity,'reviewed_supported_claims':supported,'claims':len(claims),'ready':False})

# Guided practice reference implementation
def grounded_decision(has_evidence,revision_current,condition_known,conflict=False):
    if not has_evidence or not revision_current or conflict:return 'abstain'
    if not condition_known:return 'clarify'
    return 'answer'
assert grounded_decision(True,True,True)=='answer'
assert grounded_decision(True,True,False)=='clarify'
assert grounded_decision(True,False,True)=='abstain'
assert grounded_decision(True,True,True,True)=='abstain'
print('practice: current evidence answers; missing condition clarifies; stale/conflicting evidence abstains')
```

```text
{'citation_identity': True, 'reviewed_supported_claims': 0, 'claims': 1, 'ready': False}
```

## Streaming source-grounded chat with failure states · concepts and decision

## Before you begin

Session 13: authorized citations and reviewed answer states. An async generator yields provisional events over time. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

A socket closes after two text chunks and before citation validation.

## Reason through the decision

Keep an incomplete draft, preserve the question and exclude it from the full-answer cache or approved export.

Streaming reduces perceived waiting but exposes provisional output before final validation. The client must render deltas as a draft and wait for a complete event carrying status/source identity. A disconnect after two deltas is not a completed answer and must not enter the full-answer cache. Retrieval-first streaming also needs latency measurement for the silent phase before generation begins.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Draft delta

Provisional streamed content that has not become a validated result.

### Completion event

An explicit terminal response carrying status and provenance.

### Partial-result policy

How disconnected streams are retained or excluded from cache/export.

## Learn each concept step by step

Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Draft delta

A draft delta is a fragment, not a complete answer. Append fragments to a visible draft buffer while retaining the original question. The user can see progress without the application claiming that citations, schema or factual review have finished. Rendering a delta should not mutate the approved-answer store.

## Step 2 · Completion event

A completion event signals the stream reached its normal terminal boundary and carries source IDs/status. Validate those IDs against the authorized evidence before making the result eligible for later review/cache. Completion of generation is not human factual approval; keep those states separate.

## Step 3 · Partial-result policy

A partial-result policy handles disconnect, error and cancellation explicitly. Keep the draft as incomplete, preserve the question and stop sibling work. Never let finally mean successful completion: finally also runs on failures. Full-answer caches should accept only the validated generation-complete state under the correct owner/revision key.

## Read, run and explain the complete implementation

## Walk through the data and state

1. Two delta events build provisional text.

2. Only the third event marks normal generation completion with p1.

3. Removing the last event leaves a partial stream; nonempty text alone cannot complete it.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
import asyncio
async def main():
    events=[];done=False
    async def stream():
        yield {'event':'draft_delta','text':'Unopened '}
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
        yield {'event':'draft_delta','text':'within 14 days.'}
        yield {'event':'draft_complete','source_ids':['p1']}
    async for event in stream():
        events.append(event)
        if event['event']=='draft_complete':done=True
    assert done and events[-1]['source_ids']==['p1']
    partial=events[:-1]
    assert not any(e['event']=='draft_complete' for e in partial)
    print({'partial_is_approved':False,'completed_events':len(events)})
asyncio.run(main())
```

## Observed output

```text
{'partial_is_approved': False, 'completed_events': 3}
```

Streaming reduces perceived waiting but exposes provisional output before final validation. The client must render deltas as a draft and wait for a complete event carrying status/source identity. A disconnect after two deltas is not a completed answer and must not enter the full-answer cache. Retrieval-first streaming also needs latency measurement for the silent phase before generation begins.

Add error and cancellation events, preserve the question across disconnect and show an unambiguous incomplete state. Compare time-to-first-byte with retrieval duration and full-answer latency. Validate citations only against the authorized selected evidence.

exercise.solution:
## Complete guided-practice reference

Save the entire following block as solution.py and run `python3 -I solution.py` in a new scratch directory. No prior files or provider account are needed. This is one reference implementation of the bounded practice, not a completed live capstone.

```python
import asyncio
async def main():
    events=[];done=False
    async def stream():
        yield {'event':'draft_delta','text':'Unopened '}
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
        yield {'event':'draft_delta','text':'within 14 days.'}
        yield {'event':'draft_complete','source_ids':['p1']}
    async for event in stream():
        events.append(event)
        if event['event']=='draft_complete':done=True
    assert done and events[-1]['source_ids']==['p1']
    partial=events[:-1]
    assert not any(e['event']=='draft_complete' for e in partial)
    print({'partial_is_approved':False,'completed_events':len(events)})
asyncio.run(main())

# Guided practice reference implementation
def reduce_events(events,allowed_sources):
    text='';state='incomplete';terminal=False
    for event in events:
        if terminal:raise ValueError('event after terminal completion')
        if event['event']=='draft_delta':text+=event['text']
        elif event['event']=='draft_complete':
            if not set(event['source_ids'])<=allowed_sources:raise PermissionError('citation scope')
            state='generation_complete';terminal=True
        elif event['event']=='error':state='incomplete';break
    return {'text':text,'state':state}
partial_events=[{'event':'draft_delta','text':'Draft'},{'event':'error'}]
assert reduce_events(partial_events,{'p1'})['state']=='incomplete'
assert reduce_events([{'event':'draft_complete','source_ids':['p1']}],{'p1'})['state']=='generation_complete'
try:reduce_events([{'event':'draft_complete','source_ids':['private']}],{'p1'})
except PermissionError:pass
else:raise AssertionError('private citation accepted')
try:reduce_events([{'event':'draft_complete','source_ids':['p1']},{'event':'draft_delta','text':'late'}],{'p1'})
except ValueError:pass
else:raise AssertionError('late delta accepted after completion')
print('practice: error remains incomplete; allowed completion recognized; private citation and late delta rejected')
```

## Expected reference observation

```text
{'partial_is_approved': False, 'completed_events': 3}
practice: error remains incomplete; allowed completion recognized; private citation and late delta rejected
```

## If your result differs

If an error leaves generation_complete, the reducer is treating cleanup or text presence as success. Even a valid completion still needs the factual review policy from session 13.

## Explain before continuing

Compare the changed code with the baseline: which new input or state transition is protected, and which integration behavior remains untested?

- **rerank budget, citations and stream failure** — taught in Reranking under a latency and spend budget, Grounded claims, citations and abstention, Streaming source-grounded chat with failure states. Evidence: retain those lessons’ successful case and negative check in the project report.

## Mixed-media knowledge base capstone · concepts and decision

## Before you begin

Sessions 7–14: the capstone combines intake, scoped retrieval, grounding and draft streaming. Start from the smaller offline scoring task. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

A source-grounded chat feature retrieves one wrong passage, correctly abstains once and misses another answer.

## Reason through the decision

Keep no-source and answerable denominators separate; report the missed evidence rather than hiding it as safe abstention.

Retrieval recall needs an explicit denominator. The no-source query has no relevant passage and is scored for correct abstention rather than forcing a 0/0 recall. A correct abstention on unavailable sources and an incorrect abstention caused by retrieval failure are operationally different. This three-case fixture validates scoring; a capstone needs a larger held-out set and factual review.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Source lifecycle

Received-to-active transitions with failure preservation.

### No-answer evaluation

Testing correct abstention separately from retrieval failure.

### Retrieval/answer separation

Independent scoring of evidence selection and claim quality.

## Learn each concept step by step

Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Source lifecycle

The source lifecycle determines which records can be retrieved. received and parsed are not active; activation follows indexing and checks. Keep status visible in the UI and preserve a prior working revision after replacement failure. The capstone should expose this state rather than silently search every uploaded file.

## Step 2 · No-answer evaluation

No-answer evaluation distinguishes a question with no source support from an answerable question whose evidence was missed. Only answerable queries have a relevant-passage recall denominator. Score unsupported questions for the correct abstain/clarify outcome separately, and retain failed retrieval as a failure rather than calling all abstention safe.

## Step 3 · Retrieval/answer separation

Retrieval and answer metrics diagnose different defects. Passage recall@k is |retrieved relevant IDs|/|gold relevant IDs|, averaged over answerable queries. Hit rate only asks whether at least one gold ID appears. With two gold passages and one retrieved, recall is .5 but hit rate is 1. Final claim support must still be reviewed even if recall is perfect.

## Read, run and explain the complete implementation

## Walk through the data and state

1. q1 retrieves its gold p1 within the first two results.

2. q2 has no gold and is evaluated for abstention, not passage recall.

3. q3 misses p3, so mean recall across q1 and q3 is .5.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
queries=[{'id':'q1','gold':{'p1'},'ranked':['p2','p1'],'expected':'answer','actual':'answer'},
         {'id':'q2','gold':set(),'ranked':[],'expected':'abstain','actual':'abstain'},
         {'id':'q3','gold':{'p3'},'ranked':['p4'],'expected':'answer','actual':'abstain'}]
answerable=[q for q in queries if q['gold']]
recall=sum(len(set(q['ranked'][:2])&q['gold'])/len(q['gold']) for q in answerable)/len(answerable)
assert recall==.5
assert len(queries)-len(answerable)==1
print({'recall_at_2_answerable':recall,'answerable':2,'no_source_cases':1,'behaviors_correct':2,'all_cases':3})
```

## Observed output

```text
{'recall_at_2_answerable': 0.5, 'answerable': 2, 'no_source_cases': 1, 'behaviors_correct': 2, 'all_cases': 3}
```

## Transfer beyond the fixture

Retrieval recall needs an explicit denominator. The no-source query has no relevant passage and is scored for correct abstention rather than forcing a 0/0 recall. A correct abstention on unavailable sources and an incorrect abstention caused by retrieval failure are operationally different. This three-case fixture validates scoring; a capstone needs a larger held-out set and factual review.

3. Run your change against the named normal and failure cases. Compare actual output with the reference only after making your own attempt.

4. Then complete the module integration capstone: A mixed-media knowledge base with owner-scoped uploads, provenance, hybrid/re-ranked retrieval and source-grounded streaming answers. ## Next: integration work

Ship the mixed-media knowledge-base capstone with owner-scoped uploads, parse-status UI, source-linked streaming and an evaluation report. Test unsupported questions, failed parsing, conflicting revisions, unauthorized reads and a restore; compare hybrid/reranked quality against the lexical baseline.

Complete the bounded task first. Carry its invariant and tests into this larger project. Earlier sessions and the inline integration files supply the building blocks; optional live providers must be tested separately. A successful local reference is not evidence of cloud scale, speech quality or real connector effects.

## Review before marking complete

The exercise includes staged hints, a full reference solution and diagnostic feedback. Compare after your own attempt. Practical submission is your own evidence report, not automated code inspection or certification.

## Apply the three engineering pillars

## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to A tenant-scoped source-grounded knowledge base

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Compare lexical, dense, hybrid and reranked retrieval on the same labeled queries. Report retrieval latency, reranking spend and answer quality separately.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Assert document scope and revision before retrieval. Measure recall@k/MRR on versioned relevance labels, including no-answer and conflicting-source cases.

### Context Management

Use token-aware chunks retaining page/time provenance and exceptions. Version embedding dimensions/indexes and invalidate retrieval/answer caches on source or permission changes.

## Failure and deployment work

Quarantine failed parsing, bound upload size and worker queues, activate revisions only after indexing checks, and preserve a working previous revision.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

## Before you begin

Sessions 7–14: the capstone combines intake, scoped retrieval, grounding and draft streaming. Start from the smaller offline scoring task. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

A source-grounded chat feature retrieves one wrong passage, correctly abstains once and misses another answer.

## Reason through the decision

Keep no-source and answerable denominators separate; report the missed evidence rather than hiding it as safe abstention.

Retrieval recall needs an explicit denominator. The no-source query has no relevant passage and is scored for correct abstention rather than forcing a 0/0 recall. A correct abstention on unavailable sources and an incorrect abstention caused by retrieval failure are operationally different. This three-case fixture validates scoring; a capstone needs a larger held-out set and factual review.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Source lifecycle

Received-to-active transitions with failure preservation.

### No-answer evaluation

Testing correct abstention separately from retrieval failure.

### Retrieval/answer separation

Independent scoring of evidence selection and claim quality.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Source lifecycle

The source lifecycle determines which records can be retrieved. received and parsed are not active; activation follows indexing and checks. Keep status visible in the UI and preserve a prior working revision after replacement failure. The capstone should expose this state rather than silently search every uploaded file.

## Step 2 · No-answer evaluation

No-answer evaluation distinguishes a question with no source support from an answerable question whose evidence was missed. Only answerable queries have a relevant-passage recall denominator. Score unsupported questions for the correct abstain/clarify outcome separately, and retain failed retrieval as a failure rather than calling all abstention safe.

## Step 3 · Retrieval/answer separation

Retrieval and answer metrics diagnose different defects. Passage recall@k is |retrieved relevant IDs|/|gold relevant IDs|, averaged over answerable queries. Hit rate only asks whether at least one gold ID appears. With two gold passages and one retrieved, recall is .5 but hit rate is 1. Final claim support must still be reviewed even if recall is perfect.

chapters.title: Apply the three engineering pillars
chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to A tenant-scoped source-grounded knowledge base

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Compare lexical, dense, hybrid and reranked retrieval on the same labeled queries. Report retrieval latency, reranking spend and answer quality separately.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Assert document scope and revision before retrieval. Measure recall@k/MRR on versioned relevance labels, including no-answer and conflicting-source cases.

### Context Management

Use token-aware chunks retaining page/time provenance and exceptions. Version embedding dimensions/indexes and invalidate retrieval/answer caches on source or permission changes.

## Failure and deployment work

Quarantine failed parsing, bound upload size and worker queues, activate revisions only after indexing checks, and preserve a working previous revision.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

```python
def retrieval_report(dataset,k):
    eligible=[q for q in dataset if q['gold']]
    recalls=[len(set(q['ranked'][:k])&q['gold'])/len(q['gold']) for q in eligible]
    no_source=[q for q in dataset if not q['gold']]
```

# Tool binding and workspace API permissions

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Mixed-media knowledge base capstone**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- Mixed-media knowledge base capstone (`academy-v2:ai-engineering-12-week:15`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **Source lifecycle** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: Received-to-active transitions with failure preservation.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **a permissioned workspace-agent trace**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **LangGraph state and durable human pauses**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Module 3 · Agentic Workflows & Multi-Agent Systems · system design

An agent chooses proposed steps from observations; application code controls what those steps can do. Begin with a fixed retrieval/draft pipeline and add a bounded loop only for an observed need. Tool binding supplies names and schemas, while the dispatcher supplies authenticated identity, allowed scope, argument validation and stable error categories. Gmail/Slack/calendar credentials, channel membership and calendar ownership remain outside model-generated arguments.

Represent workflow state explicitly: queued, retrieving, drafting, awaiting review, approved, claimed, committed, uncertain or failed. Durable checkpoints belong outside process memory. LangGraph exposes graph state, checkpoints and interrupts; LangChain helps compose models/tools; CrewAI offers role/task coordination. Compare each against the simpler workflow using correctness, recovery, latency, cost and maintenance. A second model persona does not create durability or authority.

Human approval binds the exact payload, actor, destination, revision and expiry. Resuming a graph may rerun a node; perform irreversible work only behind an authorized idempotent boundary. A database transaction can atomically update local records but cannot unsend an email. After a remote timeout, reconcile the existing operation key and outcome before any retry. Remote APIs differ in duplicate-prevention guarantees.

Memory should be selected by owner, source revision and relevance. Summaries can omit exceptions or stale facts; keep recoverable originals and evaluate compression on factual cases. Delegation helps independent work only when parallel latency or quality gains justify duplicate context and calls. Preserve branch provenance and define conflict arbitration rather than concatenating confident narratives.

MCP introduces a host/client/server contract for tools, resources and prompts. Discovery metadata is untrusted capability description, not permission. Negotiate capabilities, validate tool results and enforce actual actor scope. Webhook monitoring similarly needs signature/replay validation, durable inbox IDs, rapid acknowledgement and a bounded worker queue. The capstone can monitor and propose autonomously within its configured read scope; sending messages and creating invitations require the reviewed effect contract. Use local fake destinations first, and only opt into your own authorized test accounts. This course does not send messages or schedule events on your behalf.

## Module capstone

A scoped workspace agent that monitors a test channel, drafts from an authorized knowledge base and prepares/reviews calendar actions.

Weeks 6–8. Keep one versioned dataset and baseline through these sessions; do not change inputs while claiming an improvement.

## Tool binding and workspace API permissions · concepts and decision

## Before you begin

Python dictionaries and set comparison; source/owner boundaries from session 10. OAuth grants are an integration prerequisite, not model output. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

An allowlisted draft tool receives a private channel ID outside the authenticated actor scope.

## Reason through the decision

Deny at dispatch; tool discovery or a valid JSON argument cannot establish channel permission.

A function schema tells the model how to propose an operation; it does not confer permission. The dispatcher validates allowed fields, authenticated actor scope, types and effects. Real connectors also need least-privilege OAuth scopes, token storage/rotation, retry categories and destination-specific error mapping. Never accept a model-generated user/tenant ID as identity.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Tool proposal

A model-generated operation that still needs application validation.

### Connector scope

API-granted authority for channels, accounts and actions.

### Draft boundary

Local preparation that does not send or schedule externally.

## Learn each concept step by step

Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Tool proposal

Tool binding presents a function name and argument schema so a model can propose a call. The proposal is untrusted data: the application selects the registered function and validates required/extra fields and types. Never eval a function name or run code returned by the model. A schema-valid proposal can still be unauthorized.

## Step 2 · Connector scope

A connector scope is authority granted to an application for an account or resource. Slack channel membership and calendar ownership constrain it further. Bind that grant to server-established actor identity and check destination scope at dispatch. A model-supplied owner or channel cannot expand the authenticated actor’s grants.

## Step 3 · Draft boundary

A draft boundary separates local preparation from external effects. Returning status=draft can be safe without send authority; a send or create operation needs a different dispatcher contract and current approval. Whitelist effect types, rather than assuming every allowed tool is read-only. The optional connector example later supplies actual HTTP methods behind these checks.

## Read, run and explain the complete implementation

## Walk through the data and state

1. dispatch requires the exact field set channel,text.

2. The private channel fails the actor scope check even with valid field names.

3. send_reply is not registered; draft_reply on support returns a local draft.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
allowed={'draft_reply':{'fields':{'channel','text'},'effect':'local_draft'}}
def dispatch(actor,tool,args):
    contract=allowed.get(tool)
    if not contract or type(args) is not dict or set(args)!=contract['fields']:return 'rejected'
    if args['channel'] not in actor['channels']:return 'denied'
    if not all(type(value) is str for value in args.values()):return 'invalid_type'
    return {'status':'draft','owner':actor['owner'],'text':args['text']}
actor={'owner':'acme','channels':{'support'}}
assert dispatch(actor,'draft_reply',{'channel':'private','text':'hello'})=='denied'
assert dispatch(actor,'send_reply',{'channel':'support','text':'hello'})=='rejected'
assert dispatch(actor,'draft_reply',{'channel':'support','text':'hello'})['status']=='draft'
print('tool schema, application authority and draft-only effect verified')
```

## Observed output

```text
tool schema, application authority and draft-only effect verified
```

A function schema tells the model how to propose an operation; it does not confer permission. The dispatcher validates allowed fields, authenticated actor scope, types and effects. Real connectors also need least-privilege OAuth scopes, token storage/rotation, retry categories and destination-specific error mapping. Never accept a model-generated user/tenant ID as identity.

chapters.title: Module 3 · Agentic Workflows & Multi-Agent Systems · system design
chapters.body:
An agent chooses proposed steps from observations; application code controls what those steps can do. Begin with a fixed retrieval/draft pipeline and add a bounded loop only for an observed need. Tool binding supplies names and schemas, while the dispatcher supplies authenticated identity, allowed scope, argument validation and stable error categories. Gmail/Slack/calendar credentials, channel membership and calendar ownership remain outside model-generated arguments.

Represent workflow state explicitly: queued, retrieving, drafting, awaiting review, approved, claimed, committed, uncertain or failed. Durable checkpoints belong outside process memory. LangGraph exposes graph state, checkpoints and interrupts; LangChain helps compose models/tools; CrewAI offers role/task coordination. Compare each against the simpler workflow using correctness, recovery, latency, cost and maintenance. A second model persona does not create durability or authority.

Human approval binds the exact payload, actor, destination, revision and expiry. Resuming a graph may rerun a node; perform irreversible work only behind an authorized idempotent boundary. A database transaction can atomically update local records but cannot unsend an email. After a remote timeout, reconcile the existing operation key and outcome before any retry. Remote APIs differ in duplicate-prevention guarantees.

Memory should be selected by owner, source revision and relevance. Summaries can omit exceptions or stale facts; keep recoverable originals and evaluate compression on factual cases. Delegation helps independent work only when parallel latency or quality gains justify duplicate context and calls. Preserve branch provenance and define conflict arbitration rather than concatenating confident narratives.

MCP introduces a host/client/server contract for tools, resources and prompts. Discovery metadata is untrusted capability description, not permission. Negotiate capabilities, validate tool results and enforce actual actor scope. Webhook monitoring similarly needs signature/replay validation, durable inbox IDs, rapid acknowledgement and a bounded worker queue. The capstone can monitor and propose autonomously within its configured read scope; sending messages and creating invitations require the reviewed effect contract. Use local fake destinations first, and only opt into your own authorized test accounts. This course does not send messages or schedule events on your behalf.

## Module capstone

A scoped workspace agent that monitors a test channel, drafts from an authorized knowledge base and prepares/reviews calendar actions.

Weeks 6–8. Keep one versioned dataset and baseline through these sessions; do not change inputs while claiming an improvement.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Tool proposal

Tool binding presents a function name and argument schema so a model can propose a call. The proposal is untrusted data: the application selects the registered function and validates required/extra fields and types. Never eval a function name or run code returned by the model. A schema-valid proposal can still be unauthorized.

## Step 2 · Connector scope

A connector scope is authority granted to an application for an account or resource. Slack channel membership and calendar ownership constrain it further. Bind that grant to server-established actor identity and check destination scope at dispatch. A model-supplied owner or channel cannot expand the authenticated actor’s grants.

## Step 3 · Draft boundary

A draft boundary separates local preparation from external effects. Returning status=draft can be safe without send authority; a send or create operation needs a different dispatcher contract and current approval. Whitelist effect types, rather than assuming every allowed tool is read-only. The optional connector example later supplies actual HTTP methods behind these checks.

chapters.title: Read, run and explain the complete implementation
chapters.body:
## Walk through the data and state

1. dispatch requires the exact field set channel,text.

2. The private channel fails the actor scope check even with valid field names.

3. send_reply is not registered; draft_reply on support returns a local draft.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
allowed={'draft_reply':{'fields':{'channel','text'},'effect':'local_draft'}}
def dispatch(actor,tool,args):
    contract=allowed.get(tool)
    if not contract or type(args) is not dict or set(args)!=contract['fields']:return 'rejected'
    if args['channel'] not in actor['channels']:return 'denied'
    if not all(type(value) is str for value in args.values()):return 'invalid_type'
    return {'status':'draft','owner':actor['owner'],'text':args['text']}
actor={'owner':'acme','channels':{'support'}}
assert dispatch(actor,'draft_reply',{'channel':'private','text':'hello'})=='denied'
assert dispatch(actor,'send_reply',{'channel':'support','text':'hello'})=='rejected'
assert dispatch(actor,'draft_reply',{'channel':'support','text':'hello'})['status']=='draft'
print('tool schema, application authority and draft-only effect verified')
```

## Observed output

```text
tool schema, application authority and draft-only effect verified
```

## Transfer beyond the fixture

A function schema tells the model how to propose an operation; it does not confer permission. The dispatcher validates allowed fields, authenticated actor scope, types and effects. Real connectors also need least-privilege OAuth scopes, token storage/rotation, retry categories and destination-specific error mapping. Never accept a model-generated user/tenant ID as identity.

Define independent read/draft/calendar-proposal contracts for Gmail, Slack and Calendar. Keep send/create disabled until exact human approval. Record connector response IDs and test revoked scopes and a forbidden channel before any live account integration.

## LangGraph state and durable human pauses · concepts and decision

## Before you begin

Basic SQL UPDATE/WHERE and transactions. sqlite3.connect opens a file-backed store; closing and reopening tests persistence. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

A graph waits overnight for review and receives two resume requests after restart.

## Reason through the decision

Persist state durably and consume an authorized version once; in-memory personas do not provide recovery.

Persist state at a meaningful boundary, not only in a conversation buffer. A conditional state/version update prevents a duplicate resume from advancing twice. LangGraph checkpoints use a thread ID to load state; a thread ID is still not authorization. An interrupt can cause a node to execute again on resume, so work before the interrupt must be safe to repeat or isolated in idempotent tasks.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Checkpoint

A persisted workflow snapshot tied to a controlled execution boundary.

### Thread identity

A state lookup key which does not itself authorize the caller.

### Interrupt replay

Node work may run again on resume and must be safe to repeat.

## Learn each concept step by step

Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Checkpoint

A checkpoint stores enough workflow state to resume at a controlled boundary: job ID, owner, state and version. Persist before acknowledging a human pause. The SQLite example closes the connection and reopens the same file to distinguish durable records from process variables. An in-memory graph saver cannot pass a process-restart test.

## Step 2 · Thread identity

A thread/job ID locates state but does not authorize it. A conditional update includes owner as well as ID, expected state and version. rowcount=1 means this request consumed the transition; rowcount=0 means no matching authorized current state existed. Return a controlled conflict/denial rather than silently applying a stale review.

## Step 3 · Interrupt replay

Graph interrupt/resume may rerun node code preceding an interrupt. Place irreversible effects behind a durable, approved dispatcher boundary, not in code that may replay. The optional LangGraph example first demonstrates SDK control flow with an explicitly in-memory saver; the SQL baseline teaches the persistence/version behavior you must retain when choosing a durable checkpointer.

## Read, run and explain the complete implementation

## Walk through the data and state

1. Write awaiting_review/version 1 to the file and close the connection.

2. After reopen, wrong owner updates zero rows; acme/version 1 updates one.

3. A second acme/version 1 update affects zero rows because state/version changed.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
import sqlite3,tempfile
from pathlib import Path
```

chapters.body:
Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Checkpoint

A checkpoint stores enough workflow state to resume at a controlled boundary: job ID, owner, state and version. Persist before acknowledging a human pause. The SQLite example closes the connection and reopens the same file to distinguish durable records from process variables. An in-memory graph saver cannot pass a process-restart test.

## Step 2 · Thread identity

A thread/job ID locates state but does not authorize it. A conditional update includes owner as well as ID, expected state and version. rowcount=1 means this request consumed the transition; rowcount=0 means no matching authorized current state existed. Return a controlled conflict/denial rather than silently applying a stale review.

## Step 3 · Interrupt replay

Graph interrupt/resume may rerun node code preceding an interrupt. Place irreversible effects behind a durable, approved dispatcher boundary, not in code that may replay. The optional LangGraph example first demonstrates SDK control flow with an explicitly in-memory saver; the SQL baseline teaches the persistence/version behavior you must retain when choosing a durable checkpointer.
