## Approval-bound calendar and messaging proposals · concepts and decision

## Before you begin

Session 17: persisted state/version checks. Canonical JSON serialization and hashing detect payload changes; they are not authentication. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

The reviewer approved 10:00, then the event time changed to 11:00.

## Reason through the decision

Invalidate the approval and show the changed payload for review before any external event is created.

A calendar draft becomes consequential when it creates an event or invitation. The reviewed payload includes timezone, time interval, calendar, attendees and revision; editing any effect field invalidates approval. Human approval must be checked again at dispatch, including expiry and revoked roles. A hash detects changed bytes but is neither an identity system nor a remote idempotency guarantee.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Payload approval

Authority bound to exact recipients, time, destination and revision.

### Revocation check

Authority verified again when execution begins.

### Expiry

A bound after which prior approval no longer authorizes the effect.

## Learn each concept step by step

Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Payload approval

Approval authorizes an exact effect payload, not a vague task name. Include calendar/destination, start/end with timezone, recipients and revision. Canonical serialization ensures stable field ordering before hashing. Changing a time or attendee after review must change the fingerprint and invalidate approval.

## Step 2 · Revocation check

Revocation is checked at execution time: a reviewer who had authority yesterday may have lost it today. A matching hash only proves payload equality; load the approval and current role from trusted application state. Do not accept a model-generated approval dictionary as the reviewer’s actual decision.

## Step 3 · Expiry

Expiry uses a precise boundary: now < expires permits, now >= expires denies. Check time interval validity before presenting a proposal; naive times without offsets are ambiguous. Normalize equivalent instants consistently for comparison, and require end after start. Idempotency and remote reconciliation are additional requirements taught separately.

## Read, run and explain the complete implementation

## Walk through the data and state

1. The unchanged payload at time 99 with active reviewer passes.

2. Changing start from 10:00 to 11:00 changes the digest and fails.

3. At exact expiry 100, or with an inactive reviewer, the same payload fails.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
import hashlib,json
payload={'owner':'acme','destination':'calendar:team','start':'2026-11-03T10:00:00+03:00','attendees':['synthetic@example.test'],'revision':2}
def fingerprint(value):return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(value,sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
approved={'digest':fingerprint(payload),'expires_at':100,'actor':'reviewer'}
def permitted(current,now,actor_active):
    return now<approved['expires_at'] and actor_active and fingerprint(current)==approved['digest']
assert permitted(payload,99,True)
assert not permitted(dict(payload,start='2026-11-03T11:00:00+03:00'),99,True)
assert not permitted(payload,100,True) and not permitted(payload,99,False)
print('approval binds exact time, recipients, destination and active reviewer authority')
```

## Observed output

```text
approval binds exact time, recipients, destination and active reviewer authority
```

## Transfer beyond the fixture

A calendar draft becomes consequential when it creates an event or invitation. The reviewed payload includes timezone, time interval, calendar, attendees and revision; editing any effect field invalidates approval. Human approval must be checked again at dispatch, including expiry and revoked roles. A hash detects changed bytes but is neither an identity system nor a remote idempotency guarantee.

Add end time, duration, timezone validation and an expired reviewer role. In the workspace app, show the exact proposal to the human, persist the decision and prevent stale browser tabs from scheduling changed content.

1. Read the concept tutorial, trace the complete baseline and predict its assertions before running.

2. Validate a timezone-aware start/end interval before approval. Test a valid interval, a reversed interval and a naive time.

3. Run your change against the named normal and failure cases. Compare actual output with the reference only after making your own attempt.

## Next: integration work

Add end time, duration, timezone validation and an expired reviewer role. In the workspace app, show the exact proposal to the human, persist the decision and prevent stale browser tabs from scheduling changed content.

## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete.     try:a=datetime.fromisoformat(start);b=datetime.fromisoformat(end)

# Context memory, summaries and cache invalidation

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Approval-bound calendar and messaging proposals**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

Explain **Payload approval** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: Authority bound to exact recipients, time, destination and revision.

## Context memory, summaries and cache invalidation · concepts and decision

## Before you begin

Sessions 2 and 13: cache invalidation, applicability and source evidence. Summarization is lossy compression. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

A compressed history drops a policy exception and survives a permission revocation.

## Reason through the decision

Reject the stale memory and test compression against source facts; smaller context is not automatically correct.

Memory is selected application data, not permission to paste all history into every call. A rolling summary can lose exceptions, dates and unresolved decisions; evaluate it against exact source facts and keep recoverable originals. Cached summaries require source/permission invalidation and retention rules. Provider KV/prompt caches and your application memory have different lifecycles.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Selected memory

Relevant tenant-scoped state rather than the entire conversation.

### Summary fidelity

Preserving conditions, uncertainty and source revision during compression.

### Invalidation trigger

A source, role or prompt change requiring cache/memory refresh.

## Learn each concept step by step

Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Selected memory

Selected memory is a bounded subset of durable facts, recent turns and tool results. Choose by owner, permission, relevance and revision before budgeting. Persist originals separately so an omitted condition can be recovered. Pasting every historic message makes context expensive and may reintroduce revoked or stale evidence.

## Step 2 · Summary fidelity

Summary fidelity means preserving what changes a decision: dates, exceptions, scope and uncertainty. “Returns within 14 days” loses the opened-item exclusion, even if it is shorter and fluent. Evaluate compression against source facts and answer cases; token savings alone do not establish useful compression.

## Step 3 · Invalidation trigger

An invalidation trigger changes whether retained content is usable: source revision, membership, prompt/model policy, expiry or retention requirements. A different source revision gives a different cache key in the baseline, but old entries still need permission/retention checks. Application answer caches, conversation memory and provider KV caches are separate objects with different lifecycles.

## Read, run and explain the complete implementation

## Walk through the data and state

1. The v1 and v2 summaries receive different fingerprints.

2. The v1 fixture retains the exception as text.

3. The other owner cannot share the same key even for the same question/revision.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
import hashlib,json
cache={}
def memory(owner,source_revision,question,summary):
    key=hashlib.sha256(json.dumps([owner,source_revision,question]).encode()).hexdigest()
    cache[key]=summary
    return key
first=memory('acme','v1','returns','Unopened within 14 days; opened excluded.')
second=memory('acme','v2','returns','Unopened within 21 days; opened excluded.')
assert first!=second
assert 'opened excluded' in cache[first]
assert first!=memory('other','v1','returns','different tenant')
print('owner/revision memory isolation passed; exception preserved in summary fixture')
```

## Observed output

```text
owner/revision memory isolation passed; exception preserved in summary fixture
```

## Transfer beyond the fixture

Memory is selected application data, not permission to paste all history into every call. A rolling summary can lose exceptions, dates and unresolved decisions; evaluate it against exact source facts and keep recoverable originals. Cached summaries require source/permission invalidation and retention rules. Provider KV/prompt caches and your application memory have different lifecycles.

Write a memory-selection policy that budgets the recent turns, durable facts and tool outputs separately. Test a source revision and revoked membership; compare summary compression savings with a deliberately omitted exception failure.

2. Write an explicit owner/permission-aware memory selector and a reviewed summary-fidelity gate. Reject a compressed summary whose required exception is missing.

3. Run your change against the named normal and failure cases. Compare actual output with the reference only after making your own attempt.

## Next: integration work

Write a memory-selection policy that budgets the recent turns, durable facts and tool outputs separately. Test a source revision and revoked membership; compare summary compression savings with a deliberately omitted exception failure.

The exercise includes staged hints, a full reference solution and diagnostic feedback. Compare after your own attempt. Practical submission is your own evidence report, not automated code inspection or certification.

## Apply the three engineering pillars

## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

# Framework choices and multi-agent delegation

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Context memory, summaries and cache invalidation**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

## Framework choices and multi-agent delegation · concepts and decision

## Before you begin

Session 3: concurrency, and session 13: source support. A framework is an implementation choice, not an evaluator. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

Two workers retrieve the same policy and agree while doubling cost.

## Reason through the decision

Retain a single-workflow baseline and require a measured benefit before adopting delegation.

Parallel delegation can reduce wall time for independent work but also duplicate retrieval, spend and disagreement. Here two workers produce the same claim and double fixture cost without measured quality improvement. Use LangChain for provider/tool composition, LangGraph for explicit state and resumption, or CrewAI for role/task coordination only when its ownership and failure semantics fit the requirement. Framework choice does not remove an evaluator or effect permissions.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Coordination overhead

Extra calls, context duplication, communication and failure state.

### Branch provenance

Evidence and results attributable to a specific worker.

### Conflict arbitration

A rule for handling inconsistent delegated results.

## Learn each concept step by step

Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Coordination overhead

Coordination overhead includes duplicated prompts, retrieval, model calls, queueing and state. Two workers can reduce wall time only when work can overlap meaningfully. Keep a single-workflow baseline with the same input and quality bar. Compare total accepted-output spend, not only the fastest branch.

## Step 2 · Branch provenance

Branch provenance records who produced a claim, from which source/revision, with what outcome and cost. Agreement between two workers using the same source is not independent verification. Deduplicate claims for presentation, while retaining both calls in cost accounting and both provenance records for debugging.

## Step 3 · Conflict arbitration

Conflict arbitration determines what happens when branches disagree. Do not concatenate incompatible claims or count votes without evidence. A safe first policy is review when distinct supported claims conflict. LangChain, LangGraph and CrewAI organize composition, state or roles differently; adopt one only after the simpler baseline exposes a concrete requirement.

## Read, run and explain the complete implementation

## Walk through the data and state

1. Both branches return p1 and the same claim.

2. The set has one unique claim but total cost is 4, not 2.

3. No quality gain was observed, so the fixture cannot justify delegation.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
import asyncio
async def branch(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return {'branch':name,'source':'p1','claim':'Only unopened items','cost':2}
async def main():
    results=await asyncio.gather(branch('policy'),branch('account'))
    claims={r['claim'] for r in results}
    total=sum(r['cost'] for r in results)
    assert len(results)==2 and len(claims)==1 and total==4
    print({'workers':2,'unique_claims':len(claims),'total_cost':total,'quality_gain_not_established':True})
asyncio.run(main())
```

## Observed output

```text
{'workers': 2, 'unique_claims': 1, 'total_cost': 4, 'quality_gain_not_established': True}
```

Parallel delegation can reduce wall time for independent work but also duplicate retrieval, spend and disagreement. Use LangChain for provider/tool composition, LangGraph for explicit state and resumption, or CrewAI for role/task coordination only when its ownership and failure semantics fit the requirement. Framework choice does not remove an evaluator or effect permissions.

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. # MCP hosts, clients, servers and tool contracts

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **Framework choices and multi-agent delegation**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

## MCP hosts, clients, servers and tool contracts · concepts and decision

## Before you begin

Session 16: proposal/schema/authority separation. JSON-RPC is a message format; MCP adds negotiated lifecycle and capabilities. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

A newly discovered MCP tool claims it can read every workspace file.

## Reason through the decision

Treat the description as untrusted capability metadata; expose only authorized resources and validate invocations.

MCP separates a host, per-server clients and capability-providing servers. Discovery describes tools/resources/prompts; it does not authorize all discovered behavior. Validate negotiated capabilities and schema at invocation, scope credentials to the actual server and enforce the authenticated owner in the tool implementation. This JSON fixture is a discovery-contract check, not a complete MCP server or handshake.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### MCP host

The application managing clients, permissions and model interaction.

### Capability discovery

Negotiated descriptions of supported tools/resources/prompts.

### Invocation boundary

Validation and authority checks around an actual tool call.

## Learn each concept step by step

Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · MCP host

The MCP host is the user-facing application coordinating model interaction and permissions. It maintains clients that connect to servers. A server exposes bounded capabilities such as a policy lookup; it is not automatically the host or the authenticated end user. Keep credentials and resource scope attached to the actual connection.

## Step 2 · Capability discovery

Capability discovery reports what a server says it can provide: tools, resources or prompts. Initialization negotiates protocol support before discovery/invocation. Descriptions may be untrusted, and discovering a tool does not grant permission to use it. The baseline JSON object illustrates a discovery result only; the supplied SDK client/server demonstrates a real initialization and stdio round trip.

## Step 3 · Invocation boundary

The invocation boundary validates the chosen tool, argument schema, authenticated owner and returned data. An argument named owner does not authenticate anyone. Restrict filesystem or connector access in server code, and validate results before using them as model context. Transport support and cancellation behavior must be tested per server.

## Read, run and explain the complete implementation

## Walk through the data and state

1. The discovered tool set is compared to the application allowlist.

2. The proposed claimed_owner differs from authenticated_owner.

3. The fixture labels its authority source as application authentication, not discovery metadata.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
response={'jsonrpc':'2.0','id':1,'result':{'tools':[{'name':'lookup_policy','inputSchema':{'type':'object','properties':{'id':{'type':'string'}},'required':['id'],'additionalProperties':False}}]}}
allowed={'lookup_policy'}
names={tool['name'] for tool in response['result']['tools']}
assert names<=allowed
proposal={'tool':'lookup_policy','arguments':{'id':'p1'},'claimed_owner':'other'}
authenticated_owner='acme'
assert authenticated_owner!=proposal['claimed_owner']
print({'discovered_tools':sorted(names),'authority_source':'application authentication','protocol_fixture_only':True})
```

## Observed output

```text
{'discovered_tools': ['lookup_policy'], 'authority_source': 'application authentication', 'protocol_fixture_only': True}
```

## Transfer beyond the fixture

MCP separates a host, per-server clients and capability-providing servers. Discovery describes tools/resources/prompts; it does not authorize all discovered behavior. Validate negotiated capabilities and schema at invocation, scope credentials to the actual server and enforce the authenticated owner in the tool implementation. This JSON fixture is a discovery-contract check, not a complete MCP server or handshake.

Run a local MCP server with one read-only policy tool using the official SDK bundle. Test initialization, tools/list, valid/invalid calls, cancellation and a cross-owner ID. Record transport and protocol/SDK versions instead of assuming every server supports the same features.

## Complete integration: implementation and test boundaries

## Save and run the complete integration files

These files are part of this lesson, not a download assignment. Save each under the shown name in an isolated workspace. Use Python 3.12 and `python3 -m venv .venv`, then activate that environment. Only install packages for the integration you are running. Record resolved dependency versions with `python -m pip freeze > tested-dependencies.txt`; a version range is not a tested lock file. The standard-library experiment in the previous chapter needs none of these dependencies. Use synthetic data and your own authorized test accounts. Provider calls may incur charges; free academy enrollment does not include provider credits.

Install `mcp`; save both files together. Run `python mcp_client.py`. The real stdio client initializes the session, discovers the single read-only tool and calls it. The server's policy fixture is fixed and synthetic. Extend it with a denied unknown-policy case and argument validation. Do not register this toy server as a broad filesystem or connector capability: discovery describes what exists; the host and dispatcher still enforce authorization.

### mcp_policy.py

```python
"""Local stdio MCP teaching server; server-scoped single synthetic tenant.
Register: command python, arguments absolute path to this file.
No credentials, no arbitrary filesystem tool, no messaging effects.
"""
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
server=FastMCP('Synthetic policy reader')
POLICIES={'returns-v1':'Unopened items within 14 days; opened items excluded.'}
@server.tool()
def lookup_policy(policy_id:str)->dict:
    """Read an allowlisted synthetic policy; no writes or filesystem paths."""
    if policy_id not in POLICIES:return {'status':'not_found'}
    return {'status':'found','id':policy_id,'text':POLICIES[policy_id]}
if __name__=='__main__':server.run(transport='stdio')
```

### mcp_client.py

```python
"""Run beside mcp_policy.py after installing the supplied dependencies."""
import asyncio, sys
from pathlib import Path
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client
async def main():
    params=StdioServerParameters(command=sys.executable,args=[str(Path(__file__).with_name('mcp_policy.py'))])
    async with stdio_client(params) as (reader,writer):
        async with ClientSession(reader,writer) as session:
            await session.initialize()
            tools=await session.list_tools()
            assert [t.name for t in tools.tools]==['lookup_policy']
            result=await session.call_tool('lookup_policy',{'policy_id':'returns-v1'})
            assert not result.isError
            assert '14 days' in result.content[0].text
            print(result.model_dump_json())
asyncio.run(main())
```

## Practice first, then integrate

## Your practical task

1. Read the concept tutorial, trace the complete baseline and predict its assertions before running.

2. Implement a one-tool dispatcher with strict arguments and an owner check. Reject unknown tools, extra fields and cross-owner requests.

3. Run your change against the named normal and failure cases. Compare actual output with the reference only after making your own attempt.

- The baseline ran and each supplied assertion/state change is explained using the step-by-step trace.
- Implement a one-tool dispatcher with strict arguments and an owner check. Reject unknown tools, extra fields and cross-owner requests.
- The submitted implementation includes both positive and negative assertions and records actual output; its limitations are labeled.

## Next: integration work

Run a local MCP server with one read-only policy tool using the official SDK bundle. Test initialization, tools/list, valid/invalid calls, cancellation and a cross-owner ID. Record transport and protocol/SDK versions instead of assuming every server supports the same features.

Complete the bounded task first. Carry its invariant and tests into this larger project. Earlier sessions and the inline integration files supply the building blocks; optional live providers must be tested separately. A successful local reference is not evidence of cloud scale, speech quality or real connector effects.

## Review before marking complete

The exercise includes staged hints, a full reference solution and diagnostic feedback. Compare after your own attempt. Practical submission is your own evidence report, not automated code inspection or certification.

## Apply the three engineering pillars

## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to A workspace agent that proposes drafts and calendar changes

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Compare a fixed plan, bounded graph and delegated tasks. Include all tool/model calls, handoff delays and human review in the useful-output denominator.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Replay duplicate events, stale approvals, denied scopes, graph resumes and lost responses. Assert one authorized state transition; separately reconcile remote effects.

### Context Management

Persist bounded state outside the prompt. Select tenant-scoped memory, budget tool results and invalidate approval/cache when effect fields or source revisions change.

## Failure and deployment work

Verify connector scopes and actor identity outside model output, bind approval to the exact payload and destination, and handle timeout outcomes as uncertain.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

```python
    params=StdioServerParameters(command=sys.executable,args=[str(Path(__file__).with_name('mcp_policy.py'))])
    async with stdio_client(params) as (reader,writer):
```

chapters.body:
## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to A workspace agent that proposes drafts and calendar changes

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Compare a fixed plan, bounded graph and delegated tasks. Include all tool/model calls, handoff delays and human review in the useful-output denominator.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Replay duplicate events, stale approvals, denied scopes, graph resumes and lost responses. Assert one authorized state transition; separately reconcile remote effects.

### Context Management

Persist bounded state outside the prompt. Select tenant-scoped memory, budget tool results and invalidate approval/cache when effect fields or source revisions change.

## Failure and deployment work

Verify connector scopes and actor identity outside model output, bind approval to the exact payload and destination, and handle timeout outcomes as uncertain.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

- Record latency, cost and quality for the boundary taught so far; mark unmeasured provider or deployment values unknown.
- Retain the taught positive and negative checks with unchanged expectations; keep semantic review separate.
- Explain the current source/context allowance and owner boundary; later cache or distributed controls are not assumed implemented.
- Exercise the failure path taught in this stage. Future hosting, overload and distributed recovery experiments become mandatory only in their own deployment stage.

## Complete guided-practice reference

Save the entire following block as solution.py and run `python3 -I solution.py` in a new scratch directory. No prior files or provider account are needed. This is one reference implementation of the bounded practice, not a completed live capstone.

```python
response={'jsonrpc':'2.0','id':1,'result':{'tools':[{'name':'lookup_policy','inputSchema':{'type':'object','properties':{'id':{'type':'string'}},'required':['id'],'additionalProperties':False}}]}}
allowed={'lookup_policy'}
names={tool['name'] for tool in response['result']['tools']}
assert names<=allowed
proposal={'tool':'lookup_policy','arguments':{'id':'p1'},'claimed_owner':'other'}
authenticated_owner='acme'
assert authenticated_owner!=proposal['claimed_owner']
print({'discovered_tools':sorted(names),'authority_source':'application authentication','protocol_fixture_only':True})

# Guided practice reference implementation
def invoke_tool(tool,args,actor_owner):
    if tool!='lookup_policy' or type(args) is not dict or set(args)!={'id','owner'}:return 'invalid'
    if not all(type(v) is str for v in args.values()):return 'invalid'
    if args['owner']!=actor_owner:return 'denied'
    policies={('acme','p1'):'Synthetic approved policy'}
    return {'status':'found' if (actor_owner,args['id']) in policies else 'not_found'}
assert invoke_tool('lookup_policy',{'id':'p1','owner':'other'},'acme')=='denied'
assert invoke_tool('lookup_policy',{'id':'p1','owner':'acme','path':'/'},'acme')=='invalid'
assert invoke_tool('lookup_policy',{'id':'p1','owner':'acme'},'acme')['status']=='found'
assert invoke_tool('lookup_policy',{'id':'p1','owner':'other'},'other')['status']=='not_found'
print('practice: scoped invocation passed; cross-owner and extra-field requests rejected')
```

## Expected reference observation

```text
{'discovered_tools': ['lookup_policy'], 'authority_source': 'application authentication', 'protocol_fixture_only': True}
practice: scoped invocation passed; cross-owner and extra-field requests rejected
```

## If your result differs

If claimed owner overrides actor_owner, discovery/proposal data has been mistaken for authority. Passing this dispatcher does not prove MCP handshake compatibility; that is why the real SDK appendix is separate.

## Explain before continuing

Compare the changed code with the baseline: which new input or state transition is protected, and which integration behavior remains untested?

# Idempotency, remote uncertainty and reconciliation

## Learning progression and project preparation

## Before this session

Bring your notes and observed output from **MCP hosts, clients, servers and tool contracts**. Earlier completion clicks are not evidence of understanding: explain the input, output and failing case before adding this boundary.

### Specific preparation

- MCP hosts, clients, servers and tool contracts (`academy-v2:ai-engineering-12-week:21`)

If you cannot explain one of these mechanisms, return to that session’s trace and counterexample, rerun its reference, then retry your own version. The stable IDs identify lessons inside this program; no external enrollment is required.

## Readiness check from the previous session

Explain **MCP host** before continuing. Compare your explanation with this recap: The application managing clients, permissions and model interaction.

Reproduce the earlier positive case and its counterexample from your saved implementation. If you can only recall a passing output, reopen its walkthrough and explain why the counterexample must fail. Then identify what this session adds to that contract.

## Carry work forward

Build toward **a permissioned workspace-agent trace**. Keep one evidence folder for this stage: source input, implementation, unchanged expected labels, observed output and unresolved failures. Compare this lesson’s new boundary with the previous result. The complete examples are independent fixtures: deliberately map their field names and source revisions before reusing code; do not concatenate scripts and assume their data agrees.

## Next checkpoint

Next: **Slack event intake and background work**. Save your current inputs, actual output and one unresolved question so the next session can extend a known baseline.

## Idempotency, remote uncertainty and reconciliation · concepts and decision

## Before you begin

Sessions 17–18: durable state, exact approval and version checks. Local transactions cannot roll back remote effects. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

The calendar accepts an event but the acknowledgement is lost.

## Reason through the decision

Keep the same key and reconcile its destination outcome rather than retrying with a new event ID.

A timeout after a remote calendar accepts the event is uncertain. Do not infer failure and issue a new key. Save the same operation ID, inspect the remote event or idempotency record and reconcile before retrying. This dictionary is a single-process teaching fixture; multiple workers require an atomic durable claim, and remote duplicate prevention depends on the destination’s API contract.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Scoped operation key

Stable identifier for one proposed effect in one owner scope.

### Uncertain outcome

A remote write may exist despite a lost response.

### Reconciliation

Checking the original operation/destination before replay.

## Learn each concept step by step

Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Scoped operation key

A scoped operation key identifies one intended effect for one owner/payload revision. Persist it before dispatch and reuse it across retries/reconciliation. Giving each HTTP attempt a fresh key makes duplicate delivery look like a new operation. A database unique constraint can prevent duplicate local claims, but the destination has its own guarantees.

## Step 2 · Uncertain outcome

An uncertain outcome occurs when a remote system may have committed but its acknowledgement is lost. The local caller does not know whether it failed. Keep uncertain and inspect the original destination/operation ID before another write. Retrying with a new calendar ID can create a second event.

## Step 3 · Reconciliation

Reconciliation compares observed remote state with the exact approved payload and updates the ledger to committed, absent or still uncertain. Do not infer committed just because something with a similar title exists. The dictionary fixture is single-process; the durable state example shows local persistence, while remote consistency remains a separate integration test.

## Read, run and explain the complete implementation

## Walk through the data and state

1. The first approved call appends one fake effect but loses its response.

2. The ledger retains uncertain under the same scoped key.

3. The second call returns reconcile and does not append another effect.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
ledger={};effects=[]
def schedule(key,approved,lose_response=False):
    if not approved:return 'needs_review'
    if key in ledger:return 'reconcile' if ledger[key]=='uncertain' else 'already_committed'
    ledger[key]='claimed'
    effects.append({'key':key,'destination':'fake-calendar'})
    ledger[key]='uncertain' if lose_response else 'committed'
    return ledger[key]
assert schedule('acme:event-1:r2',True,True)=='uncertain'
assert schedule('acme:event-1:r2',True)=='reconcile'
assert len(effects)==1
assert schedule('acme:event-2:r1',False)=='needs_review'
print({'fake_effects':len(effects),'lost_response':'reconcile same key, never blind replay'})
```

## Observed output

```text
{'fake_effects': 1, 'lost_response': 'reconcile same key, never blind replay'}
```

## Transfer beyond the fixture

A timeout after a remote calendar accepts the event is uncertain. Do not infer failure and issue a new key. Save the same operation ID, inspect the remote event or idempotency record and reconcile before retrying. This dictionary is a single-process teaching fixture; multiple workers require an atomic durable claim, and remote duplicate prevention depends on the destination’s API contract.

Persist the ledger in PostgreSQL with a scoped unique operation key. Add two workers, a restart after the remote effect and revoked approval. Keep local transaction rollback separate from cancelling an already created external calendar event.

## Complete integration: implementation and test boundaries

## Save and run the complete integration files

These files are part of this lesson, not a download assignment. Save each under the shown name in an isolated workspace. Use Python 3.12 and `python3 -m venv .venv`, then activate that environment. Only install packages for the integration you are running. Record resolved dependency versions with `python -m pip freeze > tested-dependencies.txt`; a version range is not a tested lock file. The standard-library experiment in the previous chapter needs none of these dependencies. Use synthetic data and your own authorized test accounts. Provider calls may incur charges; free academy enrollment does not include provider credits.

Run `python workspace_state.py`. It creates a temporary SQLite database, closes/reopens it and checks duplicates, owner denial and one locally committed fake effect. This is durable local state, not a distributed exactly-once guarantee. Wire real connectors only behind the same current-payload approval and scoped operation key. For a lost remote acknowledgement, retain uncertain state, query the original destination and reconcile before replay. A local database rollback cannot undo a remote message.

### workspace_state.py

```python
"""Durable local state machine with exact review and a fake effect destination.
python workspace_state.py; no real Slack/email/calendar calls occur.
"""
import hashlib,json,sqlite3,tempfile
from pathlib import Path

def digest(payload):return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(payload,sort_keys=True,separators=(',',':')).encode()).hexdigest()

def setup(db):
    db.executescript('''CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS inbox(owner TEXT,event_id TEXT,payload TEXT,PRIMARY KEY(owner,event_id));
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS proposals(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,owner TEXT,payload TEXT,hash TEXT,approved_hash TEXT,state TEXT);
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS effects(owner TEXT,operation TEXT,payload TEXT,PRIMARY KEY(owner,operation));''')

def receive(db,owner,event_id,payload):
    encoded=json.dumps(payload,sort_keys=True)
    with db:
        prior=db.execute('SELECT payload FROM inbox WHERE owner=? AND event_id=?',(owner,event_id)).fetchone()
        if prior:return 'duplicate' if prior[0]==encoded else 'content_conflict'
        db.execute('INSERT INTO inbox VALUES(?,?,?)',(owner,event_id,encoded))
    return 'accepted'

def propose(db,identifier,owner,payload):
    with db:db.execute('INSERT INTO proposals VALUES(?,?,?,?,?,?)',(identifier,owner,json.dumps(payload),digest(payload),None,'needs_review'))

def approve(db,identifier,owner,reviewed_digest,authorized):
    if not authorized:return False
    with db:
        changed=db.execute("UPDATE proposals SET approved_hash=?,state='approved' WHERE id=? AND owner=? AND hash=? AND state='needs_review'",(reviewed_digest,identifier,owner,reviewed_digest)).rowcount
    return changed==1

def execute_fake(db,identifier,owner):
    # Fake destination shares this DB, so the transaction can be atomic here.
    # A real remote side effect needs a separate durable outbox and reconciliation.
    with db:
        row=db.execute("SELECT payload,hash,approved_hash,state FROM proposals WHERE id=? AND owner=?",(identifier,owner)).fetchone()
        if not row:return 'inaccessible'
        payload,actual,approved,state=row
        if state=='committed':return 'already_committed'
        if state!='approved' or actual!=approved:return 'needs_review'
        db.execute('INSERT INTO effects VALUES(?,?,?)',(owner,identifier,payload))
        db.execute("UPDATE proposals SET state='committed' WHERE id=? AND owner=?",(identifier,owner))
    return 'committed'

if __name__=='__main__':
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
        path=Path(folder)/'workspace.sqlite';db=sqlite3.connect(path);setup(db)
        event={'channel':'synthetic-support','question':'Returns?'}
        assert receive(db,'acme','e1',event)=='accepted'
        assert receive(db,'acme','e1',event)=='duplicate'
        payload={'destination':'fake-calendar','start':'2026-11-03T10:00:00+03:00','revision':1}
        propose(db,'p1','acme',payload)
        assert execute_fake(db,'p1','acme')=='needs_review'
        assert not approve(db,'p1','other',digest(payload),True)
        assert approve(db,'p1','acme',digest(payload),True)
        db.close();db=sqlite3.connect(path)
        assert execute_fake(db,'p1','other')=='inaccessible'
        assert execute_fake(db,'p1','acme')=='committed'
        assert execute_fake(db,'p1','acme')=='already_committed'
        assert db.execute('SELECT count(*) FROM effects').fetchone()[0]==1
        db.close()
    print('durable inbox, scoped approval, restart/resume and one fake calendar effect passed')
```

chapters.title: Idempotency, remote uncertainty and reconciliation · concepts and decision
chapters.body:
## Before you begin

Sessions 17–18: durable state, exact approval and version checks. Local transactions cannot roll back remote effects. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

The calendar accepts an event but the acknowledgement is lost.

## Reason through the decision

Keep the same key and reconcile its destination outcome rather than retrying with a new event ID.

A timeout after a remote calendar accepts the event is uncertain. Do not infer failure and issue a new key. Save the same operation ID, inspect the remote event or idempotency record and reconcile before retrying. This dictionary is a single-process teaching fixture; multiple workers require an atomic durable claim, and remote duplicate prevention depends on the destination’s API contract.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Scoped operation key

Stable identifier for one proposed effect in one owner scope.

### Uncertain outcome

A remote write may exist despite a lost response.

### Reconciliation

Checking the original operation/destination before replay.

chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Scoped operation key

A scoped operation key identifies one intended effect for one owner/payload revision. Persist it before dispatch and reuse it across retries/reconciliation. Giving each HTTP attempt a fresh key makes duplicate delivery look like a new operation. A database unique constraint can prevent duplicate local claims, but the destination has its own guarantees.

## Step 2 · Uncertain outcome

An uncertain outcome occurs when a remote system may have committed but its acknowledgement is lost. The local caller does not know whether it failed. Keep uncertain and inspect the original destination/operation ID before another write. Retrying with a new calendar ID can create a second event.

## Step 3 · Reconciliation

Reconciliation compares observed remote state with the exact approved payload and updates the ledger to committed, absent or still uncertain. Do not infer committed just because something with a similar title exists. The dictionary fixture is single-process; the durable state example shows local persistence, while remote consistency remains a separate integration test.

chapters.title: Read, run and explain the complete implementation
chapters.body:
## Walk through the data and state

1. The first approved call appends one fake effect but loses its response.

2. The ledger retains uncertain under the same scoped key.

3. The second call returns reconcile and does not append another effect.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
ledger={};effects=[]
def schedule(key,approved,lose_response=False):
    if not approved:return 'needs_review'
    if key in ledger:return 'reconcile' if ledger[key]=='uncertain' else 'already_committed'
    ledger[key]='claimed'
    effects.append({'key':key,'destination':'fake-calendar'})
    ledger[key]='uncertain' if lose_response else 'committed'
    return ledger[key]
assert schedule('acme:event-1:r2',True,True)=='uncertain'
assert schedule('acme:event-1:r2',True)=='reconcile'
assert len(effects)==1
assert schedule('acme:event-2:r1',False)=='needs_review'
print({'fake_effects':len(effects),'lost_response':'reconcile same key, never blind replay'})
```

## Observed output

```text
{'fake_effects': 1, 'lost_response': 'reconcile same key, never blind replay'}
```

## Transfer beyond the fixture

A timeout after a remote calendar accepts the event is uncertain. Do not infer failure and issue a new key. Save the same operation ID, inspect the remote event or idempotency record and reconcile before retrying. This dictionary is a single-process teaching fixture; multiple workers require an atomic durable claim, and remote duplicate prevention depends on the destination’s API contract.

Persist the ledger in PostgreSQL with a scoped unique operation key. Add two workers, a restart after the remote effect and revoked approval. Keep local transaction rollback separate from cancelling an already created external calendar event.

chapters.body:
## Save and run the complete integration files

These files are part of this lesson, not a download assignment. Save each under the shown name in an isolated workspace. Use Python 3.12 and `python3 -m venv .venv`, then activate that environment. Only install packages for the integration you are running. Record resolved dependency versions with `python -m pip freeze > tested-dependencies.txt`; a version range is not a tested lock file. The standard-library experiment in the previous chapter needs none of these dependencies. Use synthetic data and your own authorized test accounts. Provider calls may incur charges; free academy enrollment does not include provider credits.

Run `python workspace_state.py`. It creates a temporary SQLite database, closes/reopens it and checks duplicates, owner denial and one locally committed fake effect. This is durable local state, not a distributed exactly-once guarantee. Wire real connectors only behind the same current-payload approval and scoped operation key. For a lost remote acknowledgement, retain uncertain state, query the original destination and reconcile before replay. A local database rollback cannot undo a remote message.

### workspace_state.py

```python
"""Durable local state machine with exact review and a fake effect destination.
python workspace_state.py; no real Slack/email/calendar calls occur.
"""
import hashlib,json,sqlite3,tempfile
from pathlib import Path

def digest(payload):return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(payload,sort_keys=True,separators=(',',':')).encode()).hexdigest()

def setup(db):
    db.executescript('''CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS inbox(owner TEXT,event_id TEXT,payload TEXT,PRIMARY KEY(owner,event_id));
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS proposals(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,owner TEXT,payload TEXT,hash TEXT,approved_hash TEXT,state TEXT);
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS effects(owner TEXT,operation TEXT,payload TEXT,PRIMARY KEY(owner,operation));''')

def receive(db,owner,event_id,payload):
    encoded=json.dumps(payload,sort_keys=True)
    with db:
        prior=db.execute('SELECT payload FROM inbox WHERE owner=? AND event_id=?',(owner,event_id)).fetchone()
        if prior:return 'duplicate' if prior[0]==encoded else 'content_conflict'
        db.execute('INSERT INTO inbox VALUES(?,?,?)',(owner,event_id,encoded))
    return 'accepted'

def propose(db,identifier,owner,payload):
    with db:db.execute('INSERT INTO proposals VALUES(?,?,?,?,?,?)',(identifier,owner,json.dumps(payload),digest(payload),None,'needs_review'))

def approve(db,identifier,owner,reviewed_digest,authorized):
    if not authorized:return False
    with db:
        changed=db.execute("UPDATE proposals SET approved_hash=?,state='approved' WHERE id=? AND owner=? AND hash=? AND state='needs_review'",(reviewed_digest,identifier,owner,reviewed_digest)).rowcount
    return changed==1

def execute_fake(db,identifier,owner):
    # Fake destination shares this DB, so the transaction can be atomic here.
    # A real remote side effect needs a separate durable outbox and reconciliation.
    with db:
        row=db.execute("SELECT payload,hash,approved_hash,state FROM proposals WHERE id=? AND owner=?",(identifier,owner)).fetchone()
        if not row:return 'inaccessible'
        payload,actual,approved,state=row
        if state=='committed':return 'already_committed'
        if state!='approved' or actual!=approved:return 'needs_review'
        db.execute('INSERT INTO effects VALUES(?,?,?)',(owner,identifier,payload))
        db.execute("UPDATE proposals SET state='committed' WHERE id=? AND owner=?",(identifier,owner))
    return 'committed'

if __name__=='__main__':
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
        path=Path(folder)/'workspace.sqlite';db=sqlite3.connect(path);setup(db)
        event={'channel':'synthetic-support','question':'Returns?'}
        assert receive(db,'acme','e1',event)=='accepted'
        assert receive(db,'acme','e1',event)=='duplicate'
        payload={'destination':'fake-calendar','start':'2026-11-03T10:00:00+03:00','revision':1}
        propose(db,'p1','acme',payload)
        assert execute_fake(db,'p1','acme')=='needs_review'
        assert not approve(db,'p1','other',digest(payload),True)
        assert approve(db,'p1','acme',digest(payload),True)
        db.close();db=sqlite3.connect(path)
        assert execute_fake(db,'p1','other')=='inaccessible'
        assert execute_fake(db,'p1','acme')=='committed'
        assert execute_fake(db,'p1','acme')=='already_committed'
        assert db.execute('SELECT count(*) FROM effects').fetchone()[0]==1
        db.close()
    print('durable inbox, scoped approval, restart/resume and one fake calendar effect passed')
```

## Software-first practice

Build interfaces, asynchronous services, API adapters and recoverable data flows before studying algorithm derivations. Use mathematics to explain a measured engineering decision.

## Production evidence

A notebook or chat demo is an early prototype. Graduation builds toward operational evidence: deployment/readiness, bounded work, rate limits, error recovery and persisted state. Early checkpoints assess only boundaries already taught; future deployment controls are planned rather than claimed complete. The 10% framing is a teaching heuristic, not a measured universal percentage.

## Apply the three pillars to A workspace agent that proposes drafts and calendar changes

### Latency vs. Cost vs. Quality

Compare a fixed plan, bounded graph and delegated tasks. Include all tool/model calls, handoff delays and human review in the useful-output denominator.

### Deterministic Evaluation

Replay duplicate events, stale approvals, denied scopes, graph resumes and lost responses. Assert one authorized state transition; separately reconcile remote effects.

### Context Management

Persist bounded state outside the prompt. Select tenant-scoped memory, budget tool results and invalidate approval/cache when effect fields or source revisions change.

## Failure and deployment work

Verify connector scopes and actor identity outside model output, bind approval to the exact payload and destination, and handle timeout outcomes as uncertain.

## Evaluation precision

Automate repeatable checks with fixed inputs and versioned expectations. Model judges, faithfulness scores and semantic reviews can be stochastic; record judge/configuration versions and disagreement rather than calling them deterministic truth.

## Module evidence to retain

module-engineering-evidence.json: dataset/release IDs; latency/cost/quality comparison; automated checks and critical failures; context and cache policy; deployment/failure observations. Mark unmeasured fields as not tested.

## Complete guided-practice reference

Save the entire following block as solution.py and run `python3 -I solution.py` in a new scratch directory. No prior files or provider account are needed. This is one reference implementation of the bounded practice, not a completed live capstone.

```python

assert schedule('acme:event-2:r1',False)=='needs_review'

# Guided practice reference implementation
def reconcile(key,remote_keys):
    if ledger.get(key)!='uncertain':return ledger.get(key,'unknown')
    if key in remote_keys:ledger[key]='committed'
    return ledger[key]
key='acme:event-1:r2'
assert reconcile(key,set())=='uncertain' and len(effects)==1
assert reconcile(key,{key})=='committed' and len(effects)==1
assert schedule(key,True)=='already_committed' and len(effects)==1
print('practice: original operation reconciled without redispatch; one fake effect retained')
```

```text
{'fake_effects': 1, 'lost_response': 'reconcile same key, never blind replay'}
practice: original operation reconciled without redispatch; one fake effect retained
```

If effects grows during reconciliation, the implementation is retrying rather than observing. A missing observation may reflect eventual consistency, so this teaching policy keeps the outcome uncertain until a destination-specific resolution rule exists.

## Slack event intake and background work · concepts and decision

## Before you begin

Sessions 17 and 22: durable state and duplicate operation handling. The connector appendix introduces signature verification. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

The same Slack event is delivered twice during a provider outage.

## Reason through the decision

Verify the event, store it once and retain a retryable job; acknowledge only after durable enqueue.

Webhooks can be redelivered. Verify signatures over the exact raw body before trusting payloads, enforce replay windows and acknowledge quickly after durable enqueue. Work in the request handler risks provider timeout and duplicate deliveries. The memory fixture illustrates deduplication only; its printed storage label explicitly does not claim durable enqueue. A polling connector also needs a cursor and retention-aware replay policy.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Durable inbox

Accepted events persisted before background processing.

### Delivery deduplication

Repeated delivery logged without creating duplicate work.

### Signature/replay checks

Authenticating the exact inbound payload and its freshness.

## Learn each concept step by step

Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Durable inbox

A durable inbox stores a verified delivery ID and payload digest before acknowledging acceptance. Then a worker can retry processing after restart without requiring the webhook sender to reproduce lost data. An in-memory set only teaches the deduplication shape; it loses accepted work when the process exits.

## Step 2 · Delivery deduplication

Deduplication is scoped by owner/event ID. Repeated identical content is a duplicate; the same ID with changed content is a conflict worth retaining/rejecting, not silently overwriting. Worker retry state belongs to the stored job. A provider outage must not remove the already accepted inbox record.

## Step 3 · Signature/replay checks

Signature/replay checks authenticate the exact raw body and timestamp before parsing/trusting its event fields. Do not serialize parsed JSON again before signature validation, because whitespace/key order can change signed bytes. A valid signature is distinct from allowed workspace/channel scope. Check freshness, identity and destination authority independently.

## Read, run and explain the complete implementation

## Walk through the data and state

1. Two deliveries are logged but only one memory job is created.

2. The worker changes the existing job to retry_wait rather than deleting it.

3. The printed storage label is memory, explicitly showing the durability gap.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
seen=set();deliveries=[];jobs=[]
def receive(event):
    deliveries.append(event['id'])
    if event['id'] in seen:return 'duplicate'
    seen.add(event['id']);jobs.append({'id':event['id'],'state':'queued'})
    return 'accepted'
event={'id':'slack-event-7','channel':'support','text':'Returns?'}
assert receive(event)=='accepted' and receive(event)=='duplicate'
assert len(deliveries)==2 and len(jobs)==1
# A worker failure does not remove the accepted job.
jobs[0]['state']='retry_wait'
assert jobs[0]['id']=='slack-event-7'
print({'deliveries':2,'durable_design_jobs':1,'worker_state':jobs[0]['state'],'storage_in_this_fixture':'memory'})
```

## Observed output

```text
{'deliveries': 2, 'durable_design_jobs': 1, 'worker_state': 'retry_wait', 'storage_in_this_fixture': 'memory'}
```

## Transfer beyond the fixture

Webhooks can be redelivered. Verify signatures over the exact raw body before trusting payloads, enforce replay windows and acknowledge quickly after durable enqueue. chapters.title: Learn each concept step by step
chapters.body:
Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Durable inbox

A durable inbox stores a verified delivery ID and payload digest before acknowledging acceptance. Then a worker can retry processing after restart without requiring the webhook sender to reproduce lost data. An in-memory set only teaches the deduplication shape; it loses accepted work when the process exits.

## Step 2 · Delivery deduplication

Deduplication is scoped by owner/event ID. Repeated identical content is a duplicate; the same ID with changed content is a conflict worth retaining/rejecting, not silently overwriting. Worker retry state belongs to the stored job. A provider outage must not remove the already accepted inbox record.

## Step 3 · Signature/replay checks

Signature/replay checks authenticate the exact raw body and timestamp before parsing/trusting its event fields. Do not serialize parsed JSON again before signature validation, because whitespace/key order can change signed bytes. A valid signature is distinct from allowed workspace/channel scope. Check freshness, identity and destination authority independently.

chapters.body:
## Walk through the data and state

2. The worker changes the existing job to retry_wait rather than deleting it.

```python
seen=set();deliveries=[];jobs=[]
def receive(event):
    deliveries.append(event['id'])

print({'deliveries':2,'durable_design_jobs':1,'worker_state':jobs[0]['state'],'storage_in_this_fixture':'memory'})
```

## Complete guided-practice reference

Save the entire following block as solution.py and run `python3 -I solution.py` in a new scratch directory. No prior files or provider account are needed. This is one reference implementation of the bounded practice, not a completed live capstone.

```python
seen=set();deliveries=[];jobs=[]
def receive(event):
    deliveries.append(event['id'])
    if event['id'] in seen:return 'duplicate'
    seen.add(event['id']);jobs.append({'id':event['id'],'state':'queued'})
    return 'accepted'
event={'id':'slack-event-7','channel':'support','text':'Returns?'}
assert receive(event)=='accepted' and receive(event)=='duplicate'
assert len(deliveries)==2 and len(jobs)==1
# A worker failure does not remove the accepted job.
jobs[0]['state']='retry_wait'
assert jobs[0]['id']=='slack-event-7'
print({'deliveries':2,'durable_design_jobs':1,'worker_state':jobs[0]['state'],'storage_in_this_fixture':'memory'})

# Guided practice reference implementation
import sqlite3,tempfile,hashlib
from pathlib import Path
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path=Path(folder)/'inbox.sqlite';db=sqlite3.connect(path)
    db.execute('CREATE TABLE inbox(owner TEXT,event TEXT,digest TEXT,state TEXT,PRIMARY KEY(owner,event))')
    def accept(owner,event,raw):
        digest=hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest()
        old=db.execute('SELECT digest FROM inbox WHERE owner=? AND event=?',(owner,event)).fetchone()
        if old:return 'duplicate' if old[0]==digest else 'conflict'
        with db:db.execute('INSERT INTO inbox VALUES(?,?,?,?)',(owner,event,digest,'queued'))
        return 'accepted'
    assert accept('acme','e1',b'original')=='accepted'
    assert accept('acme','e1',b'original')=='duplicate'
    assert accept('acme','e1',b'changed')=='conflict'
    db.close();db=sqlite3.connect(path)
    assert db.execute('SELECT state FROM inbox').fetchall()==[('queued',)]
    db.close()
print('practice: scoped inbox survived reopen; duplicate/conflict did not create extra jobs')
```

```text
{'deliveries': 2, 'durable_design_jobs': 1, 'worker_state': 'retry_wait', 'storage_in_this_fixture': 'memory'}
practice: scoped inbox survived reopen; duplicate/conflict did not create extra jobs
```

If restart loses the job, the durable path was not used or committed. This serial SQLite example does not prove multi-worker claim safety; use atomic insert/conflict handling and a shared store for that integration.

## Workspace agent capstone · concepts and decision

## Before you begin

Sessions 16–23: dispatch authority, checkpoints, approvals, selected memory, reconciliation and inbox deduplication. Use Python3.12 with assertions enabled. All core practice runs offline with the standard library; provider accounts are only for separately labeled integration work.

## The case

The agent monitors a support test channel, drafts an answer and proposes a meeting.

## Reason through the decision

Require authorization/review at the effect boundary and prove no unauthorized send/invitation on duplicate or stale input.

The workspace fixture actually runs proposal, authorization, approval, duplicate and uncertain-outcome branches. Returned states and the effect list must agree; comparing literal expected/actual strings would not exercise a dispatcher. This is still a single-process fake destination, not durable remote exactly-once delivery. The live adapters and durable local state examples are subsequent integration pieces.

## Vocabulary used in this session

### Bounded autonomy

Monitoring/proposing within configured scope with controlled effects.

### Reviewed action

A consequential operation carrying exact current authorization.

### Connector evidence

Observed permissions, errors and IDs for a particular integration.

## Learn each concept step by step

Read these three explanations before running the specimen. Each connects a definition to the decision it controls.

## Step 1 · Bounded autonomy

Bounded autonomy means the system can monitor and prepare within declared read scopes while consequential writes stay controlled. First build a deterministic event→evidence→draft→review pipeline. Add agent choice only where a fixed workflow demonstrably lacks required behavior. The capstone does not need unrestricted tool access to be useful.

## Step 2 · Reviewed action

A reviewed action passes current scope, source support, exact-payload approval and duplicate/uncertain-operation checks at dispatch. A proposal is not permission. Test state transitions by actually invoking the dispatcher with revoked scope and stale data; literal expected/actual strings cannot test behavior.

## Step 3 · Connector evidence

Connector evidence records what a particular granted integration actually did: scope, request/event IDs, stable error category and observed destination state. Fake destinations allow deterministic tests without sending messages. Live connector availability, OAuth refresh and factual quality are separate observations; do not treat a successful fake call as those observations.

## Read, run and explain the complete implementation

## Walk through the data and state

1. The capstone fixture computes outcomes through a dispatcher rather than copying expected labels.

2. An unapproved proposal remains a draft; revoked scope is denied.

3. A lost acknowledgement produces uncertain and a repeated key is reconciled without a second effect.

## Predict before execution

Save this entire block as example.py in an empty directory. Run `python3 -I example.py` with assertions enabled. It uses only the Python standard library, includes its synthetic data and performs no provider calls. Explain each assertion before running.

```python
import hashlib,json
def review(proposal):
    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(proposal,sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
class WorkspaceFixture:
    def __init__(self):self.ledger={};self.effects=[];self.payloads={}
    def process(self,event_id,proposal,scope,evidence,approval,lose_response=False):
        if not scope or proposal['owner']!='acme' or proposal['channel']!='support':return 'deny'
        if not evidence:return 'abstain'
        if approval!=review(proposal):return 'needs_review'
        key=(proposal['owner'],event_id,proposal['revision'])
        if key in self.ledger:
            if self.payloads[key]!=review(proposal):return 'payload_conflict'
            return 'reconcile' if self.ledger[key]=='uncertain' else 'already_committed'
        self.ledger[key]='claimed';self.payloads[key]=review(proposal)
        self.effects.append({'key':key,'text':proposal['text']})  # Fake local destination.
        self.ledger[key]='uncertain' if lose_response else 'committed'
        return self.ledger[key]
service=WorkspaceFixture()
proposal={'owner':'acme','channel':'support','text':'Unopened items only','revision':1}
assert service.process('e1',proposal,True,True,None)=='needs_review'
assert service.process('e1',proposal,False,True,review(proposal))=='deny'
assert service.effects==[]
assert service.process('e1',proposal,True,True,review(proposal))=='committed'
assert service.process('e1',proposal,True,True,review(proposal))=='already_committed'
assert service.process('e2',proposal,True,True,review(proposal),lose_response=True)=='uncertain'
assert service.process('e2',proposal,True,True,review(proposal))=='reconcile'
changed={**proposal,'text':'Changed under reused event ID'}
assert service.process('e1',changed,True,True,review(changed))=='payload_conflict'
assert len(service.effects)==2
print({'fake_effects':2,'duplicate_did_not_write':True,'lost_response':'uncertain then reconcile'})
```

### workspace_connectors.py

```python
"""Optional connector adapters. Importing this module performs no calls.
Use your own authorized sandbox; OAuth issuance/refresh is an operator prerequisite.
Requires httpx. No write is retried after an uncertain response.
"""
import hashlib,hmac,json,time
import httpx

def verify_slack(raw, timestamp, signature, signing_secret, now=None):
    now=time.time() if now is None else now
    if abs(now-int(timestamp))>300:raise ValueError('stale event')
    expected='v0='+hmac.new(signing_secret.encode(),b'v0:'+str(timestamp).encode()+b':'+raw,hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    if not hmac.compare_digest(expected,signature):raise ValueError('bad signature')
    return json.loads(raw)

def payload_hash(payload):return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(payload,sort_keys=True,separators=(',',':')).encode()).hexdigest()

def require_review(payload,approval,owner,now=None):
    now=time.time() if now is None else now
    if not approval or approval['owner']!=owner or approval['hash']!=payload_hash(payload) or approval['expires']<=now:
        raise PermissionError('current exact-payload approval required')
    # Approval is loaded from your trusted DB, never accepted directly from model arguments.

class Connectors:
    def __init__(self,slack_token,google_token,allowed_channels,allowed_calendar):
        self.slack_token=slack_token;self.google_token=google_token
        self.allowed_channels=set(allowed_channels);self.allowed_calendar=allowed_calendar
    async def history(self,channel):
        if channel not in self.allowed_channels:raise PermissionError('channel scope')
        # Requires membership and the corresponding Slack history read scope.
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:
            r=await client.get('https://slack.com/api/conversations.history',headers={'Authorization':'Bearer '+self.slack_token},params={'channel':channel,'limit':20})
            r.raise_for_status();data=r.json()
            if not data.get('ok'):raise RuntimeError('connector rejected history')
            return {'messages':data['messages'],'next_cursor':data.get('response_metadata',{}).get('next_cursor','')}
    async def gmail_metadata(self,message_id):
        from urllib.parse import quote
        # Requires a granted Gmail metadata/read scope; never implies send authority.
        url='https://gmail.googleapis.com/gmail/v1/users/me/messages/'+quote(message_id,safe='')
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:
            r=await client.get(url,headers={'Authorization':'Bearer '+self.google_token},params={'format':'metadata'})
            r.raise_for_status();data=r.json()
            return {'id':data['id'],'threadId':data.get('threadId'),'headers':data.get('payload',{}).get('headers',[])}
    async def gmail_reviewed_draft(self,owner,operation,to,subject,body,approval):
        import base64
        from email.message import EmailMessage
        payload={'operation':operation,'to':to,'subject':subject,'body':body}
        require_review(payload,approval,owner)
        message=EmailMessage();message['To']=to;message['Subject']=subject;message.set_content(body)
        raw=base64.urlsafe_b64encode(message.as_bytes()).decode()
        # Gmail compose scope can be broad. The app exposes draft creation only.
        # Persist the intent first. A lost response is uncertain, not a safe retry.
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:
            try:
                r=await client.post('https://gmail.googleapis.com/gmail/v1/users/me/drafts',headers={'Authorization':'Bearer '+self.google_token},json={'message':{'raw':raw}})
            except (httpx.TimeoutException,httpx.NetworkError):return {'state':'uncertain','operation':operation}
            r.raise_for_status();return {'state':'draft_created','draft_id':r.json()['id']}
    async def freebusy(self,start,end):
        # Requires calendar.freebusy or an appropriately scoped read grant.
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:
            r=await client.post('https://www.googleapis.com/calendar/v3/freeBusy',headers={'Authorization':'Bearer '+self.google_token},json={'timeMin':start,'timeMax':end,'items':[{'id':self.allowed_calendar}]})
            r.raise_for_status();data=r.json()
            calendar=data.get('calendars',{}).get(self.allowed_calendar,{})
            if calendar.get('errors') or 'busy' not in calendar:raise RuntimeError('availability unavailable')
            return calendar['busy']
    async def create_reviewed_event(self,owner,operation,event,approval):
        from urllib.parse import quote
        payload={'calendar':self.allowed_calendar,'event':event,'operation':operation}
        require_review(payload,approval,owner)
        # Stable base32hex-compatible ID; same scoped operation maps to same destination ID.
        event_id=hashlib.sha256((owner+':'+operation).encode()).hexdigest()
        base='https://www.googleapis.com/calendar/v3/calendars/'+quote(self.allowed_calendar,safe='')+'/events'
        headers={'Authorization':'Bearer '+self.google_token}
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:
            try:r=await client.post(base,headers=headers,params={'sendUpdates':'none'},json={**event,'id':event_id})
            except (httpx.TimeoutException,httpx.NetworkError):return {'state':'uncertain','destination_id':event_id}
            if r.status_code==409:
                observed=await client.get(base+'/'+event_id,headers=headers);observed.raise_for_status()
                # Caller compares actual event fields to the approved canonical payload.
                return {'state':'needs_reconciliation','destination_id':event_id,'observed':observed.json()}
            r.raise_for_status();return {'state':'committed','destination_id':r.json()['id']}
```

## Step 3 · Connector evidence

Live connector availability, OAuth refresh and factual quality are separate observations; do not treat a successful fake call as those observations.
